category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: Any break in the body tissue, occurring either externally or internally; both terms are considered synonymous pathological entities.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: How is 'Injury' defined legally according to the Pakistan Penal Code?
back: Any harm illegally caused to any person in body, mind, reputation, or property.
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): Injury is any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Contrast the legal usage of the terms 'wound' and 'hurt'.
back: The law has not defined 'wound' and specifically prefers to use the term 'hurt' instead.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: A victim survives an assault with impaired organ function. Define this legally.
back: Hurt: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or impairing/disabling/dismembering any organ without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: On what two primary bases is Hurt classified legally?
back:
1. Part of the body involved.
2. Manner of infliction.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): It is typed on the basis of part of body involved and manner of infliction, each having further subtypes.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define the specific legal term 'Itlaf-i-udw'.
back: Causing dismemberment, amputation, or severing of any limb or organ of the body.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Table 4.2: Itlaf-i-Udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ of the body.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Distinguish between 'Shajjah' and 'Jurh' based on anatomical site.
back:
* Shajjah: Hurt located on the head or face.
* Jurh: Hurt on any part of the body other than the head or face.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Table 4.2: Shajjah: Hurt on the head or face... Jurh: Hurt on part of the body other than the head and face bearing mark of wound.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Compare Jaifah and Ghayr-jaifah in terms of body cavity involvement.
back:
* Jaifah: Hurt extending into the body cavity of the trunk.
* Ghayr-jaifah: Hurt that does not extend to the body cavity.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Table 4.2: Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk. Ghayr-jaifah: Hurt not amounting to Jaifah.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw' regarding organ capacity.
back: Destroying or permanently impairing the function/capacity of an organ or causing permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Table 4.2: Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ of the body or causing permanent disfigurement.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: List the three legal compensation terms introduced for criminal hurt.
back:
1. Arsh (Law-specified compensation)
2. Daman (Court-determined compensation)
3. Diyat (Compensation for heirs in qatl/certain hurts)
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Table 4.1: Arsh: Compensation specified in law... Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court... Diyat: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt payable to the heirs.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the legal definition of "Injury" according to the Pakistan Penal Code?
back:
Any harm illegally caused to a person in:
- Body or Mind
- Reputation
- Property
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury is any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define "Wound" from a medical-pathological perspective.
back:
- Any break in the continuity of body tissue.
- Can be external (skin) or internal (organs/membranes).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Contrast the medical versus legal use of the term "Wound" in Pakistan.
back:
- Medical: Synonymous with injury (tissue break).
- Legal: The law does not define "wound" and uses the term "Hurt" instead.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Legally classify an assault that impairs an organ but does not result in death.
back: Classified as **Hurt**. It includes causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or disabling/dismembering any body part.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Which two factors determine the specific classification of a "Hurt"?
back:
1. The part of the body involved (e.g., head, face, or others).
2. The manner of infliction.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [It is typed on the basis of part of body involved and manner of infliction, each having further subtypes.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What are the components included in the definition of "Hurt" under current law?
back:
- Pain or harm
- Disease or infirmity
- Injury
- Impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Under the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance 1991, what term replaced "Injury"?
back: The term **Hurt**. (Similarly, "Murder" was replaced by the term "Qatl").
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Qisas & Diyat Ordinance 1991 has replaced terms of murder with qatl and injury with hurt and also gave new classifications.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Differentiate "Injury" from "Hurt" regarding their legal scope.
back:
- Injury: Broad; includes property, mind, and reputation.
- Hurt: Specific to bodily harm/impairment without causing death.
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury is any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Explain the pathological relationship between medical "Injury" and "Wound".
back: They are synonymous in meaning and represent a **single pathological entity** involving a break in tissue.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What does the term "Infirmity" signify within the legal definition of Hurt?
back: It refers to a state of weakness or illness caused by the offender, contributing to the legal criteria for Hurt.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury...]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How are mechanical injuries primarily classified based on the causative weapon's edge?
back:
- Blunt weapon injuries (Abrasion, Bruise, Laceration).
- Sharp cutting edge injuries (Incised wounds).
- Sharp pointed edge injuries (Penetrating/Puncturing).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What defines the mechanism of an incised wound compared to a laceration?
back:
- Incised: Produced by a sharp-edged weapon dividing tissues cleanly.
- Lacerated: Produced by a blunt-edged weapon crushing or stretching tissues over bone.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Examples are incised and lacerated wounds produced by sharp edged and blunt edged weapons.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify thermal injuries based on the state of the causative heat agent.
back:
- Dry Heat: Flame or heated metallic objects.
- Moist Heat: Hot liquids (scalding) or pressure steam.
- Extreme Cold: Frostbite.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Temperature—Heat, Cold; Flame; Hot liquid.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Which two categories of weapons are classified as having 'multiple causative factors'?
back:
- Fire-arms (including Shotguns and Rifled weapons).
- Bomb blasts (involving blast waves and fragments).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR: Bomb blast; Fire-arm]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify corrosive injuries based on the chemical nature of the agent.
back:
- Strong Mineral Acids (e.g., Sulfuric acid).
- Weak Organic Acids (e.g., Carbolic acid/Phenol).
- Strong Alkalis (e.g., Sodium Hydroxide/Caustic Soda).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Corrosive—Acid, Alkali.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What is the defining physical characteristic of a penetrating wound regarding its dimensions?
back:
- Produced by a sharp-edged and pointed weapon.
- Its greatest dimension is its internal depth, exceeding length/breadth.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Penetrating & puncturing wound is produced by thrusting sharp edged and pointed weapon... depth, which is the greatest dimension]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How are electrical injuries classified based on voltage and contact quality?
back:
- Voltage: Low voltage (Domestic) vs. High voltage (Industrial).
- Contact: Loose contact (Spark/Metallization) vs. Firm contact (Blister/Burn).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Electricity—Low voltage, High voltage; Loose contact, Firm contact.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Differentiate rifled firearm entry from shotgun entry at a distance.
back:
- Rifled: Single hole with inverted margins and characteristic ring.
- Shotgun (Far): Multiple individual pellet holes without a central mass or charring.
citation: Page 74 (Book Page): [Main difference is that rifled wound has single hole whereas shotgun has many holes depending upon distance of fire.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify radiation injuries on the basis of atomic effect.
back:
- Ionizing radiation (e.g., X-rays, radioactive isotopes).
- Non-ionizing radiation.
- Source can be Artificial or Natural.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Radiation—Artificial, Natural; Ionizing, Non-ionizing.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What are the three sub-types of blunt weapon lacerations based on mechanism?
back:
- Split (crush) laceration: Skin split against bone.
- Over-stretch laceration: Pressure and push.
- Grinding compression: e.g., vehicle wheel over limb.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split, also called crush laceration; Over-stretch laceration; Grinding compression laceration]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: List the three categories of mechanical weapons based on their wounding edges.
back:
1. Blunt weapons.
2. Sharp cutting-edge weapons.
3. Sharp pointed-edge weapons.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How do blunt and sharp weapons differ in their wounding mechanism?
back: Blunt weapons cause tissue crushing and tearing (lacerations), while sharp weapons overcome tissue resistance by cutting or splitting (incised/penetrating wounds).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Type of weapon directly controls and determines the appearance of the wound. Examples are incised and lacerated wounds produced by sharp edged and blunt edged weapons.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Contrast the wound margins produced by blunt versus sharp cutting implements.
back: Blunt weapons produce irregular, bruised margins with tissue bridging. Sharp weapons produce clean-cut, smooth margins with sharp angles.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins... Page 59 (Book Page): [It shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: A wound presents with bridging tissue tags. What is the likely causative weapon?
back: A blunt weapon. Bridging tissue tags (nerves, vessels, and fibers crossing the wound gap) are pathognomonic for blunt force lacerations.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are... walls that have bridging tissue tags]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify fire-arms based on the causative factors described in the text.
back:
They are multiple causative factor weapons categorized into: 
1. Shot guns (smooth bore).
2. Rifled weapons (low/high velocity bullets).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR... Fire-arm: Shot gun; Rifled weapon—Low velocity bullet, High velocity bullet]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What are the four types of single factor agents causing burn-like lesions?
back:
1. Temperature (Heat/Cold).
2. Electricity.
3. Radiation.
4. Corrosives (Acids/Alkalis).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Other: Temperature—Heat, Cold... Electricity... Radiation... Corrosive—Acid, Alkali.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Which specific weapon causes a 'split laceration' that resembles an incised wound?
back: A blunt weapon. This occurs when skin is crushed against underlying bone, such as the scalp or forehead.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split laceration occurs on scalp, forehead, chin or any other part of the body where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. It may resemble an incision wound.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Differentiate between wounds caused by sharp-pointed versus sharp-cutting weapons.
back: Sharp-pointed weapons cause penetrating wounds where depth is the greatest dimension. Sharp-cutting weapons cause incised wounds where length is greater than depth.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Most of the characteristics of this wound are similar to those of an incised wound, except the depth, which is the greatest dimension.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How does weapon velocity influence the resulting tissue damage?
back: High velocity (bullets) produces temporary cavitation and shatters target organs, whereas low velocity blunt weapons cause localized crushing/tearing.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet, on the other hand, additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally... energy radiations causing damage proportionate to diameter of the bullet.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Define the weapon-assault relationship through 'imprint abrasions'.
back: Imprint abrasions are caused by the strike of a rough object (e.g., shoe heel, rope), providing a pattern that identifies the causative implement.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like shoe-heel... Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define "Injury" from a strictly medical perspective.
back: Any break in the body tissue, whether occurring externally or internally.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define "Wound" from a medical standpoint and its relationship to injury.
back: A break in the continuity of soft tissues (skin or serous membrane); medically synonymous with injury.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Contrast the legal definition of "Injury" with its medical definition.
back: Legally, injury is any harm caused illegally to a person's body, mind, reputation, or property.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Law also defines injury as any harm caused illegally to any person in body, mind, reputation or property.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: A victim is struck illegally causing non-fatal pain and organ impairment. Define this legally.
back: Legally termed as "Hurt" under the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define "Itlaf-i-Udw" according to the classification of Hurt.
back: The dismemberment, amputation, or severing of any limb or organ of the body.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Itlaf-i-Udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ of the body.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What criteria define "Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw"?
back: Destroying or permanently impairing the functional capacity of an organ, or causing permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ of the body or causing permanent disfigurement.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define "Shajjah" and its specific anatomical boundary.
back: Any hurt inflicted specifically on the head or face that does not amount to Itlaf-i-Udw.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Shajjah: Hurt on the head or face which does not amount to thaf-i-Udw or itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Distinguish "Jaifah" from "Ghayr-Jaifah" hurts.
back: Jaifah: Extends into the body cavity of the trunk. Ghayr-Jaifah: A wound on the body that does not enter a cavity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk. Ghayr-Jaifah: Hurt not amounting to Jaifah.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define the legal term "Jurh".
back: Hurt on any part of the body other than the head or face which leaves a mark of a wound.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Jurh: Hurt on part of the body other than the head and face bearing mark of wound which may be.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define "Shajjah-i-Mudihah" by its defining clinical feature.
back: A hurt on the head or face where the bone is exposed but not fractured.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the legal definition of "Injury" according to the Pakistan Penal Code?
back: Any harm caused illegally to a person in: • Body • Mind • Reputation • Property
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury: any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What constitutes a "wound" from a strictly medical and pathological perspective?
back: • Any break in body tissue. • May occur externally or internally. • Considered a single pathological entity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: How does the legal definition of injury differ from the medical definition?
back: • Medical: limited to tissue breaks. • Legal: includes non-physical harm to mind, reputation, or property.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Law also defines injury as any harm caused illegally to any person in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: If a victim suffers internal liver rupture without external marks, is this a medical wound?
back: • Yes. • Medical wounds include any tissue break, whether "externally or internally."
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Which specific legal term has replaced "injury" in the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance 1991?
back: • The term "Hurt." • It is used to classify specific types of bodily damage.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Qisas & Diyat Ordinance 1991 has replaced terms of murder with qatl and injury with hurt]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What are the specific criteria required to legally define an act as "Hurt"?
back: Causing of: • Pain, harm, or disease. • Infirmity or injury. • Disabling/dismembering organs without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Does the term "Injury" legally encompass non-physical damage like harm to reputation?
back: • Yes. • The definition explicitly includes illegal harm to "mind, reputation or property."
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury: any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the formal status of the word "wound" in Pakistani statute law?
back: • It has no formal legal definition. • The law prefers to use the term "hurt" instead.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What condition must be absent for bodily harm to be classified as "Hurt"?
back: • The harm must be caused "without causing death." • If death results, it is classified as Qatl.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as... disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Pathologically, what is the relationship between the words "wound" and "injury"?
back: • They are synonymous. • They describe the same pathological entity (tissue break).
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Injury' according to the Pakistan Penal Code.
back:
Any harm illegally caused to any person in:
- Body
- Mind
- Reputation
- Property
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury is any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the defining medical pathology of a wound or injury?
back: A break in any body tissue, occurring either externally or internally.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Contrast the medical vs. legal standing of the term 'Wound'.
back:
- Medically: Synonymous with injury.
- Legally: Undefined; the law uses the term 'Hurt' instead.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Hurt' as per the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or impairing/disabling/dismembering any organ or part without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Which four specific domains are included in 'Injury' but excluded from 'Hurt'?
back:
- Mind
- Reputation
- Property
(Hurt is restricted to physical body harm/pain).
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury is any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: A person suffers illegal psychological distress and a damaged car. Classify this legally.
back: This is classified as an 'Injury' (harm to mind and property), not 'Hurt'.
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury is any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Under the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance 1991, what term substituted 'Injury'?
back: The term 'Hurt'.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Qisas & Diyat Ordinance 1991 has replaced terms of murder with qatl and injury with hurt.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Why is 'Hurt' not applicable if the victim dies from the assault?
back: The definition of Hurt explicitly requires the harm to be 'without causing death'.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as... causing of pain, harm... or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Differentiate a medical 'Wound' from a legal 'Injury' in a defamation case.
back:
- Medical Wound: Requires a physical tissue break.
- Legal Injury: Includes non-physical harm like loss of reputation.
citation: Page 15 (Book Page) & 30: [Injury is any harm... in body, mind, reputation or property] vs [any break in the body tissue... is termed as wound].

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What are the pathological characteristics of a 'Wound' medically?
back: It is a single pathological entity representing any interruption of tissue continuity, whether deep or superficial.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the legal definition of 'injury' according to the Pakistan Penal Code?
back:
Any harm whatever illegally caused to any person in: 
1. Body or Mind
2. Reputation
3. Property.
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury: Any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: How is 'wound' or 'injury' defined from a medical and pathological perspective?
back: Any break in the body tissue, occurring either externally or internally. Both terms are medically synonymous and represent a single pathological entity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the legal status of the word 'wound' in current legislation?
back: Law has not specifically defined the word 'wound'; instead, it prefers to use the term 'hurt' to denote such bodily damage.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Under what circumstances is a non-fatal bodily harm legally classified as 'Hurt'?
back:
When there is causing of: 
1. Pain or harm
2. Disease or infirmity
3. Impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ/part without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define the legal compensation term 'Arsh' as applied to 'Hurt'.
back: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt, payable by the offender to the victim or their heirs.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Arsh: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt by the offender to the victim or his heirs.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the defining criteria for the legal term 'Daman' in cases of hurt?
back: Compensation not liable to Arsh; the value is determined by the court and payable by the offender to the victim/heirs.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court for causing hurt and payable by offender to the victim or his heirs]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Contrast the scope of 'Injury' versus 'Hurt' in the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back:
1. Injury: Broadly includes illegal harm to mind, reputation, and property.
2. Hurt: Specifically restricted to bodily pain, harm, or organ impairment without death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Law also defines injury as any harm caused illegally to any person in body, mind, reputation or property... Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ...]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Which specific physical conditions are legally excluded from the definition of 'Hurt'?
back: Any harm that results in death is excluded; 'Hurt' must be non-fatal by definition.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means... without causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: How is 'Hurt' primarily classified for legal typing purposes?
back:
1. Based on the part of the body involved.
2. Based on the manner of infliction.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [It is typed on the basis of part of body involved and manner of infliction, each having further subtypes.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Diyat' in the context of criminal compensation.
back: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt, payable specifically to the heirs of the victim by the offender.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Diyat: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt payable to the heirs of the victim, by the offender.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How are wounding implements classified based on the number of causative factors?
back:
1. Single Causative Factor: Mechanical (blunt/sharp), Temperature, Electricity, Radiation, Corrosives.
2. Multiple Causative Factor: Fire-arms and Bomb blasts.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Typing due to weapon used includes single causative factor injury by blunt and sharp edged weapon and other is fire arm injury due to multiple causative factors weapon like smooth/rifled barrel weapons and bomb blast.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What defines the mechanism of tissue disruption in wounds caused by blunt weapons?
back: They cause wounding through crushing, over-stretching, or grinding compression, resulting in abrasions, bruises, or lacerated wounds.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Lacerated wound is an open wound showing breach of skin... caused by strike of blunt weapon... there are of three types: Split, also called crush laceration; Over-stretch laceration; Grinding compression laceration]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Contrast the margins of wounds caused by sharp-edged vs. blunt-edged weapons.
back:
1. Sharp-edged (Incised): Clean-cut margins, sharp angles, smooth walls.
2. Blunt-edged (Lacerated): Irregular/jagged margins, ill-defined angles, bridging tissue tags.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Examples are incised and lacerated wounds produced by sharp edged and blunt edged weapons.] Page 59 (Book Page): [It shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Identify the likely weapon for a spindle-shaped wound with clean-cut margins and sharp angles.
back: A sharp-edged cutting weapon, such as a knife or glass fragment, producing an incised wound.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Incised wound... result of cutting or incision... common instrument causing it is a knife... generally linear or spindle shaped... shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How are chemical wounding agents (corrosives) classified?
back:
1. Strong Mineral Acids (Sulfuric, Nitric, Hydrochloric).
2. Weak Organic Acids (Carbolic/Phenol, Oxalic).
3. Strong Alkalis (Sodium/Potassium Hydroxide, Ammonia).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Corrosive—Acid, Alkali.] Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong mineral acids are sulfuric acid... Weak organic acids are carbolic acid... Important strong alkalis are sodium hydroxide...]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Which weapon category produces a wound where depth is the greatest dimension?
back: Sharp-pointed weapons (with or without edges), resulting in penetrating or puncturing wounds that pierce body cavities.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Penetrating & puncturing wound is produced by thrusting sharp edged and pointed weapon... depth, which is the greatest dimension.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify firearm weapons based on the internal design of the barrel.
back:
1. Smooth-bore weapons: (e.g., Shot-gun).
2. Rifled-bore weapons: (e.g., Revolver, Pistol, Rifle) featuring spiral grooves and lands.
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Firearms weapons as a group contain weapons like revolver, rifle, shot-gun... barrel from point of view design is... smooth and rifled.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: A linear scalp wound has clean margins but bridging tissue. Determine the weapon type.
back: A blunt weapon. This is a 'split' or 'crush' laceration occurring where skin is stretched over bone, often simulating an incised wound.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split, also called crush laceration occurs on scalp... where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. Sudden compression... split them. It may resemble an incision wound.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify thermal wounding agents based on the causative medium.
back:
1. Dry Heat: Flame or heated metallic objects.
2. Moist Heat: Scalds from liquids at boiling point or pressure steam.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Thermal burn is caused by application of heat... includes all types of thermal lesions whether produced by heated metallic object, flame, fluids at or near boiling point and pressure steam.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What weapon effect produces a pattern reflecting the causative agent's shape on the skin?
back: An imprint abrasion, caused by a strike from a patterned object (e.g., shoe-heel, tire) or hard ligature (e.g., rope).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like sheo-heel... its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back: Any break in the body tissue, occurring either externally or internally. Pathologically, both terms are considered synonymous and represent a single entity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: How does the law define 'injury' under the Pakistan Penal Code?
back:
Any harm caused illegally to any person in four specific areas:
- Body
- Mind
- Reputation
- Property
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Law also defines injury as any harm caused illegally to any person in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the legal definition of 'Hurt' under current Pakistani law?
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, or injury, or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ/part of the body without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
coreConcept: Legal preference of Hurt vs Wound
front: Q: Why is the term 'hurt' utilized in criminal courts instead of 'wound'?
back: Law has not formally defined the word 'wound.' It prefers the term 'hurt' to classify non-fatal physical harm for legal compensation purposes.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead,]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Which specific ordinance replaced the term 'injury' with 'hurt' in Pakistan?
back: The Qisas and Diyat Ordinance of 1991. This ordinance also replaced the legal term 'murder' with 'qatl.'
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Qisas & Diyat Ordinance 1991 has replaced terms of murder with qatl and injury with hurt and also gave new classifications denoting specific meanings.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What are the two primary factors used to type 'Hurt' legally?
back:
- The part of the body involved (e.g., head/face vs. others).
- The manner of infliction.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [It is typed on the basis of part of body involved and manner of infliction, each having further subtypes.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: How is 'Hurt' on the head or face specifically categorized legally?
back: It is classified as Shajjah, provided the injury does not amount to Itlaf-i-udw (dismemberment) or Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw (loss of function).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt on the head or face which does not amount to itlaf-i-Udw or itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw, (is Shajjah)]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the critical threshold that separates 'Hurt' from homicide?
back: The occurrence of death. To qualify as 'Hurt,' the harm or impairment must be inflicted 'without causing death.'
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [means causing of pain, harm... or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What does 'Itlaf-i-udw' signify in the context of 'Hurt'?
back: The dismemberment, amputation, or severing of any limb or organ of the body.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ of the body]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw' as per the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back: Destroying or permanently impairing the functional capacity of an organ, or causing permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ of the body or causing permanent disfigurement]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the legal definition of "Injury" under the Pakistan Penal Code?
back:
Any harm caused illegally to any person in:
- Body or mind
- Reputation
- Property
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury: Any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What constitutes a "wound" or "injury" from a strictly medical perspective?
back: A single pathological entity characterized by any break in body tissue, occurring either externally (skin) or internally (membranes/organs).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: How does the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance differentiate the terms "Injury" and "Hurt"?
back:
- The Ordinance replaced the legal term "injury" with "hurt" for criminal offenses.
- Law does not provide a specific definition for "wound."
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Qisas & Diyat Ordinance 1991 has replaced terms of murder with qatl and injury with hurt... Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Categorize a facial hurt exposing the bone without fracture under the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance.
back:
Category: Shajjah-i-Mudihah.
Definition: Any hurt on the head or face that exposes the bone without causing a fracture.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What legal term describes the compensation for "Hurt" that is not liable to Arsh?
back:
Term: Daman.
Definition: Compensation determined by the court, payable by the offender to the victim or their heirs.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court for causing hurt and payable by offender to the victim or his heirs.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the comprehensive legal definition of "Hurt"?
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or impairing/disabling/dismembering any part of the body without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Categorize the permanent physical loss or amputation of a limb under the law.
back:
Category: Itlaf-i-Udw.
Definition: Causing disarticulation, dismemberment, amputation, or severance of any limb or organ.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-Udw: Causing of disarticulation, dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ of the body.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Differentiate Itlaf-i-Udw from Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw based on anatomical outcome.
back:
- Itlaf-i-Udw: Total physical loss (severance/amputation).
- Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Permanent impairment of function, capacity, or permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ of the body or causing permanent disfigurement.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What local physiological responses accompany the "breaking of body tissue" in wounding?
back:
- Localized: Pain and bleeding.
- Generalized: Sweating and transient loss of consciousness.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Breaking of body tissue is also associated with other local manifestations at site like pain and bleeding and general body responses like sweating, transient loss of consciousness.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Which two terms are considered synonymous in medical pathology regarding tissue breaks?
back: The terms "Wound" and "Injury" are synonymous in meaning and represent a single pathological entity.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Injury' as per the legal definition in the Pakistan Penal Code.
back: Any harm whatever illegally caused to any person in body, mind, reputation, or property.
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): [Injury is any harm whatever illegally caused to any person, in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a 'Wound' or 'Injury'?
back: Any break in the body tissue, occurring either externally or internally.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Contrast the medical and legal status of the terms 'Wound' and 'Injury'.
back: Medically: Synonymous terms for a single pathological entity. Legally: 'Injury' denotes illegal harm; the law uses 'Hurt' instead of 'Wound'.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity... Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Does an illegal financial loss constitute an 'Injury' under Section 44 PPC?
back: Yes. The legal definition specifically includes illegal harm caused to 'property'.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Law also defines injury as any harm caused illegally to any person in body, mind, reputation or property.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Hurt' as per the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or impairing/disabling/dismembering any organ or part without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What is the essential criteria for 'Hurt' regarding the victim's outcome?
back: The harm must be inflicted 'without causing death'.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain... withoutt causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Under which legal framework was the term 'Injury' replaced by 'Hurt'?
back: The Qisas & Diyat Ordinance 1991.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Qisas & Diyat Ordinance 1991 has replaced terms of murder with qatl and injury with hurt and also gave new classifications denoting specific meanings.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: A victim survives an assault but loses function of an organ. Which legal term applies?
back: The term 'Hurt' applies, as it includes 'impairing' or 'disabling' any organ without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means... impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Pathologically, how is the relationship between 'Injury' and 'Wound' described?
back: They are considered a single pathological entity defined by a break in tissue.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What two anatomical locations are specified for a 'Wound' medically?
back: External and internal body tissues.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Injury' from a strictly medical perspective.
back: Any break in the body tissue, whether occurring externally or internally.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
coreConcept: Pathological Synonymity of Wound and Injury
front: Q: How do the terms 'Injury' and 'Wound' relate pathologically?
back: They are synonymous in meaning and constitute a single pathological entity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Contrast the legal and medical definitions of 'Injury'.
back: Medically: A tissue break. Legally: Any illegal harm to a person's body, mind, reputation, or property.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Law also defines injury as any harm caused illegally to any person in body, mind, reputation or property.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: A victim's arm is amputated during an assault. Classify this specific 'Hurt'.
back: Itlaf-i-Udw: Disfigurement, dismemberment, amputation, or severing of any limb or organ.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Itlaf-i-Udw: Causing of disfigurement, dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ of the body.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Hurt' as per the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, or injury/impairment to any organ without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: What are the four primary classifications of 'Hurt' in Pakistani law?
back: 1. Itlaf-i-Udw; 2. Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw; 3. Shajjah; 4. Jurh.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Names of Hurt: Itlaf-i-Udw, Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw, Shajjah, Jurh.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Differentiate between 'Arsh' and 'Daman' regarding compensation.
back: Arsh: Compensation specified in law. Daman: Compensation not specified, determined by the court.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Arsh: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt... Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: A victim presents with a head wound exposing bone but no fracture. Name the Shajjah.
back: Shajjah-i-Mudirah.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-Mudirah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Jurh' and its two primary sub-categories.
back: Jurh: Hurt on parts other than head/face leaving a mark. Subtypes: Jaifah (trunk cavity) and Ghayr-Jaifah.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Jurh: Hurt on part of the body other than the head and face bearing mark of wound... Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk. Ghayr-Jaifah: Hurt not amounting to Jaifah.

category: Define injury, wound and hurt
front: Q: Define 'Diyat' in the context of criminal hurt.
back: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt, payable by the offender to the victim's heirs.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Diyat: Compensation specified in Taw for causing hurt payable to the heirs of the victim, by the offender.

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How are mechanical injuries classified based on the weapon's physical properties?
back:
- Blunt weapons (e.g., club, hammer).
- Sharp cutting edge weapons (e.g., knife, razor).
- Sharp pointed edge weapons (e.g., needle, ice-pick).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [WOUNDING IMPLEMENT (Weapon) HAVING SINGLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What is the mechanism of wound formation by blunt force weapons?
back:
- Results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil.
- Causes internal vessel rupture (bruising) or skin splitting (laceration) against underlying bone.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Bruise also called contusion is a closed wound caused by strike of a blunt weapon. It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Differentiate the physical characteristics of incised versus lacerated wounds.
back:
- Incised: Clean-cut margins, sharp angles, no tissue bridging.
- Lacerated: Irregular/jagged margins, poorly defined angles, presence of bridging tissue tags.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Incised wound... shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls... Lacerated wound... varied shapes with irregular margins, ill defined angles and walls that have bridging tissue tags]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Describe the diagnostic features of a contact rifled firearm entry wound.
back:
- Circular hole with inverted margins.
- Signs of fire-blast: flame scorching, smoke blackening (soot), and powder tattooing (stippling).
- Stellate shape over bony areas.
citation: Page 71 (Book Page): [Riffled weapon entry wound is typically circular hole with inverted margins... Characteristics... include abrasion, bruising, flame scorching, tattooing, smoke and grease effect and gross splitting.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Contrast the tissue effects of high-velocity versus low-velocity projectiles.
back:
- Low-velocity: Energy radiates laterally proportionate to diameter.
- High-velocity: Creates temporary cavitation, massive tissue disintegration, and shatters dense structures like bone.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally... characteristic of damage... is disintegration and disorganization of large areas]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What are the three primary types of thermal injury based on causative agents?
back:
- Scalds: Moist heat (boiling liquids, steam).
- Burns: Dry heat (flame, heated objects).
- Corrosives: Chemical action (strong acids or alkalis).
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Thermal burn is caused by application of heat... whether by heated metallic object, flame, fluids at or near boiling point and pressure steam.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Why is a bomb blast injury categorized as having multiple causative factors?
back:
- Primary: Pressure waves (mechanical).
- Secondary: Flying debris/shrapnel (penetrating).
- Tertiary: Victim thrown against barriers (deceleration).
- Other: Hot gases/flame (thermal).
citation: Page 76 (Book Page): [These elements cause external injuries... in four ways: Primary effect; Secondary effect; Tertiary effect; Other effect]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Compare the skin lesions of 'loose contact' vs 'firm contact' electrical injuries.
back:
- Loose (Spark): Dry burn, central parchment, and 'metallization' (pitted metallic particles).
- Firm: Raised blister containing gas/fluid with a full-thickness white slough.
citation: Page 66 (Book Page): [Loose contact lesion, also called spark lesion is an area of dry burn... showing multiple pricked or pitted metallization... Firm contact lesion... is a raised blister... white slough]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What defines a penetrating wound compared to a simple incised wound?
back:
- Caused by sharp-pointed weapons.
- Greatest dimension is internal depth (piercing into cavities).
- External length/breadth are smaller than the track depth.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Penetrating & puncturing wound is produced by thrusting sharp edged and pointed weapon... except the depth, which is the greatest dimension]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: List the diagnostic hallmarks of a corrosive acid ingestion injury.
back:
- Localized corrosion of lips, tongue, and throat.
- Dark brown 'coffee-ground' vomitus (altered blood).
- Possible stomach perforation and inflammatory edema of the glottis.
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong corrosive substance has the property of destroying the texture of the tissue it meets... Stomach may contain blood stained or of dark brown color]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What are the two primary categories of wounding implements based on the number of causative factors?
back:
- Single Causative Factor: Mechanical, Thermal, Electrical, Corrosive.
- Multiple Causative Factor: Firearms, Bomb blasts.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [WOUNDING IMPLEMENT (Weapon) HAVING SINGLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR ... HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: List the mechanical weapons classified as having a Single Causative Factor.
back:
- Blunt weapons.
- Sharp cutting edge weapons.
- Sharp pointed edge weapons.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How are firearms classified under Multiple Causative Factor weapons based on barrel design?
back:
- Shotgun (smooth bore).
- Rifled weapons (low velocity or high velocity bullet).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Fire-arm: Shot gun; Rifled weapon—Low velocity bullet, High velocity bullet]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Categorize thermal causative agents listed under the Single Causative Factor classification.
back:
- Temperature: Heat, Cold, Flame, Hot liquid.
- Radiation: Artificial, Natural, Ionizing, Non-ionizing.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Other: Temperature—Heat, Cold; Flame; Hot liquid. Radiation—Artificial, Natural; Ionizing, Non-ionizing.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify corrosive wounding agents based on their chemical composition in Forensic Medicine.
back:
- Acids: Mineral or Organic acids (e.g., Sulfuric, Nitric).
- Alkalis: Strong bases (e.g., Caustic soda, Potassium hydroxide).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Corrosive—Acid, Alkali.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Which specific external injuries are typical of blunt versus sharp Single Causative Factor weapons?
back:
- Blunt: Abrasions, Bruises, Lacerations.
- Sharp: Incised, Penetrating, Puncturing wounds.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge ... Resultant Injuries: External—Closed: Abrasion, Bruise ... Open: Incised, Lacerated]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How is electricity classified as a Single Causative Factor weapon based on exposure characteristics?
back:
- Voltage: Low vs High voltage.
- Contact quality: Loose vs Firm contact.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Electricity—Low voltage, High voltage; Loose contact, Firm contact.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Why are bomb blasts classified as Multiple Causative Factor wounding implements?
back: They involve multiple mechanisms: primary (blast wave pressure), secondary (missiles/debris), tertiary (physical displacement), and thermal (heat/gases).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR Bomb blast]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Name the two kinetic factors in a mechanical weapon that determine the appearance of a wound.
back:
- Weight of the weapon.
- Velocity of the weapon.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What is the defining feature of 'Single Causative Factor' mechanical injuries?
back: They result from the application of force by an implement possessing only one type of mechanical action (Blunt, Sharp-edged, or Pointed).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [HAVING SINGLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Name the three primary categories of mechanical weapons having a single causative factor.
back:
1. Blunt
2. Sharp cutting edge
3. Sharp pointed edge
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [WOUNDING IMPLEMENT (Weapon) HAVING SINGLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Explain why a blunt strike causes a laceration on the head but a bruise on the buttock.
back: It depends on the architecture of the part struck. Scalp stretched over bone splits (laceration), whereas soft tissue like the buttock absorbs force through subcutaneous bleeding (bruise).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Head has scalp stretched over a bone whereas buttock comprises mostly of soft tissues of skin, fat and muscles... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Contrast the margins of wounds caused by sharp cutting edges versus blunt weapons.
back:
Sharp edge (Incised wound): Clean-cut, everted margins.
Blunt weapon (Lacerated wound): Irregular, bruised margins with tissue bridging.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Incised wound... shows clean cut margins... Lacerated wound... Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins... that have bridging tissue tags]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: A victim presents with a linear wound on the shin after a club strike. What is the injury type?
back: Split (Crush) Laceration. It occurs where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone, causing a linear breach that mimics an incision.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split, also called crush laceration... occurs on scalp, forehead, chin or any other part of the body where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. It may resemble an incision wound.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Categorize weapons having multiple causative factors.
back:
1. Fire-arms (Shotgun or Rifled weapons)
2. Bomb blasts
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR Bomb blast Fire-arm: Shot gun; Rifled weapon]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What is the defining diagnostic dimension of a wound caused by a sharp pointed weapon?
back: Depth is the greatest dimension. These are classified as penetrating or puncturing wounds.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Penetrating & puncturing wound is produced by thrusting sharp edged and pointed weapon... Most of the characteristics of this wound are similar to those of an incised wound, except the depth, which is the greatest dimension.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Define 'Mechanical Injury' in a forensic context.
back: Wounding of body tissue caused mechanically by blunt, sharp-edged, or sharp-pointed implements.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Wounding when caused mechanically is called mechanical injuries.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Differentiate the external presentation of injuries caused by flame versus scalding liquids.
back:
Flame: Singeing of hair, charred skin, small vesicles.
Scalding (Hot liquids): No singeing, large vesications, soaked clothing.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.5: Flame... Hair singeing present... Vesicles Very small. Hot liquids... Hair singeing absent... Vesicles Large.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Which two factors in a weapon determine the kinetic energy and resulting wound appearance?
back: Weight and Velocity. (K.E. = 1/2 MV²). High velocity projectiles produce greater tissue damage through energy radiation.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: List three external 'closed' injuries caused by blunt weapons.
back:
1. Abrasion
2. Bruise (Contusion)
3. Burn (Thermal blunt impact)
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [RESULTANT INJURIES External—Closed: Abrasion, Bruise, Burn]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How are wounding implements (weapons) broadly classified based on causative factors?
back:
1. Single Causative Factor: Mechanical, Temperature, Electricity, Radiation, and Corrosives.
2. Multiple Causative Factor: Bomb blasts and Fire-arms (Shotguns/Rifled weapons).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [WOUNDING IMPLEMENT (Weapon) HAVING SINGLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR... HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR Bomb blast Fire-arm: Shot gun; Rifled weapon]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify mechanical weapons based on their physical characteristics.
back:
1. Blunt implements (e.g., club, stone).
2. Sharp cutting edge (e.g., knife).
3. Sharp pointed edge (e.g., needle, pick).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How are Fire-arm weapons sub-classified in forensic terminology?
back:
1. Shotgun (smooth-bore).
2. Rifled weapons: subdivided into Low velocity and High velocity bullet types.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Fire-arm: Shot gun; Rifled weapon—Low velocity bullet, High velocity bullet]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Which specific weapon class causes 'Closed' versus 'Open' mechanical injuries?
back:
1. Closed: Blunt weapons (Abrasions, Bruises).
2. Open: Sharp edged (Incised), Sharp pointed (Penetrating), and Fire-arms.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [RESULTANT INJURIES External—Closed: Abrasion, Bruise, Burn; Open: Incised, Lacerated, Fire-arm]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify non-mechanical agents under the 'Single Causative Factor' group.
back:
1. Temperature (Heat, Cold, Flame, Hot liquid).
2. Electricity (Low/High voltage).
3. Radiation (Ionizing/Non-ionizing).
4. Corrosives (Acid/Alkali).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Other: Temperature—Heat, Cold; Flame; Hot liquid. Electricity—Low voltage, High voltage... Radiation—Artificial, Natural... Corrosive—Acid, Alkali.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What is the defining characteristic of a 'Multiple Causative Factor' weapon?
back: These are weapons that utilize multiple propulsive or destructive forces simultaneously, specifically identified as Fire-arms and Bomb blasts.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR Bomb blast Fire-arm: Shot gun; Rifled weapon]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: A wound shows bridging tissue tags and irregular margins. Identify the causative weapon class.
back: Mechanical: Blunt weapon (causing a lacerated wound).
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Lacerated wound is an open wound showing breach of skin... caused by strike of blunt weapon... walls that have bridging tissue tags]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Contrast the resultant injuries of low-velocity vs high-velocity rifled weapons.
back:
1. Low velocity: Simple track proportionate to bullet diameter.
2. High velocity: Produces temporary cavitation and extensive tissue disorganization.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [Low velocity bullet... energy radiates laterally causing damage proportionate to diameter... High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How is the 'Weight and Velocity' of a weapon used in forensic classification?
back: They determine the Kinetic Energy (K.E.=1/2mv²) and the appearance of the wound; high velocity/low mass (bullet) may cause more damage than low velocity/high mass (stone).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon... control and determine appearance of the wound... A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Which category do 'Corrosives' fall into when classifying based on weapon factors?
back: Single Causative Factor (Non-Mechanical).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [HAVING SINGLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR... Corrosive—Acid, Alkali.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How are wounding implements (weapons) classified based on the number of causative factors?
back:
1. Having Single Causative Factor (Mechanical, Thermal, Electrical, Corrosive).
2. Having Multiple Causative Factor (Fire-arms, Bomb blast).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [WOUNDING IMPLEMENT (Weapon) HAVING SINGLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR ... HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of mechanical injury production by blunt-edged weapons.
back: Blunt force causes sudden tissue indentation and recoil, resulting in bruises (closed) or lacerations (open) with irregular margins and tissue bridging.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Bruise also called contusion is a closed wound caused by strike of a blunt weapon. It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Contrast the wound characteristics of sharp-edged versus blunt-edged weapons.
back: Sharp-edged weapons produce incised wounds with clean-cut margins and sharp angles. Blunt weapons produce lacerations with irregular margins and crushed hair bulbs.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Incised wound ... shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls ... contrasting features ... Lacerated wound ... irregular margins, ill defined angles]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: In a fire-arm injury, what determines the production of temporary cavitation in tissues?
back: High-velocity bullets (above 2000 ft/sec). The kinetic energy dissipates radially, creating a permanent cavity larger than the bullet diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet, on the other hand, additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify chemical corrosive weapons on the basis of their chemical nature.
back:
1. Strong Mineral Acids (Sulfuric, Nitric).
2. Weak Organic Acids (Carbolic, Oxalic).
3. Strong Alkalis (Caustic Soda, Ammonia).
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong mineral acids are sulfuric acid, nitric acid ... Weak organic acids are carbolic acid ... Important strong alkalis are sodium hydroxide]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What are the diagnostic entry wound features of a shotgun (smooth-bore) weapon?
back: Depends on distance: single en-mass entry with irregular margins at close range, or multiple isolated pellet holes at far range.
citation: Page 74 (Book Page): [Entry wound shotgun differs from rifled wound ... Contact wound makes single en-mass entry ... Far distance wound ... pellets with wider dispersion make individual holes]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify injuries resulting from mechanical blunt force based on skin continuity.
back:
1. Closed wounds: Abrasions (moving, imprint, friction) and Bruises.
2. Open wounds: Lacerations (split, over-stretch, grinding compression).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [External—Closed: Abrasion, Bruise ... Open: Incised, Lacerated, Fire-arm]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Define the four-tier classification of injuries caused by a bomb blast weapon.
back:
1. Primary: Direct pressure wave effects.
2. Secondary: Flying debris/missiles.
3. Tertiary: Impact against fixed objects.
4. Other: Thermal burns or noxious gases.
citation: Page 76 (Book Page): [These elements cause external injuries to the victims in the vicinity of blast in four ways: Primary effect Secondary effect Tertiary effect Other effect]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Classify thermal wounding implements based on the causative agent.
back:
1. Dry Heat: Flame and heated solids (burns).
2. Moist Heat: Hot liquids and pressure steam (scalds).
3. Extreme Cold.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Temperature—Heat, Cold; Flame; Hot liquid.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What is the defining feature of a wound caused by a sharp-pointed thrusting weapon?
back: Penetrating or puncturing wound. The internal depth is the greatest dimension, determined by the length of the weapon's blade.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Penetrating & puncturing wound is produced by thrusting sharp edged and pointed weapon ... depth, which is the greatest dimension.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: How are wounding implements classified based on the number of causative factors?
back:
- Single Causative Factor: Mechanical (blunt/sharp), Thermal, Electrical, Corrosive.
- Multiple Causative Factors: Firearms (shotguns/rifled) and Bomb blasts.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [WOUNDING IMPLEMENT (Weapon) HAVING SINGLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR... HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR: Bomb blast; Fire-arm]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Classify injuries caused specifically by single-factor mechanical weapons.
back:
- Blunt edge: Abrasion, Bruise, Laceration.
- Sharp cutting edge: Incised wound.
- Sharp pointed edge: Penetrating or Puncture wound.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge... RESULTANT INJURIES... Abrasion, Bruise... Incised, Lacerated]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Identify the sub-types of weapons classified under Multiple Causative Factors.
back:
- Firearms: Shotguns (smooth bore) and Rifled weapons (low/high velocity).
- Explosives: Bomb blasts (incorporating heat, fragments, and pressure).
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR: Bomb blast; Fire-arm: Shot gun; Rifled weapon—Low velocity bullet, High velocity bullet]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: A victim presents with 'central wounding' and 'peripheral non-wounding stamping.' Identify the causative weapon.
back: A firearm. The central hole is from the projectile; peripheral stamping is caused by smoke, unburned powder, and grease (tattooing).
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Entry wound by fire-arm has two types of Findings: Central wounding; Peripheral non-wounding stamping]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: How are thermal wounding agents classified in forensic practice?
back:
- Heat/Flame: Dry burns.
- Hot liquids/Steam: Scalds.
- Cold: Frostbite or local lesions.
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [Other: Temperature—Heat, Cold; Flame; Hot liquid... RESULTANT INJURIES... Burn]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Contrast the resultant open injuries caused by blunt vs. sharp cutting weapons.
back:
- Blunt weapon: Lacerated wound (irregular margins, tissue bridging).
- Sharp cutting weapon: Incised wound (clean-cut margins, sharp angles, no tissue bridging).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Examples are incised and lacerated wounds produced by sharp edged and blunt edged weapons.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Classify corrosive weapons based on their chemical composition and forensic importance.
back:
- Strong Mineral Acids: Sulfuric, Nitric, Hydrochloric.
- Weak Organic Acids: Carbolic (Phenol), Oxalic.
- Strong Alkalis: Caustic Soda (Sodium Hydroxide).
citation: Page 175 (Book Page): [Strong mineral acids... Weak organic acids... Important strong alkalis]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: A wound's internal depth is its greatest dimension. Identify the specific mechanical weapon type.
back: A sharp pointed edge weapon (e.g., knife or glass shard), causing a penetrating or puncturing wound.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Penetrating & puncturing wound is produced by thrusting sharp edged and pointed weapon... depth, which is the greatest dimension.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Classify electrical weapons based on contact type and voltage effect.
back:
- Low Voltage (Domestic): Spark (loose contact) or Raised Blister (firm contact).
- High Voltage (Industrial): Arcing (flash burns) or Carbonization.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): [Contact with above mentioned three voltages produce three effects... Domestic lesions are further divided into two types: loose and firm contact lesion.]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Identify the causative weapon producing injuries through primary, secondary, and tertiary effects.
back:
Bomb blasts. 
- Primary: Pressure wave.
- Secondary: Flying debris (missiles).
- Tertiary: Body being propelled against obstacles.
citation: Page 76 (Book Page): [These elements cause external injuries to the victims in the vicinity of blast in four ways: Primary effect; Secondary effect; Tertiary effect; Other effect]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: How is mechanical wounding classified based on the causative implement's edge or point?
back:
Injuries are classified as: 
1. Blunt weapon injuries (abrasions, bruises, lacerations)
2. Sharp cutting edge injuries (incised wounds)
3. Sharp pointed edge injuries (penetrating/puncturing wounds)
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [WOUNDING IMPLEMENT (Weapon) HAVING SINGLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR Mechanical: Blunt; Sharp cutting edge; Sharp pointed edge]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: What defines weapons with 'multiple causative factors' compared to simple mechanical weapons?
back:
These weapons produce damage through a combination of components (flame, hot gases, smoke, projectiles). Examples include:
1. Bomb blasts
2. Fire-arms (Shotguns and Rifled weapons)
citation: Page 52 (Book Page): [HAVING MULTIPLE CAUSATIVE FACTOR Bomb blast Fire-arm: Shot gun; Rifled weapon—Low velocity bullet, High velocity bullet]

category: Classify injuries on the basis of causative weapons
front: Q: Contrast the wound margins produced by sharp-edged versus blunt-edged mechanical weapons.
back:
• Sharp-edged: Produce incised wounds with clean-cut, regular margins and sharp angles.
• Blunt-edged: Produce lacerated wounds with irregular margins, bruising, and characteristic bridging tissue tags.
