front: Q: Define the legal term 'Diyat'.
back: Compensation specified in the law for causing death or hurt, payable to the victim's heirs.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Diyat: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt payable to the heirs of the victim, by the offender.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What defines a 'Shajjah-i-mudihah' injury?
back: A head or face injury where the bone is exposed but not fractured.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Name the classification for a displaced fracture of the skull or face.
back: Shajjah-i-munaqqilah.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-munaqqilah: Fracturing of bone with displacement.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Differentiate 'Jaifah' from 'Ghayr-Jaifah' injuries.
back:
• Jaifah: Hurt extending into the body cavity (trunk).
• Ghayr-Jaifah: Hurt not extending into the body cavity.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk. Ghayr-Jaifah: Hurt not amounting to Jaifah.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What is 'Shajjah-i-ammah'?
back: A head or face injury where the fracture touches the brain membranes (meninges).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-ammah: Fracturing of bone and the wound touching the membranes of the brain.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What defines 'Shajjah-i-khafifah'?
back: Hurt on the head or face where the bone is not exposed.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-khafifah: Hurt withoutt exposing of bone.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: How is 'Hurt' defined under the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance?
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ or part of the body without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What is the defining anatomical feature of Shajjah-i-damighah?
back: A fracture of the skull bone that is accompanied by the rupturing of the brain membranes.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-damighah: Fracturing of bone with rupturing of the brain membranes.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Contrast the legal terms Arsh and Daman as per the Act.
back:
• Arsh: Compensation specified/fixed in law for causing hurt.
• Daman: Unspecified compensation determined by the court.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Arsh: Compensation not is specified in law for causing hurt... Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court for causing hurt.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: A victim presents with a skull fracture where the wound touches the brain membranes; classify this injury.
back: Shajjah-i-ammah.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-ammah: Fracturing of bone and the wound touching the brain membranes.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What specific functional loss constitutes Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw?
back: Destroying or permanently impairing the function or capacity of a body organ, or causing permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ of the body or causing permanent disfigurement

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What is the diagnostic criteria for a 'Jaifah' injury?
back: A 'Jurh' (wound) that extends into the body cavity of the trunk.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: How is Shajjah-i-mudihah distinguished from Shajjah-i-khafifah?
back:
• Khafifah: Hurt without exposing bone.
• Mudihah: Hurt where the bone is exposed but not fractured.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-khafifah: Hurt withoutt exposing of bone. Shajjah-i-mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Contrast 'Madihah' and 'Mudihah' based on body region and weapon type.
back:
• Mudihah: Head/face hurt exposing bone.
• Madihah: Ghayr-jaifah hurt (rest of body) exposing bone, specifically caused by a sharp weapon.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture... Madihah: ...exposing the bone. (Sharp weapon).

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What anatomical event differentiates Shajjah-i-munaqqilah from Shajjah-i-hashimah?
back: Both involve fracture, but Munaqqilah involves the displacement of the bone fragments.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-hashimah: Fracturing of bone withoutt displacement. Shajjah-i-munaqqilah: Fracturing of bone and its displacement.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Define the injury known as Itlaf-i-udw.
back: Dismemberment, amputation, or severing of any limb or organ of the body.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Itlaf-i-Udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ of the body.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Define "Hurt" according to the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, or injury; or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What is the pathophysiological difference between Itlaf-i-udw and Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw?
back:
- Itlaf-i-udw: Physical dismemberment, amputation, or severing of a limb/organ.
- Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw: Permanent impairment of the function/capacity of an organ or permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Itlaf-i-udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ... Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ... or causing permanent disfigurement.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Contrast Arsh, Diyat, and Daman as specified under the Act.
back:
- Arsh: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt.
- Daman: Court-determined compensation for hurt not liable to Arsh.
- Diyat: Specified compensation payable to heirs of the victim.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Arsh: Compensation not is specified in law for causing hurt... Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court... Diyat: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt payable to the heirs.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: A victim presents with a stab wound that penetrates the abdominal cavity. Identify this hurt.
back: Jaifah. It is defined as hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk (cranium, chest, or abdomen).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What defines the transition from Shajjah-i-mudihah to Shajjah-i-hashimah?
back: The occurrence of a fracture. Shajjah-i-mudihah involves exposing bone without fracture; Shajjah-i-hashimah involves fracturing bone without displacement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture. Shajjah-i-hashimah: Fracturing of bone withoutt displacement.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: List the diagnostic criteria for Shajjah-i-damighah.
back:
1. Injury on head or face.
2. Fracture of the skull bone.
3. Rupture of the brain membranes (meninges).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-damighah: Fracturing of bone with rupturing of the brain membranes.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Distinguish between the Jurh categories Damiyah and Badiha.
back:
- Damiyah: Rupturing of the skin with bleeding.
- Badiha: Cutting the flesh without exposing the bone.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Damiyah: Rupturing of the skin with bleeding. Badiha: Cutting the fas exposing the bone. (Sharp weapon)

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: A patient has a displaced skull fracture after an assault. Which specific Shajjah is this?
back: Shajjah-i-munaqqilah. It involves fracturing the skull bone and the displacement of the fractured fragments.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-munaqqilah: Fracturing of bone with displacement.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What distinguishes Shajjah from Jurh in terms of anatomical site?
back: Shajjah is exclusively hurt on the head or face. Jurh is hurt on any part of the body other than the head or face.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah: Hurt on the head or face which does not amount to itlaf-i-Udw... Jurh: Hurt on part of the body other than the head and face bearing mark of wound.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: How does the law define "Injury" compared to medical "Wound"?
back: Injury is any harm illegally caused to a person's body, mind, reputation, or property. Wound (medical) is simply a break in body tissue.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Law also defines injury as any harm caused illegally to any person in body, mind, reputation or property. Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it.

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the three primary factors determining the appearance and production of a mechanical wound?
back:
1. Subject: Architecture and movement of the body part.
2. Object: Weight and type of weapon.
3. Contact: Velocity and manner of execution.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients... Weight and velocity Movement of the part]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How is the kinetic energy of a weapon calculated in the mechanism of wounding?
back:
K.E. = 1/2mv². 
High velocity is more critical than weight; a small bullet at high speed causes greater damage than a larger, slower object.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv². A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone bigger in size.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why does a blunt strike produce different wounds on the scalp versus the buttocks?
back:
Due to Subject Architecture:
- Scalp: Thin tissue over bone produces lacerations.
- Buttocks: Soft tissue (fat/muscle) absorbs force, producing bruises.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Head has scalp stretched over a bone whereas buttock comprises mostly of soft tissues... This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Compare wounding mechanisms in a strike to a stationary head versus a moving head.
back:
- Stationary: Produces local scalp injury at the contact site.
- Moving: Forces are widely distributed, causing deeper intracranial damage (e.g., deceleration/contre-coup injuries).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact... in a moving head hitting a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is wider.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Distinguish between direct and indirect contact in mechanical wound production.
back:
- Direct: Injury at the site of contact.
- Indirect: Injury distant from contact site (e.g., clavicle fracture from a fall on an outstretched hand).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution... direct and indirect. Latter causes injury at a place away from the site of contact.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does bone elasticity in the subject change with age during injury contact?
back:
- Infants: Higher elasticity leads to greenstick fractures.
- Elderly: Bones are brittle and break easily under less force.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the object's type specifically control the resultant wound class?
back:
- Sharp-edged object: Incised wound.
- Blunt-edged object: Lacerated wound.
- Pointed object: Penetrating/Puncturing wound.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Type of weapon directly controls and determines the appearance of the wound. Examples are incised and lacerated wounds produced by sharp edged and blunt edged weapons.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the content of hollow subject organs affect their wounding mechanism?
back: Hollow organs (stomach, bladder) are more likely to burst if they contain fluid or semi-solids at the time of blunt impact.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Stomach, intestine, heart... are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids of different density... shapes along with size and density of bone have relation to the outcome.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain the 'Split Laceration' mechanism regarding subject and object interaction.
back: It occurs when soft tissue is suddenly compressed and crushed between a blunt object and an underlying bone (e.g., scalp, forehead, or chin).
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues between the weapon and the underlying bone split them. It may resemble an incision wound.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Which two factors of the wounding object determine the sum-total appearance of the wound?
back: Weight and Velocity. These determine the kinetic energy and the force of execution during contact.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Define 'Hurt' as per the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury, or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Contrast 'Shajjah' and 'Jurh' based on anatomical location.
back:
• Shajjah: Injuries specifically on the head or face.
• Jurh: Injuries on any part of the body other than the head or face.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah: Hurt on the head or face... Jurh: Hurt on part of the body other than the head and face bearing mark of wound which may be temporary or permanent.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Differentiate between 'Arsh' and 'Daman' compensation.
back:
• Arsh: Compensation specified in the law for causing specific hurt.
• Daman: Compensation not specified by law, determined by the court.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Arsh: Compensation not is specified in law for causing hurt by the offender to the victim or his heirs. Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court for causing hurt.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: A victim presents with a scalp wound exposing the skull bone but no fracture. Classify this hurt.
back: Shajjah-i-Mudihah.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Distinguish between 'Itlaf-i-Udw' and 'Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw'.
back:
• Itlaf-i-Udw: Disarticulation, amputation, or severing of a limb/organ.
• Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying or permanently impairing the function/capacity of an organ.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-Udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ... Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ of the body or causing permanent disfigurement.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What is the defining criteria for a 'Jaifah' injury?
back: Hurt on the trunk that extends into the body cavity.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: How is 'Shajjah-i-Damighah' distinguished from 'Shajjah-i-Ammah'?
back:
• Shajjah-i-Ammah: Fracture touches the brain membranes.
• Shajjah-i-Damighah: Fracture ruptures the brain membranes.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Ammah: Fracturing of bone and the wound touching the membranes of brain. Shajjah-i-Damighah: Fracturing of bone with rupturing of the brain membranes.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Differentiate 'Mutalahimah' and 'Mudihah' under 'Ghayr-Jaifah' injuries.
back:
• Mutalahimah: Lacerating the flesh.
• Mudihah: Exposing the bone (caused by a sharp weapon).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Mutalahimah: Lacerating the flesh. Mudihah: the fas exposing the bone. (Sharp weapon)]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Describe the progression of 'Shajjah-i-Hashimah' to 'Shajjah-i-Munaqqilah'.
back:
• Hashimah: Bone fracture without displacement.
• Munaqqilah: Bone fracture with displacement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Hashimah: Fracturing of bone withoutt displacement. Shajjah-i-Munaqqilah: Fracturing of bone with displacement.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Define 'Shajjah-i-Khafifah'.
back: A hurt on the head or face that does not expose the bone.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Khafifah: Hurt withoutt exposing of bone.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How is a wound defined from a medical perspective?
back:
• Any break in body tissue
• Can be external or internal
• Synonymous with the medical term 'injury'
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Which physical formula determines the wounding potential of a weapon (object)?
back:
• $K.E. = 1/2 mv^2$
• Velocity has a greater influence on kinetic energy than weight
• High velocity produces greater tissue destruction
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2. A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone bigger in size with less velocity shall produce greater damage.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast direct versus indirect execution of a weapon in wound production.
back:
• Direct: Injury occurs exactly at the point of impact
• Indirect: Force causes injury at a site remote from contact (e.g., fractured clavicle from a fall on the hand)
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution or infliction of weapon; direct and indirect. Direct causes injury at the site of impact whereas indirect causes injury at a place away from the site of contact.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why does a club strike produce a laceration on the scalp but a bruise on the buttocks?
back:
• Scalp: Skin is stretched over hard bone, causing it to split (split laceration)
• Buttocks: Soft tissue (fat/muscle) absorbs force, resulting in a bruise instead of a breach
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club, a blunt weapon, having same force on different body parts having different architecture will produce different shaped injuries i.e. on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the mechanical step in the 'Resistance mechanism with hard inclusion' regarding scalp injuries?
back:
• Skin and subcutaneous tissues are suddenly compressed between the weapon and underlying bone
• This results in a split or crush laceration
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Resistance mechanism with hard inclusion i.e. scalp having soft scalp over it... Scalp laceration with skull fracture.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: List the three primary factors in a weapon (object) that control wound appearance.
back:
• Type of weapon (e.g., sharp vs. blunt edge)
• Weight of the weapon
• Velocity of the weapon
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Type of weapon directly controls and determines the appearance of the wound... Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the movement of the subject's head affect the outcome of an impact?
back:
• Stationary head: Produces local injury at the site of contact
• Moving head: Impact with a stationary object often results in wider, more severe intracranial trauma
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact and damage may extend even to deeper part... whereas if a moving head strikes a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is severer.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Compare how solid vs. hollow organs (subject) respond to blunt force contact.
back:
• Solid (Liver/Spleen): Fracture or disintegrate
• Hollow (Stomach/Bladder): Rupture based on the density of their fluid or semi-solid contents
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Stomach, intestine, heart, gall and urinary bladder are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids... because of the design of these organs, they have different behavior character.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why is bone elasticity a critical subject factor in pediatric versus geriatric wounding?
back:
• Infants: Highly elastic bones, often resulting in greenstick fractures
• Adults/Elderly: Brittle bones that break easily due to higher calcification
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bone elasticity depends upon person's age... Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What legal term does Pakistani Law use instead of 'wound' for criminal injuries?
back:
• 'Hurt'
• Defined as causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, or injury without causing death
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead. Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing... without causing death.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the two primary factors that control the shape of a mechanical injury?
back:
1. Factors in the weapon (Object)
2. Factors in the part struck (Subject)
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does velocity influence the mechanism of wound production in mechanical injuries?
back: Velocity provides kinetic energy ($K.E.=1/2 mv^2$). A high-velocity object (e.g., a bullet) produces significantly more tissue destruction than a larger object at lower velocity.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2. A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone bigger in size.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast the mechanism of direct vs. indirect manners of weapon execution.
back:
• Direct: Injury occurs at the point of impact.
• Indirect: Injury occurs at a site remote from contact (e.g., a clavicle fracture resulting from a fall on the hand).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Direct causes injury at site of impact... Indirect causes injury at a place away from site of impact]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why does the same force cause a laceration on the scalp but only a bruise on the buttocks?
back: Subject Architecture: The scalp is stretched over rigid bone, causing it to split. The buttocks have thick, elastic soft tissue (fat/muscle) that absorbs force, resulting in vessel rupture (bruise) instead of a tear.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike with a club... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain the mechanical step leading to a 'split laceration'.
back: Sudden compression of skin between the weapon and underlying bone causes the tissue to split. This often mimics an incised wound due to the linear nature of the underlying bone support.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues betweenn the weapon and the underlying bone split them. It may resemble an incision wound.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the three defining characteristics of a lacerated wound produced by blunt force contact?
back:
• Irregular margins
• Ill-defined angles
• Bridging tissue tags in the wound walls
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins, ill defined angles and walls that have bridging tissue tags]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does subject movement (stationary vs. moving) alter the mechanism of head trauma?
back:
• Stationary head: Strike produces localized scalp injury and potentially deep focal damage.
• Moving head: Impact against a stationary object produces diffuse trauma due to acceleration-deceleration forces.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a’stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp... whereas if a moving head strikes a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is more diffuse]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Analyze the mechanism and clinical risk of 'grinding compression' injuries from automobile wheels.
back: Mechanism involves localized pressure plus a tangential tangential push. This separates skin/muscles from bone and crushes tissue, frequently precipitating fatal fat embolism or renal failure.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [grinding compression... skin and muscles are also separated from underlying bone... They precipitate fat embolism... causing death from renal failure.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Describe the 'blowback phenomenon' in contact firearm wounds over bony subjects.
back: High-pressure explosive gases enter the wound but are resisted by the underlying bone. The gases return forcefully, distending and lacerating the skin into a stellate or ragged shape.
citation: Page 72 (Book Page): [When there is hard bone as in scalp or cheek, it resists entry of gases, which return with extreme force; blowback phenomenon causing stellate or ragged wound]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the subject's age modify the mechanism of bone fractures?
back: Infant bones are more elastic, often resulting in greenstick fractures. Adult and elderly bones are brittle and break easily at the point of impact or via lever action.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How is a mechanical wound or injury defined from a medical perspective?
back: Any break in the body tissue, either externally or internally, that is synonymous with the term injury.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the three primary factors in a weapon (object) that determine wound appearance?
back:
1. Type of weapon (sharp vs blunt).
2. Weight of the weapon.
3. Velocity of the weapon.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Type of weapon directly controls and determines the appearance of the wound... Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Distinguish between direct and indirect execution of a weapon contact.
back:
1. Direct: Injury occurs at the site of impact.
2. Indirect: Injury occurs at a site remote from contact (e.g., clavicle fracture from falling on hands).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution... direct and indirect. Indirect causes injury at a place away from the site of contact... fracture of clavicle produced by fall on hands.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: A club strike causes a head laceration but a buttock bruise. Which 'subject' factor explains this?
back: Architecture of the part struck. Scalp is stretched over rigid bone (split), while buttocks have soft, elastic fat/muscle that absorbs force (bruise).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Architecture of part struck... Strike with a club... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference... is due to the difference in architecture.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the physical formula used to calculate the wounding energy of an object?
back: K.E. = 1/2 mv². Velocity is critical; a small high-velocity bullet produces more damage than a large, slow object.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2. A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone bigger in size.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: List the three specific mechanisms for the production of mechanical abrasions.
back:
1. Moving abrasion (grazes/scratches).
2. Imprint abrasion (contact with patterned objects).
3. Friction abrasion.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Types of mechanical abrasion... Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain the mechanical process involved in the production of a 'split laceration'.
back: Sudden compression of skin and soft tissue between a blunt object and an underlying rigid bone causes the tissue to split.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split laceration... Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues betweenn the weapon and the underlying bone split them.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: A victim has neck abrasions from a heavy necklace. How is the contact mechanism evaluated?
back: Ante-mortem contact shows vital reactions (bleeding/hyperemia). Post-mortem contact/handling causes dry, parchment-like skin without vital reaction.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Anle-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction... Postmortem removal of epidermis by rawgh handling of corpse... with passage of time after drying develops parchment appearance.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Describe the mechanism and consequence of 'grinding compression' contact.
back: A heavy weight (e.g., vehicle wheel) moves over a limb, compressing and rotating tissue, which separates skin/muscle and causes internal crushing.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Grinding compression laceratign... movement of heavy body... automobile wheel over limbs... skin and muscles are also separated from each other and underlying bone.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the internal architecture of the subject (hollow vs solid organs) affect wound type?
back:
1. Solid organs (liver/spleen): Shatter easily.
2. Hollow sacs (stomach/bladder): Rupture depending on fluid/food density and contents.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Stomach, intestine, heart, gall and urinary bladder are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids of different density... these organs have different behavior character.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Under the Qisas and Diyyat Act, how is "Hurt" defined?
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ/part of the body without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Contrast the mechanisms of Itlaf-i-Udw and Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw.
back:
• Itlaf-i-Udw: Physical dismemberment, amputation, or severing of a limb/organ.
• Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying/permanently impairing function/capacity or causing permanent disfigurement of an organ.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-Udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ... Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ of the body or causing permanent disfigurement]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What is the primary difference between Arsh and Daman?
back:
• Arsh: Compensation specifically stated in the law for certain hurts.
• Daman: Compensation not specified as Arsh, to be determined by the court.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Arsh: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt by the offender to the victim or his heirs. Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court for causing hurt]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: A head injury exposes the bone but no fracture is present. Name the category.
back: Shajjah-i-Mudiha.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Mudiha: Hurt on the head or face... Exposing of bone without its fracture.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: List the sub-categories of Shajjah (injuries to head or face) in increasing severity.
back:
1. Khafifah (no bone exposure)
2. Mudiha (bone exposed)
3. Hashimah (fracture without displacement)
4. Munaqqilah (displaced fracture)
5. Ammah (reaches brain membrane)
6. Damighah (membrane ruptured)
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Table 4.2: Shajjah-i-Khafifah... Shajjah-i-Mudiha... Shajjah-i-Hashimah... Shajjah-i-Munaqqilah... Shajjah-i-Ammah... Shajjah-i-Damighah]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: What is the defining criteria for a Jaifah injury?
back: A hurt on any part of the body other than head or face that extends into the body cavity of the trunk.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: How is 'Jurh' conceptually divided under the Act?
back:
• Jaifah: Extends into the trunk cavity.
• Ghayr-jaifah: Hurt not amounting to Jaifah (does not enter trunk cavity).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Jurh: Hurt on part of the body other than the head and face bearing mark of wound... Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk. Ghayr-jaifah: Hurt not amounting to Jaifah.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Distinguish Shajjah-i-Ammah from Shajjah-i-Damighah.
back:
• Shajjah-i-Ammah: The wound touches the membranes of the brain.
• Shajjah-i-Damighah: The brain membranes are actually ruptured.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Ammah: Fracturing of bone and the wound touching the membranes of brain. Shajjah-i-Damighah: Fracturing of bone with rupturing of the brain membranes.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: List the six types of Ghayr-jaifah injuries.
back:
1. Damiyah
2. Badihah
3. Mutalahimah
4. Mudiyah
5. Hashimah
6. Munaqqilah
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Table 4.2: Ghayr-jaifah... Damiyah, Badihah, Mutalahimah, Mudiyah, Hashimah, Munaqqilah]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Q: Define 'Diyat' according to the Act's legal terms.
back: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt, payable to the heirs of the victim by the offender.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Table 4.1: Diyat: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt payable to the heirs of the victim, by the offender.]

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Define Hurt according to the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance 1991.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, or injury, or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Differentiate between Itlaf-i-udw and Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw regarding organ damage.
back: Itlaf-i-udw: Dismemberment, amputation, or severing of a limb/organ. Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw: Destroying or permanently impairing the function/capacity of an organ, or causing permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Itlaf-i-Udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ of the badly ... Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ of the body or causing permanent disfigurement

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Contrast the diagnostic features of Shujjah-i-khafifah and Shujjah-i-mudihah.
back: Khafifah involves hurt where no bone is exposed. Mudihah involves hurt where the bone is exposed but not fractured.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shujjah-i-khafifah: Hurt withoutt exposing of bone. Shujjah-i-mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: What criteria must an injury meet to be classified as Jaifah?
back: The hurt must extend into the body cavity of the trunk.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Classify the first three sub-types of Ghayr-Jaifah based on tissue damage depth.
back: 1. Damiyah: Skin rupture with bleeding. 2. Badi'ah: Cutting of flesh. 3. Mutalahimah: Lacerating of flesh.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Damiyah: Rupturing of the skin with bleeding. Badi'ah: Cutting of the flesh. Mutalahimah: Lacerating of the flesh.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Define the diagnostic threshold for Shujjah-i-ammah.
back: A head/face injury involving a bone fracture where the wound specifically touches the 'meninger' (membranes) of the brain.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shujjah-i-Ammah: Fracturing of bone and the wound touching the meninger of brain

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: How is the compensation amount for Daman determined?
back: Daman is compensation not specified as Arsh in law; the court determines the amount payable to the victim or heirs.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court for causing hurt and payable by offender to the victim or his heirs

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Compare Shujjah-i-hashimah and Shujjah-i-munaqqilah based on bone state.
back: Hashimah: Bone is fractured but not displaced. Munaqqilah: Bone is fractured and displaced.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shujjah-i-hashimah: Fracturing of bone withoutt displacement. Shujjah-i-munaqqilah: Fracturing of bone with displacement.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: Define Arsh as specified under the Ordinance.
back: Compensation that is specifically listed/quantified in the law for causing particular types of hurt.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Arsh: Compensation is specified in law for causing hurt by the offender to the victim or his heirs.

category: Classify injuries as per Qisas and Diyyat Act
front: To which anatomical regions does the classification 'Shujjab' apply?
back: Specifically to injuries on the head or face that do not result in total loss of organ or function.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shujjab: Hurt on the head or face which does not amount to itlaf-i-Udw or itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw.

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What three primary factors control the appearance and shape of a mechanical injury?
back:
1. Factors in the weapon (Weight, velocity).
2. Factors in the part struck (Architecture, movement).
3. Manner of execution (Direct or indirect contact).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients... Weight and velocity, Manner of execution, Architecture, Movement of the part]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the mechanical process behind the production of a bruise (contusion)?
back:
1. Sudden tissue indentation by a blunt object.
2. Tissue recoil and rupture of small blood vessels.
3. Extravasation of blood into surrounding interstitial spaces.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil... Blood from the broken small vessels spreads into the surrounding tissue.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How do incised and lacerated wounds differ by mechanical contact?
back:
• Incised: Caused by a sharp edge moving across tissue (incision/cutting).
• Lacerated: Caused by a blunt strike crushing or over-stretching tissue beyond its elastic limit.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page), 59: [Lacerated wound... caused by strike of blunt weapon... Incised wound resulting from cutting or incision of skin... Movement of the weapon is necessary ingredient]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: A blunt strike to the scalp creates a linear wound with minimal bruising. Diagnosis and mechanism?
back:
• Split (Crush) Laceration.
• Mechanism: Tissues are forcefully compressed and split between the blunt weapon and the underlying rigid bone.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split, also called crush laceration... skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues betweenn the weapon and the underlying bone split them.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the three mechanical sub-types of lacerations based on contact mechanism?
back:
1. Split (Crush) laceration.
2. Over-stretch laceration.
3. Grinding compression laceration.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Depending upon mechanism of tts causation, there are of three types: Split, also called crush laceration, Over-stretch laceration, Grinding compression laceratign]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the three types of mechanical abrasions based on contact?
back:
1. Moving abrasion (e.g., grazes/scratches).
2. Imprint abrasion (e.g., ligature marks).
3. Friction abrasion.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the architecture of the part struck (Subject) determine injury type?
back:
A blunt strike of identical force produces different wounds based on tissue consistency:
• Scalp (stretched over bone): Laceration.
• Buttock (soft tissue/fat): Bruise.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club... same force on different body parts... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Define the difference between direct and indirect contact in bone fractures.
back:
• Direct: Fracture occurs at the specific point of impact.
• Indirect: Force is transmitted along the bone (acting as a lever) to fracture a remote, weaker point.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Long bone fracture of adult occurs either at point of impact or bone acting as a lever divert the force to other remote weaker point, which gets fractured.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What mechanical sequence produces a 'grinding compression' injury?
back:
1. A moving object (e.g., wheel) passes over a limb.
2. Skin is pinned and rotated against the surface.
3. Underlying muscles are crushed and separated from skin.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Grinding compression... produced by moving automobile wheel over limbs... skin and muscles are also separated from each other and underlying bone.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What physical formula determines the potential wounding energy of a weapon (Object)?
back: Kinetic Energy (K.E.) = 1/2 MV² (where M = Mass, V = Velocity). Velocity is more critical than mass.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What defines a medical 'wound' or 'injury'?
back:
* Any physical break in body tissue.
* Can be external (skin) or internal (serous membranes/organs).
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view. any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Which formula determines the kinetic energy and wounding potential of a weapon?
back:
* K.E. = 1/2 mv².
* Velocity (v) has a greater impact on damage than mass (m).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv².]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Distinguish between 'direct' and 'indirect' manners of weapon execution.
back:
* Direct: Injury occurs exactly at the contact site.
* Indirect: Injury occurs away from contact (e.g., fractured clavicle from a fall on the hand).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Indirect causes injury at a place away from the site of contact... e.g. fracture of clavicle produced by fall on hand.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: A club strike causes a laceration on the head but a bruise on the buttocks. Why?
back:
* Tissue architecture.
* Scalp is thin/stretched over rigid bone (splits).
* Buttocks have thick, elastic soft tissue and fat (absorbs force).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Head has scalp stretched over a bone whereas buttock comprises mostly of soft tissues... This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does bone elasticity change with age during contact with a weapon?
back:
* Infants: Bones are relatively elastic and resist breaking.
* Adults/Elderly: Bones are brittle and break easily under less force.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the two primary factors controlling the shape of a mechanical injury?
back:
1. Factors in the weapon (weight, velocity, execution).
2. Factors in the part struck (architecture, movement).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Compare wound production in stationary versus moving body parts.
back:
* Stationary head: Produces localized contact injury.
* Moving head (striking object): Produces widespread trauma due to force distribution.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a’stationary head will produce a local injury... whereas if the head is in motion and hits a stationary object, the resultant trauma... will be widespread.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How do hollow organs (stomach/bladder) differ from solid organs (liver/spleen) upon impact?
back:
* Solid: Shatter or rupture directly.
* Hollow: Act as sacs; damage depends on internal fluid density and transmission of force.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Stomach, intestine, heart, gall and urinary bladder are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids... they have different behavior character.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What happens when a weapon's distortion exceeds the limit of bone elasticity?
back:
* The bone fractures.
* Initial indentation/recoil occurs first if force is within limits.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Force beyond the limit of bone elasticity will cause fracture... starting at point of maximum convexity.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why are soft tissues like skin and fat considered 'elastic' in wound mechanics?
back: * They absorb and distribute force more effectively than rigid tissues like bone or ligaments.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Human body is composed of different types of tissues. They are soft and elastic like skin, fat, muscle and internal organ.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back:
* Any break in the body tissue, whether external or internal.
* It is considered a single pathological entity.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does velocity influence the mechanism of wound production?
back:
* Determined by Kinetic Energy ($K.E.=1/2mv^2$).
* High velocity (e.g., bullets) produces significantly more tissue damage than larger, slower objects.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv^2.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast direct versus indirect manners of weapon execution.
back:
* Direct: Injury occurs at the exact site of impact.
* Indirect: Injury occurs at a site remote from contact (e.g., clavicle fracture from falling on an outstretched hand).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution of weapon; direct and indirect... indirect causes injury at a place away from site of impact.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain why a blunt strike causes a laceration on the head but a bruise on the buttocks.
back:
* Tissue Architecture: Scalp is thin and stretched over rigid bone, facilitating a split (laceration).
* Soft tissue/fat in buttocks absorbs force, causing internal bleeding (bruise) without breaking skin.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the age of the subject affect bone fracture mechanisms?
back:
* Infants: Bones are more elastic, leading to greenstick fractures or indentations.
* Adults/Elderly: Bones are brittle and break easily upon impact.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the defining mechanical feature of a moving abrasion?
back:
* Heaping or piling up of the epidermis at the far end of the injury.
* Indicates the specific direction of the abrasive force.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Compare wound outcomes for a strike to a stationary head versus a moving head.
back:
* Stationary: Localized trauma at the site of contact (scalp/skull damage).
* Moving: Hitting a stationary object causes widespread, diffuse brain trauma (acceleration/deceleration injury).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury... In a moving head hitting a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is widespread.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How do internal organ consistencies affect their mechanism of injury?
back:
* Solid organs (liver, spleen): Shatter or rupture upon impact.
* Hollow organs (bladder, stomach): May burst if filled with fluid/air due to hydrostatic pressure changes.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Lungs are spongy... Stomach, intestine... are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids... they have different behavior character.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the mechanism of a 'split' or 'crush' laceration?
back:
* Skin is caught between a blunt weapon (object) and an underlying bone (subject).
* The skin is compressed until it splits through its full thickness.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split, also called crush laceration... Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues betweenn the weapon and the underlying bone split them.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the two primary factor categories that control the shape of a mechanical injury?
back:
1. Factors in the weapon (object) - weight, velocity, type.
2. Factors in the part struck (subject) - tissue elasticity, architecture, movement.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How is a wound defined from a medical point of view?
back: Any break in the body tissue, whether externally or internally. Medically, the terms "wound" and "injury" are synonymous and represent a single pathological entity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How do weight and velocity interact to determine wound severity?
back: They determine Kinetic Energy (K.E.=1/2mv²). Higher velocity (like a bullet) produces greater injury compared to a slower, heavier object (like a stone).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv².]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast direct versus indirect manners of weapon execution.
back:
* Direct: Injury occurs at the specific site of contact.
* Indirect: Injury occurs at a site distant from contact (e.g., clavicle fracture following a fall on an outstretched hand).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [direct and indirect. Direct causes injury at contact site and indirect causes injury at a place away from contact example fracture of clavicle produced by fall on hand.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
coreConcept: Impact of tissue architecture on wounding
front: Q: A club strike causes a scalp laceration but only a buttock bruise. Why?
back: Architecture of the part (subject) determines shape. Scalp is stretched over rigid bone, causing splitting (laceration), while buttocks have soft, elastic fat and muscle that absorb force (bruise).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club, a blunt weapon, having same force on different body parts having different architecture will produce different shaped injuries i.e. on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the movement of the subject part affect wounding outcomes?
back: A strike to a stationary part (e.g., the head) produces more localized, severe damage at the contact site compared to a part that is already in motion.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Movement of the part also affects the outcome. Difference can be appreciated by noting injuries produced when the part is stationary or in motion. It is best manifested when a body cavity like head or chest is involved.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the two primary categories of factors controlling injury shape?
back:
* Factors in the weapon (Object): Type, weight, velocity, manner of execution.
* Factors in the part struck (Subject): Architecture and movement.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients, (Table 6.1)]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How do solid and hollow organs (subject) respond differently to contact?
back:
* Solid organs (liver, spleen): Often crushed or ruptured.
* Hollow organs (stomach, heart): Contain fluids of different densities that transmit pressure waves.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Stomach, intestine, heart, gall and urinary bladder are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids of different density in them]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: A body is dragged against a rough road. What specific wound mechanism occurs?
back: Moving abrasion (graze). Friction between the skin (subject) and the rough object (object) causes irregular removal of the epidermis, often piling it at the far end.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of "local deformation" in skull fracturing.
back: Force forms a shallow cone. The apex stretches the inner-table (fracturing it first) and compresses the outer-table. Larger force eventually fractures both tables.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. Apex of cone stretches the inner-table and compresses the outer table... inner-table at the apex of the cone fractures before the outer table]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What defines the contact mechanism of a "penetrating" wound?
back: It is produced by thrusting a sharp, pointed weapon (object) into a body cavity (subject). The greatest dimension is the internal depth, exceeding length and breadth.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [produced by thrusting sharp edged and pointed weapon into part of the body having a cavity like cranium, chest and abdomen... depth, which is the greatest dimension]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a wound or injury?
back:
- Any break in the body tissue.
- Can be external (skin and underlying tissue) or internal (serous membranes and organs).
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view. any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How do the object's (weapon) weight and velocity influence wound appearance?
back:
- They determine the Kinetic Energy (K.E. = 1/2 mv²).
- Higher velocity or weight produces greater tissue damage and influences wound shape.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv².]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast a blunt strike on the head (scalp) versus the buttocks.
back:
- Head: Produces a laceration because the scalp is stretched over hard bone.
- Buttocks: Produces a bruise due to soft tissue architecture (fat/muscle).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Describe the wounding mechanism when a stationary head is struck by a moving weapon.
back:
- Produces local injury at the contact site.
- Damage may extend to deeper structures through force transmission.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact and damage may extend even to deeper structures.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Differentiate between direct and indirect execution of force in wounding.
back:
- Direct: Injury occurs at the impact site.
- Indirect: Injury occurs distant from impact (e.g., clavicle fracture from a fall on the hand).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution... direct and indirect. Indirect causes injury at a place away from the site of contact.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the three primary factors controlling the shape of a mechanical injury?
back:
- The Object (Weapon factors).
- The Subject (Part struck factors).
- The Contact (Manner of execution).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury each having its ingredients. (Table 6.1) a. Factors in weapon: b. Factors in part struck:]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does bone elasticity affect the outcome of a mechanical strike?
back:
- Slight force within elastic limits causes indentation and recoil without breaking.
- Force beyond elastic limits causes fracture at the point of maximum convexity.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Slight force within the limit of bone elasticity will cause a local indentation... without breaking bone... Greater force beyond the limit of bone elasticity will cause a break.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain why a moving head hitting a stationary object causes specific trauma patterns.
back:
- Resultant trauma depends on deceleration forces.
- Often results in injuries distant from the contact point (e.g., contre-coup injuries).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [in the case of head in motion striking a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head and also its internal contents is far more serious.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How do organ consistencies (solid vs. hollow) affect internal wound production?
back:
- Solid (liver/spleen): Prone to bruising or rupture.
- Hollow (stomach/bladder): Damage depends on the density of fluid/semi-solid contents.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Stomach, intestine, heart... are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids of different density... these organs have different behavior character.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What defines 'direct' injury mechanism during weapon execution?
back: - The injury is produced precisely at the site of contact with the weapon.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [direct... causes injury at the site of contact.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What two primary factors control the resulting shape and appearance of a mechanical injury?
back:
* The weapon used (object)
* The body part struck (subject)
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the velocity of an object disproportionately influence the kinetic energy of a wound?
back:
* Calculated by $K.E. = 1/2mv^2$
* Doubling velocity quadruples energy
* High velocity (e.g., bullets) produces significantly more damage than mass alone
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2. A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone bigger in size with less velocity shall produce greater damage]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact

back:
* Scalp: Skin stretched over rigid bone results in a laceration.
* Buttocks: Soft tissue (fat/muscle) absorbs force, resulting in a bruise.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of 'indirect' weapon execution in wound production.
back:
* The injury occurs at a site distant from the point of contact.
* Example: Fracture of the clavicle resulting from a fall onto an outstretched hand.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [indirectly causes injury at a place away from contact e.g. fracture of clavicle produced by fall on the hand]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the 'subject' factor of age alter the mechanism of bone fracturing?
back:
* Infants: Bones are relatively elastic, requiring more force to snap.
* Adults/Elderly: Bones are brittle due to calcification, breaking easily under impact.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the defining characteristic of a 'cavity' subject (e.g., abdomen) in wound production?
back:
* Contains organs of varying density (solid, spongy, or hollow sacs).
* Force transmission depends on fluid/gas content (e.g., blood in heart, air in lungs).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [These cavities have organs in them... Liver, spleen and kidney are solid; Lungs are spongy... Stomach, intestine, heart... are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids of different density]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain the 'Contact' mechanism when a moving head strikes a stationary object.
back:
* Deceleration injury
* Resultant trauma is typically extensive due to the momentum of the subject (head) upon sudden stop.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [a moving head strikes a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is generally extensive]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: In the mechanism of wound production, how does a stationary head react to a moving object?
back:
* Produces local injury at the site of contact.
* Damage may extend deeply to intracranial structures depending on the force of the object.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact and damage may extend even to deeper structures]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does organ consistency (solid vs. hollow) affect wound production in the abdomen?
back:
* Solid organs (liver/spleen) suffer direct parenchymal rupture.
* Hollow organs (stomach/bladder) respond based on the density of internal contents (water, food, or urine).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Because of the design of these organs, they have different behavior character: Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Stomach, intestine... are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids of different density]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the three essential components of 'Object' (weapon) factors in wounding?
back:
* Type (sharp vs. blunt)
* Weight and Velocity (Kinetic Energy)
* Manner of execution (Direct vs. Indirect)
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factors in weapon: Type of weapon... Weight and velocity... Manner of execution]

citation: Page 53 (Book Page): Examples are incised and lacerated wounds produced by sharp edged and blunt edged weapons.

back:
• Stationary: Maximum energy absorbed at contact site (local scalp injury).

back:
Stationary head: Local injury at contact site, possibly extending deep.

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Identify the mechanism and characteristic finding of a 'grinding compression' injury.
back: Passage of a heavy wheel over a limb. Tissues are crushed and moved, causing multiple skin tears and potentially fat embolism.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Caused by the passage of an automobile wheel over limbs... producing grinding compression of the muscles... characteristics of such a wound are multiple tears... precipitate fat embolism.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What sequence leads to the production of an 'over-stretch' laceration?
back: Localized pressure pushes the skin until it is stretched beyond its limit of elasticity, causing a breach (tear).
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Localized pressure along with push... skin is stretched beyond the limit of elasticity and it tears. Characteristics of such laceration are breach of skin.]

front: Q: How does bone age/calcification alter the mechanism of fracture production?
back:
Infants: Elastic bones undergo local indentation and recoil. 
Adults: Brittle, calcified bones break easily at points of maximum convexity.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily... Slight force within the limit of bone elasticity will cause a local indentation... recoil back.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the two primary factors controlling the shape and appearance of a mechanical injury?
back:
- Factors in the weapon (object).
- Factors in the part struck (subject).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does weapon velocity determine the kinetic energy and resultant wound severity?
back:
- Calculated by K.E. = 1/2mv².
- High velocity (e.g., a bullet) causes more damage than a larger, slower object (e.g., a stone).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2. A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone bigger in size with less velocity shall produce greater damage.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why does a strike with a blunt club produce different wounds on the scalp versus the buttocks?
back:
- Scalp: Skin is stretched over bone (architecture), producing a laceration.
- Buttocks: Soft tissue and fat (architecture) produce a bruise.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club, a blunt weapon, having same force on different body parts having different architecture will produce different shaped injuries i.e. on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
coreConcept: Direct vs Indirect Manner of Execution
front: Q: Identify the manner of force execution when a fall on an outstretched hand causes a clavicle fracture.
back:
- Manner: Indirect execution.
- Mechanism: Force is transmitted from the point of contact to a remote, weaker point.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Indirect causes injury at a place away from the site of contact. Fracture of clavicle produced by fall on out stretched hand.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the movement of the head at the moment of contact change the trauma outcome?
back:
- Stationary head: Produces localized injury at the contact site.
- Moving head: Impact against a stationary object produces diffuse trauma and internal brain injury.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact... When the head is in motion and strikes a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is more diffuse.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: List the three components of ballistics used to explain the mechanism of firearm wounding.
back:
- Interior ballistics (inside barrel).
- Exterior ballistics (flight to target).
- Wound-complex ballistics (interaction with body).
citation: Page 68 (Book Page): [Study of understanding of their cause-effect relationship of wounding with them is based upon a knowledge of special ballistics subject having three components: Interior ballistics, Exterior ballistics, Wound-complex ballistics.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What defines the mechanism of a 'split' or 'crush' laceration regarding subject and object?
back:
- Subject: Skin firmly supported by bone.
- Object: Blunt weapon.
- Mechanism: Sudden compression splits the skin between the weapon and bone.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split laceration occurs on scalp, forehead, chin or any other part of the body where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues between the weapon and the underlying bone split them.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: A victim presents with multi-linear skin tears and muscle evisceration after a vehicular run-over. Name the mechanism.
back:
