- Mechanism: Grinding compression.
- Interaction: Rotation of the wheel (object) over a limb (subject) causes tissue ripping and fat embolism risk.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [grinding compression laceration occurs due to rotation of automobile wheel over limbs of the body... characteristics of such a wound are multi-linear skin tears which are also separated from the underlying tissue.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How do 'high velocity' bullets produce damage beyond their own diameter in tissue?
back:
- Mechanism: Temporary cavitation.
- Contact: Rapid dissipation of energy causes tissues to expand and collapse, creating a permanent cavity larger than the bullet.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally... creating instant cavitation... leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why are infants' bones less likely to suffer complete fractures compared to adults?
back:
- Bones are relatively more elastic (subject factor).
- Adult/elderly bones are more brittle and break easily under similar force.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How is a wound medically defined in forensic practice?
back: Any break in body tissue, occurring either externally or internally. The terms 'wound' and 'injury' are synonymous pathological entities.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How do weapon weight and velocity determine kinetic energy in wounding?
back: Kinetic energy (K.E. = 1/2mv²) dictates damage. A high-velocity, small-mass projectile (bullet) can produce significantly greater tissue destruction than a larger, slow-moving object.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv².]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast the wound produced by blunt force on the scalp versus the buttocks.
back: Architecture determines the shape: a blunt strike produces a laceration on the scalp (skin stretched over bone) but a bruise on the buttocks (thick soft tissue).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the mechanism of injury when a moving head strikes a stationary object?
back: This is a deceleration injury. The force is generalized throughout the cranial cavity, often causing internal damage distant from the impact site (contre-coup).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [In the case of a moving head striking a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is more generalized.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Define the indirect manner of weapon execution in wounding.
back: Indirect execution causes injury at a site remote from the point of impact, such as a clavicle fracture resulting from a fall on an outstretched hand.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution of infliction of weapon; direct and indirect. The later causes injury at a place away from the site of impact example fracture of clavicle produced by fall on the out-stretched hand.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: List the three architectural categories of human tissue relative to elasticity.
back:
1. Soft/Elastic: Skin, muscle, fat, organs.
2. Rigid/Less Elastic: Ligaments, cartilage.
3. Hard/Limited Elastic: Bones (elasticity varies with age).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Human body is composed of different types of tissues. They are soft and elastic like skin, fat, muscle... relatively rigid and less elastic like ligament... and hard and limited elastic like bones.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does movement of the 'Subject' affect the outcome of a strike?
back: A strike to a stationary part results in localized damage at the contact point, whereas a strike during motion causes generalized force distribution and internal trauma.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Movement of the part also affects the outcome... A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact... whereas in the case of a moving head... the resultant trauma... is more generalized.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Compare the wounding potential of blunt force on solid versus hollow organs.
back: Solid organs (liver/spleen) are prone to rupture upon impact, while hollow organs (stomach/bladder) respond based on the density and volume of their fluid contents.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Stomach, intestine, heart, gall and urinary bladder are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids of different density in them... shapes along with size and density of bone have relation to the outcome.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why do infant bones resist fractures more effectively than elderly bones?
back: Higher elasticity. Slight force within the limit of bone elasticity causes temporary indentation followed by recoil without breaking, whereas brittle elderly bones fracture easily.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Slight force within the limit of bone elasticity will cause a local indentation at site of impact withoutt breaking bone and then recoil back to its original shape... Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What defines a 'Penetrating' wound regarding the mechanism of contact?
back: It is produced by thrusting a sharp-edged, pointed weapon into a body cavity. The depth is always the greatest dimension of the wound.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Penetrating & puncturing wound is produced by thrusting sharp edged and pointed weapon into part of the body having a cavity like cranium, chest and abdomen which gets pierced... the depth, which is the greatest dimension.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Define a medical abrasion.
back: An injury involving the mechanical removal of the epidermis caused by a blunt weapon or rough surface.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is an injury caused by the mechanical removal of the epidermis by a blunt weapon or rough surface.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the morphological feature indicating force direction in moving abrasions.
back: The epidermis is heaped or piled up at the far end of the injury.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Contrast ante-mortem and post-mortem abrasions.
back: Ante-mortem abrasions show vital reaction; post-mortem abrasions appear dry and lack vital reaction.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Anle-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction... Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying gives a different appearance.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: A victim is dragged across a rough road. Classify this injury.
back: It is a moving abrasion, specifically classified as a graze.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: How is an imprint abrasion formed?
back: By a strike or contact with a rough object, like a shoe-heel, that mimics the object's pattern.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like shoe-heel or ligature abrasion by hard ligature material around neck.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What are the three primary types of abrasions based on mechanism?
back:
1. Moving abrasion
2. Imprint abrasion
3. Friction abrasion
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion; Imprint abrasion; Friction abrasion]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: In a hanging case, why is the ligature mark considered an imprint abrasion?
back: It shows indentation and frictional rub that provides corroborative evidence of the causative agent.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub. Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: A corpse shows dry, parchment-like skin on the neck without inflammation. Identify the timing.
back: Post-mortem abrasion (occurred after death due to rough handling or rubbing).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem removal of epidermis by rough handling of corpse or rubbing against hard object occurs during postmortem period... lacks vital reaction.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the timeline for scab formation and shedding in an abrasion.
back: Soft scab forms in 2 days; hardens in 3-4 more days; retracts and falls off by 7-10 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What dictates the color changes in the effused serum of a healing abrasion?
back: The amount of blood mixed with the serum, ranging from straw to yellow to brown.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown, depending upon the amount of blood.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Define "Abrasion" from a medical perspective.
back: Removal of the surface layer (epidermis) of the skin or mucous membrane caused by the strike of a blunt weapon or rough surface.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Abrasion is defined as, “removal of the surface layer (epidermis) of the skin or mucous membrane due to the strike of a blunt weapon or rough surface.”

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: List the three main types of abrasions based on mechanism.
back:
1. Moving abrasion
2. Imprint abrasion
3. Friction abrasion
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Type of abrasion on the basis of mechanism of its causation are of three types: Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What feature of a moving abrasion indicates the direction of force?
back: Heaping or piling up of the epidermis at the far end of the wound.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Differentiate between a "scratch" and a "graze".
back:
• Scratch: Caused by a sharp-pointed object (fingernail, pin).
• Graze: Caused by dragging against rough objects (e.g., road in traffic accidents).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail pin or thorn. Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Define "Imprint Abrasion" and its forensic value.
back:
• Definition: Caused by a strike of a rough object (e.g., shoe-heel) or hard ligature.
• Value: Its pattern identifies the specific causative weapon/agent.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Imprint abrasion is caused by strike of a rough object on skin like sheo-heel or frictional abrasion by hard ligature material around neck. Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What is the typical color progression of drying serum in a fresh abrasion?
back: Ranges from straw to yellow to brown, depending on the amount of blood mixed with the serum.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown, depending upon the amount of blood.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Outline the chronological healing stages of a scab in an abrasion.
back:
• Soft scab: ~2 days.
• Hard scab: 4-6 days.
• Retraction/Falling off: 7-10 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: How is an antemortem abrasion distinguished from a postmortem one?
back: Antemortem abrasions show vital reaction (congestion/exudation), whereas postmortem abrasions become dry, brownish, and parchment-like.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying acquire a brown parchment like appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: A victim dragged by a vehicle shows wide, irregular epidermal loss. Name the lesion.
back: Graze (a form of moving abrasion).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What type of abrasion is characteristic of hanging or strangulation?
back: Imprint abrasion (often showing indentation and frictional rub from the ligature).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Which specific layer of the skin is destroyed in the production of an abrasion?
back: The most superficial layer, known as the epidermis.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is destruction and removal of the most superficial layer of the skin (epidermis) by blunt weapon.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the mechanism by which a 'moving abrasion' indicates the direction of force.
back: The abrasive force scrapes the skin, causing the epidermis to heap or pile up at the far end.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Contrast the production mechanism of a graze with a scratch.
back:
- Scratch: Scrape from a fingernail, pin, or thorn.
- Graze: Result of body surface dragging against a rough object (e.g., a road).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail pin or thorn. Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: How is the mechanism of a graze typically produced in clinical forensic scenarios?
back: The body surface is dragged across a rough object, commonly seen in vehicular accidents.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What are the two distinct mechanical steps involved in producing a ligature-based imprint abrasion?
back:
1. Indentation (static pressure from the ligature).
2. Frictional rub (movement between the skin and ligature).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the primary diagnostic criterion used to differentiate ante-mortem from post-mortem abrasions?
back: The presence of a vital reaction in ante-mortem injuries.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion especially when on vital region like neck... Ante-moriem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Apply the principle of epithelial heaping to determine the terminal point of an abrasive strike.
back: The far end (terminal point) is identified by the side where the epidermis has piled up.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Differentiate post-mortem neck abrasions from homicidal throttling in the case of a victim wearing jewelry.
back: Post-mortem jewelry abrasions occur from rough handling/drying and lack vital reaction; throttling shows internal and external vital markers.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem removal of epidermis by rough handling of corpse or rubbing against hard object occurs... Ante-moriem abrasion shows vital reaction. Example is a case of newly wedded women... had three post-mortem abrasions... caused by heavy sliver necklace. Police during initial inquiry labeled her death due to throttling.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Outline the chronological physiological changes in an abrasion's effused serum during the first week.
back:
- Day 1-2: Formation of a soft scab (serum mixed with blood).
- Day 3-6: The scab hardens.
- Day 7-10: Scab retracts and falls away.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [It is followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Define the core mechanism that produces an 'imprint abrasion'.
back: A strike from a rough object or pressure from hard material that results in an indentation reflecting the object's shape.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [imprint abrasion is caused by strike of a rough object on skin like shoe-heel or by hard ligature material around neck. Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Define a medical abrasion.
back: - A closed mechanical injury involving destruction and removal of the skin's superficial layer (epidermis) by blunt force trauma.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is a closed wound of the body surface caused by the strike of a blunt weapon. It consists of the destruction and removal of the superficial layer of the skin (epidermis).]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Classify the three primary types of abrasions based on mechanism.
back:
1. Moving abrasion
2. Imprint abrasion
3. Friction abrasion
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Type of abrasions are: Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the defining characteristic of a moving abrasion.
back: - Shows direction of force by heaping up or piling of epithelial cells at the far end of the injury.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Contrast a 'scratch' from a 'graze' moving abrasion.
back:
- Scratch: Caused by a point (fingernail, pin, thorn).
- Graze: Irregular epithelial removal from dragging against rough objects (road accidents).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail pin or thorn. Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging such as road as seen vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What defines an 'imprint abrasion' in medicolegal practice?
back: - A pattern abrasion caused by vertical strike or pressure where the mark reflects the shape of the causative agent (e.g., shoe-heel).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like sheo-heel... Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Differentiate ante-mortem from post-mortem abrasions.
back:
- Ante-mortem: Presence of vital reaction (swelling/inflammation).
- Post-mortem: Lacks vital reaction; acquires a dry, parchment-like appearance.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying has parchment appearance. Ante-moriem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the chronological color changes in an abrasion's effused serum.
back: - Varies from straw to yellow to brown, depending on the volume of blood mixed with serum.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown, depending upon the amount of blood.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Outline the timeline for scab hardening and detachment in abrasions.
back:
- Soft scab: forms in ~2 days.
- Hardens: in ~3-4 days.
- Falls off: in ~7-8 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: A corpse has parchment-like neck marks without vital reaction. Diagnosis?
back: - Post-mortem abrasion (likely due to rough handling or jewelry rubbing after death).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem removal of epidermis by rawgh handling of corpse... Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying has parchment appearance. Ante-moriem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What characterizes a ligature imprint abrasion in hanging?
back: - Shows both indentation and frictional rub, with the pattern reflecting the specific ligature material.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub. Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Define an abrasion from a medicolegal perspective.
back:
- A closed mechanical injury caused by blunt force
- Characterized by the removal of the epidermis
- The deeper layer of the dermis remains intact.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is a closed mechanical injury caused by blunt force applied to the skin surface. It is resultant from frictional rub causing removal of the epidermis, while the deeper layer of the dermis remains intact.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the pathological mechanism of a moving abrasion.
back:
- Abrasive force moves across the skin surface
- Results in heaping or piling up of the epidermis at the far end of the injury.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end. Appearance is characteristic.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Differentiate between a scratch and a graze.
back:
- Scratch: Produced by a sharp/pointed object (fingernail, pin, thorn)
- Graze: Irregular epidermal removal from dragging against rough surfaces (e.g., road in accidents).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail, pin or thorn. Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: A victim shows irregular epidermal loss and dirt embedded in the skin. Identify the injury type.
back:
- Graze (a form of moving abrasion)
- Common in vehicular accidents due to body surface dragging.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Outline the chronological steps of scab formation in an abrasion.
back:
- Soft scab: Forms in approximately 2 days
- Hard scab: Occurs in another 3 to 4 days
- Retraction/Falling off: Takes another 3 to 4 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [It is followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: List the three primary varieties used to classify abrasions.
back:
1. Moving abrasion
2. Imprint abrasion
3. Friction abrasion
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [There are three varieties of abrasions; Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Explain the diagnostic significance of an imprint abrasion.
back:
- Caused by a rough object's strike or hard ligature
- Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of the specific causative weapon (e.g., shoe-heel).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like shoe-heel. Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: How is an antemortem abrasion differentiated from a postmortem one?
back:
- Antemortem: Shows vital reaction (hyperemia/effused serum)
- Postmortem: Lacks vital reaction and assumes a dark brown, parchment-like appearance upon drying.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion especially when on vital region like neck. Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying assume a different appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the color changes in effused serum used for dating an abrasion.
back:
- Varies from straw to yellow to brown
- Dependent on the amount of blood mixed with the serum and time elapsed.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown, depending upon the amount of blood.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Which specific anatomic structure is removed in a friction abrasion?
back: The epidermis.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion... resultant from frictional rub causing removal of the epidermis, while the deeper layer of the dermis remains intact.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What is the medical definition of an abrasion?
back:
* Superficial mechanical injury.
* Involves only the epidermis of the skin.
* Caused by friction or strike of a blunt weapon.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Wounding involving only epidermis is called an abrasion. It is the purest form of superficial mechanical injury caused by friction or a strike of a blunt weapon.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Explain the mechanism behind a moving abrasion (graze).
back:
* Abrasive force moves across skin surface.
* Removes epidermis irregularly.
* Shows heaping or piling up of skin on the far end.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end. Appearance is characteristic... irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging... also called a graze.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Contrast a moving abrasion from an imprint abrasion.
back:
* Moving: Shows direction; heaping of skin at distal end; includes scratches/grazes.
* Imprint: No direction; reflects shape of rough object; includes ligature marks/shoe-heels.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end... Page 55 (Book Page): imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like shoe-heel... Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: A victim is found with irregular skin removal on the arm after a vehicular drag. Identify the injury.
back:
* Type: Graze (Moving abrasion).
* Feature: Irregular removal of epidermis.
* Clinical sign: Heaping of skin at the end indicates direction of movement.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Outline the chronological steps of scab formation in an abrasion.
back:
* Day 2: Soft scab forms from dry fluid.
* Day 5-6: Scab hardens.
* Day 8-10: Hard scab retracts and eventually falls away.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What are the diagnostic criteria for an antemortem abrasion?
back:
* Presence of vital reaction (swelling/redness).
* Congestion in surrounding tissues.
* Effusion of serum mixed with blood.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction... Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum, which occasionally may also get mixed with blood.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Apply the concept of imprint abrasions to the diagnosis of hanging.
back:
* Ligature mark: An imprint abrasion.
* Features: Shows indentation and frictional rub.
* Value: Pattern reflects the texture and shape of the hard ligature material.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub. Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: How do you differentiate a postmortem abrasion from an antemortem one?
back:
* Antemortem: Shows vital reaction and hyperemia.
* Postmortem: Lacks vital reaction; initially pale; dries into a brown, parchment-like, translucent area.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Post-mortem abrasion... with passage of time after drying presents translucent appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the physiological fluid progression in a fresh abrasion.
back:
* Rupture of superficial vessels.
* Effusion of serum (may mix with blood).
* Drying of fluid: Color shifts from straw/yellow to brown.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown, depending upon the amount of blood.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: List the three primary types of abrasions based on mechanism.
back:
1. Moving abrasion (e.g., scratches, grazes).
2. Imprint abrasion (e.g., patterned strikes).
3. Friction abrasion (e.g., rubbing injuries).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion... Imprint abrasion... Friction abrasion.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Define an abrasion according to its mechanical production.
back: A closed wound involving a breach of only the surface layer (epidermis), caused by the strike of a blunt weapon.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is a closed wound showing breach of only surface layer of the skin, the epidermis, caused by a strike of blunt weapon.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the primary mechanism of a moving abrasion (graze)?
back: Friction or dragging against a rough object, characterized by the heaping or piling up of the epidermis at the far end.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end... dragging against the rough object such as road... graze.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Contrast the production of imprint abrasions versus moving abrasions.
back:
• Imprint: Perpendicular strike by a rough object.
• Moving: Parallel friction or dragging across a surface.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like sheo-heel... Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: In a forensic examination, how do you determine force direction in a graze?
back: By identifying the site where the epidermis is 'piled up'; the heaping occurs at the destination point of the force.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What chemical changes occur in the healing of an abrasion?
back:
• 0-2 days: Effused serum dries into a soft scab.
• 2-6 days: Scab hardens.
• 7-10 days: Hard scab retracts and falls off.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown... It is followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Identify the diagnostic criteria for an ante-mortem abrasion.
back: Presence of a vital reaction (hyperemia or hemorrhage) and exudation of serum, distinguishing it from post-mortem parchment-like changes.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Anle-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction. Post-mortem abrasion... after drying presents parchment like appearance.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Apply the mechanism of 'imprint abrasion' to a hanging case.
back: The hard ligature material (e.g., rope) exerts pressure against the neck skin, causing both indentation and a frictional rub.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Why is the 'heaping' of the epidermis a hard differential in forensic cases?
back: It requires distinguishing between fresh epidermal tags (ante-mortem) and post-mortem rough handling which lacks inflammatory response.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem removal of epidermis by rawgh handling of corpse or rubbing against hard object occurs during postmortem period... Anle-moriem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: How is 'friction abrasion' technically produced during constriction?
back: Through a frictional rub caused by sliding or tightening an object against the skin, often combined with indentation.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Frictional rub and indentation of neck skin... produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck... shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What anatomic layer is specifically spared in a mechanical abrasion?
back: The dermis and deeper tissues; abrasions only breach the superficial epidermis.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is a closed wound showing breach of only surface layer of the skin, the epidermis.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Define an abrasion and identify the primary skin layer involved in its production.
back: An abrasion is a closed wound resulting from mechanical removal of the epidermis by impact with a blunt force or rough object.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Abrasion is a closed wound... caused by the mechanical removal of the surface layer (epidermis) of the skin by the impact of a blunt weapon or rough object.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of a moving abrasion and how it indicates force direction.
back: Friction against a rough surface (e.g., road) causes irregular removal of epidermis, heaping or piling up the skin at the far end.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Contrast the visual diagnostic features of ante-mortem versus post-mortem abrasions.
back: Ante-mortem: Shows vital reaction (redness/scab). Post-mortem: Becomes yellow, translucent, and parchment-like after drying, lacking vital inflammatory response.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying gives a parchment appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: A victim presents with a patterned neck abrasion resembling a rope weave. Identify the specific type.
back: This is an imprint abrasion. The skin records the pattern of a rough object (like ligature material) providing corroborative evidence.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck... pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the sequence of scab maturation used to estimate the age of an abrasion?
back:
1. Soft scab: 2 days.
2. Hardened scab: 3-4 additional days.
3. Retraction and falling off: Another 3-4 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Classify abrasions into three main categories based on the specific mechanism of infliction.
back:
1. Moving abrasion (Graze/Scratch).
2. Imprint abrasion.
3. Friction abrasion.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Mechanisms of production of abrasions are of three types: Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: How can a heavy silver necklace on a corpse produce a false throttling indicator?
back: Post-mortem removal of the epidermis by jewelry rubbing during handling creates an abrasion that dries and simulates throttling without vital reaction.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): She... had three post-mortem abrasions; two in front of the neck... caused by heavy sliver necklace. Police during initial inquiry labeled her death due to throttling.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Differentiate between a scratch and a graze based on the wounding implement used.
back: Scratch: Produced by a sharp point (e.g., fingernail, pin). Graze: Produced by body dragging across broad, rough objects (e.g., road).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail, pin or thorn. Another example is... dragging against the rough object such as road... also called a graze.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the early physiological changes in the effused serum of an abrasion.
back: Serum effuses at the site, mixes with blood, and dries into a fluid varying from straw to yellow or brown.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Why are superficial abrasions considered low-yield for permanent scarring?
back: Because they involve only the epidermis, they heal rapidly through serum effusion and scab formation without leaving a permanent mark.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Age of abrasion is difficult especially when superficial. It heals rapidly leaving no permanent mark.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Define an abrasion based on the depth of tissue involvement.
back: A superficial injury involving only the removal of the epidermis of the skin.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is defined as a superficial injury involving removal of the epidermis only.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the primary mechanical mechanism that produces an abrasion?
back: Mechanical impact or friction caused by a blunt weapon or contact with a rough surface.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [It is produced by mechanical impact of a blunt weapon or contact with rough surface.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: How is the direction of force determined in a moving abrasion?
back: By observing the heaping or piling up of the epidermis on the far end of the injury.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: A victim presents with a 'graze' after a road accident. Describe the production mechanism.
back: Irregular removal of the epidermis occurring as the body surface drags against a rough object.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What defines the mechanism of production for an 'imprint' abrasion?
back: A vertical strike or pressure from a rough object, mimicking the pattern of the causative agent.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like shoe-heel etc. Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the defining microscopic or visual difference between antemortem and postmortem abrasions?
back: Antemortem abrasions exhibit vital reactions (reddening/scabbing); postmortem abrasions appear yellow/brown and parchment-like.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Anle-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction. ...Postmortem abrasion with passage of time after drying acquires yellow to brown parchment like appearance.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Explain the mechanism behind a 'friction abrasion' seen in hanging cases.
back: Pressure from hard ligature material causing both indentation and a frictional rub on the neck skin.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: A woman's corpse has neck marks from a heavy necklace. Why might these be mistaken for throttling?
back: Postmortem handling or rubbing against hard jewelry causes abrasions that mimic antemortem violence.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem removal of epidermis by rough handling of corpse or rubbing against hard object occurs during postmortem period. Postmortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion especially when on vital region like neck.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the sequence of serum changes used to estimate the age of an abrasion.
back: Effused serum dries (straw/yellow/brown) → soft scab (2 days) → hard scab (3-4 more days) → retraction.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum ... followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Which specific layers are lost during the production of a scratch abrasion?
back: The epidermis is removed, typically via a sharp point like a fingernail, pin, or thorn.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail, pin or thorn.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Define an 'Abrasion' from a forensic medical perspective.
back: A superficial mechanical injury characterized exclusively by the removal of the epidermis due to friction or pressure.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is a superficial mechanical injury involving the skin... it is a result of friction or pressure against the body surface leading to the removal of the epidermis.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the general mechanical mechanism of abrasion production.
back: It is caused by a blunt strike or interaction with a rough surface, resulting in the scraping or crushing of skin without breaking deeper tissues.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Wounding when caused mechanically is called mechanical injuries... caused by the mechanical strike of a blunt weapon or rough surface against the body... result of friction or pressure.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Differentiate the mechanisms of 'Moving' versus 'Imprint' abrasions.
back:
• Moving: Directional friction (e.g., scratches/grazes).
• Imprint: Direct vertical pressure replicating the object's shape (e.g., shoe heel).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page)-55: [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force... Imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like shoe-heel... Its pattern provides corroborative evidence.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: A victim is dragged on asphalt during a car crash. Identify the abrasion type and mechanism.
back: The injury is a 'Graze,' a form of moving abrasion caused by directional friction against a rough surface.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: How is the direction of force determined in a moving abrasion?
back: By observing the heaping or 'piling up' of the epidermis, which occurs at the far end of the stroke.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: List the diagnostic criteria for a patterned imprint abrasion.
back:
• Strike by a rough object.
• Replicates the object's shape/surface characters.
• Caused by vertical pressure.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin... Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Identify the mechanism and classification of a hard ligature mark in hanging.
back: Classified as an imprint abrasion, caused by mechanical indentation and frictional rub against the neck skin.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Differentiate ante-mortem abrasions from post-mortem ones based on morphology.
back:
• Ante-mortem: Shows vital reaction (redness/exudate).
• Post-mortem: Dry, parchment-like appearance due to post-death drying.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem abrasion... with passage of time after drying presents parchment appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Outline the chronological healing stages (scab formation) of an abrasion.
back:
• Soft scab: ~2 days.
• Hard scab: ~4-5 days.
• Scab retraction/fall: ~7-10 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Which specific anatomical layer is affected in a simple abrasion?
back: The Epidermis only; the continuity of the underlying dermis remains intact.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is a superficial mechanical injury... it is a result of friction or pressure against the body surface leading to the removal of the epidermis.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the fundamental mechanical mechanism of an abrasion?
back: The removal of the superficial layer of the skin (epidermis) caused by the mechanical application of force against the body surface.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Abrasion is removal of the superficial layer of the skin (epidermis). It is caused by mechanical application of force against the body surface.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: How is a "moving abrasion" mechanically produced?
back: It results from force applied linearly, causing the epidermis to heap or pile up at the terminal end of the force.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What characterizes the mechanism of a "graze" in road accidents?
back: Irregular removal of the epidermis occurring when the body surface is dragged against a rough object, such as a road.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: A victim presents with a patterned mark matching a shoe-heel. Identify the mechanism.
back: Imprint abrasion; produced by a strike or perpendicular pressure of a rough object against the skin surface.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like sheo-heel or abrasion by hard ligature material around neck.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What two mechanical forces create a ligature mark in hanging cases?
back:
1. Indentation (perpendicular pressure).
2. Frictional rub (sliding pressure against the skin).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: How is a "scratch" mechanically differentiated from other abrasions?
back: It is a moving abrasion specifically produced by a sharp-pointed object like a fingernail, pin, or thorn.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Appearance is characteristic. Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail pin or thorn.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What determines the color changes in a healing abrasion?
back: The drying of effused serum (sometimes mixed with blood), changing from straw-colored to yellow or brown.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Compare the mechanism of ante-mortem vs post-mortem abrasions.
back:
1. Ante-mortem: Shows vital reaction (inflammation/scab).
2. Post-mortem: Result of rough handling; skin dries to a dark brown appearance without vital reaction.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Postmortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion... Post-mortem abrasion shows with passage of time after drying a dark brown appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the timeline for scab formation in the mechanism of abrasion repair.
back:
1. Soft scab: Forms in approximately 2 days.
2. Hard scab: Forms in 3-4 additional days.
3. Retraction: Occurs in another 3-4 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the most high-yield diagnostic feature of a moving abrasion?
back: The piling up of the epidermis at the far end, which confirms the direction of the causative force.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the anatomical definition and primary tissue involvement in the production of an abrasion?
back: * Superficial injury involving epidermis only* Caused by friction or pressure against a rough object* Results in loss of skin continuity.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Abrasion is an injury, which results from the loss of continuity of the epidermis caused by friction or pressure of a rough object.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the mechanical process leading to the parchment-like appearance of postmortem abrasions.
back: * Loss of epidermis occurs after death* Exposed dermis undergoes rapid evaporation* Results in a dry, yellow, leather-like texture.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying produces a parchment appearance. ...Post-mortem abrasion lacks vital reaction.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Contrast the forensic significance of antemortem versus postmortem abrasions in trauma cases.
back: * Antemortem: Shows vital reaction (inflammation/swelling)* Postmortem: Lacks vital reaction; often caused by rough handling/jewelry.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion lacks vital reaction. ...Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: A hanging victim presents with a neck groove showing indentation and frictional rub. Identify the mechanism.
back: * Imprint abrasion* Caused by direct pressure of hard ligature material (rope)* Pattern matches the causative agent's surface.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the biological step-wise transition of effused serum in the healing of an abrasion.
back: * Serum dries to straw-yellow fluid* Soft scab formation (~2 days)* Hard scab development (~4-5 days)* Scab retraction/shedding (~7-10 days).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the primary diagnostic criterion used to estimate the age of an abrasion?
back: * Condition and color of the scab* Extent of serum drying* Degree of scab retraction from margins.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days... Hard scab retracts in another three or four days.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Apply the mechanism of epidermal removal to explain why grazes are extensive in vehicular accidents.
back: * Significant friction during body surface dragging* Large-scale irregular removal of the epidermis* Often contains environmental debris (grit).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: A deceased with a heavy silver necklace has neck marks. Distinguish these from homicidal throttling.
back: * These are postmortem abrasions* Caused by jewelry rubbing during handling* Lacks internal muscle bruising/vital reaction.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem removal of epidermis by rough handling of corpse... she, besides vaginal damage also had three post-mortem abrasions... on the neck... caused by heavy sliver necklace.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: Explain the physiological loop of scab retraction and shedding in epidermal repair.
back: * New epidermis grows beneath the protective layer* Scab shrinks as it dries further* Eventually falls away without leaving permanent scars.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [It heals rapidly leaving no permanent mark. ...Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Describe mechanism of production of abrasions
front: Q: What is the macroscopic effect produced on the skin by the mechanism of an imprint abrasion?
back: * Mirror image or pattern of the object* Results from direct crushing strike* Example: Patterned shoe-heel marks.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [imprint abrasion is caused by strike of a rough object on skin like shoe-heel... Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Define an abrasion and state which specific layer of skin is removed.
back:
- Definition: Injury caused by a rough mechanical weapon or object.
- Layer involved: Epidermis only.
- Characteristics: No scarring upon healing; bleeding is minimal or absent.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Abrasion is removal of the epidermis by a rough mechanical weapon or an object. Abrasion is the simplest form of wounding and does not leave a permanent scar.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What morphological feature in a moving abrasion determines the direction of force?
back:
- Heaping or piling up of the epidermis.
- The epidermis is pushed toward the far end of the injury, indicating the weapon's exit direction.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: How is an imprint abrasion differentiated from a moving abrasion?
back:
- Mechanism: Caused by a direct strike/pressure (imprint) vs. sliding motion (moving).
- Feature: Shows the specific pattern or shape of the causative object (e.g., shoe heel, ligature).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like shoe-heel. Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Identify the specific type of abrasion typically seen in dragging vehicular accidents.
back:
- Type: Graze (a form of moving abrasion).
- Mechanism: Irregular removal of epidermis due to body dragging against rough surfaces like roads.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the unique characteristics of an imprint abrasion produced by a hard ligature.
back:
- Morphological Features: Indentation (groove) and frictional rub.
- Forensic Value: Pattern of the ligature material (e.g., rope weaves) is imprinted on the skin.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What is the primary diagnostic indicator distinguishing ante-mortem from post-mortem abrasions?
back:
- Vital Reaction: Present in ante-mortem abrasions (hyperemia/exudate).
- Post-mortem: Lacks vital reaction and develops a brown, parchment-like appearance due to drying.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying acquires a different appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Name the two specific features of a 'scratch' abrasion type.
back:
- Tool: Fingernails, pins, or thorns.
- Pattern: A linear moving abrasion indicating a sharp or pointed sliding force.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Example of this variety [moving abrasion] is a scratch produced with fingernail pin or thorn.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: A victim presents with a brown, stiff, parchment-like abrasion. Interpret this finding.
back:
- Diagnosis: Post-mortem abrasion.
- Reason: Drying of the denuded skin surface without vital circulation leads to hardening and browning.
citation: Page 140 (Book Page): Denuded area dries rapidly and presents a brown parchment like appearance which may be mistaken for scratches or abrasions.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Outline the chronological aging of a superficial abrasion based on scab formation.
back:
- 0-2 days: Serum effusion/drying into a soft scab.
- 2-4 days: Scab hardens.
- 4-7+ days: Scab retracts and eventually falls away.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What are the three primary categories of abrasions based on mechanism?
back:
1. Moving abrasion.
2. Imprint abrasion.
3. Friction abrasion.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Types of abrasion] Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Name the three primary types of abrasions based on the mechanism of causation.
back:
• Moving abrasion (Graze)
• Imprint abrasion
• Friction abrasion
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Classification of abrasions: Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What morphological feature of a moving abrasion indicates the direction of force?
back: • Heaping or piling up of the epidermis at the far end of the injury.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: How do imprint abrasions assist in identifying the weapon of offense?
back: • They mirror the pattern of the rough object (e.g., shoe-heel or ligature), providing corroborative evidence of the causative agent.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent. Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope... shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: A victim is dragged along a road in a vehicular accident. What specific type of abrasion is this?
back: • A graze (a form of moving abrasion caused by irregular removal of epidermis against a rough object).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the chronologic healing step for a scab in a standard abrasion.
back:
• Soft scab: Forms in about 2 days.
• Hard scab: Develops in 3-4 more days.
• Retraction/Falling: After another 3-4 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: List the diagnostic criteria distinguishing antemortem from postmortem abrasions.
back:
• Antemortem: Shows vital reaction (bleeding/inflammation).
• Postmortem: Dries to a parchment-like appearance; lacks vital reaction.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying gives a different appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: How is the age of a superficial abrasion estimated based on effused serum?
back: • Fluid color changes: Straw to yellow to brown, depending on blood mixture and drying time.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown, depending upon the amount of blood.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: In cases of throttling, what specific marks accompany abrasions on the neck?
back: • Fingernail marks (crescentic scratches) caused by the assailant's pressure.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Appearance is characteristic. Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail pin or thorn.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the tissue fluid process that occurs immediately after an abrasion is sustained.
back: • Serum effusion: Serum leaks from damaged capillaries, which later dries to form a scab.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum, which occasionally may also get mixed with blood.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Define a friction abrasion in the context of forensic pathology.
back: • Abrasion caused by rubbing of a rough object against the skin, often seen alongside indentation in ligature marks.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Name the three primary varieties of mechanical abrasions.
back:
* Moving abrasion (Scratches/Grazes).
* Imprint abrasion (Patterned).
* Friction abrasion (Frictional rub).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Three varieties of mechanical abrasions are recognized; Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: How is the direction of force determined in a moving abrasion?
back:
* The epidermis is detached at the start of the injury.
* It is heaped up/piled at the far end, indicating the direction of weapon movement.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Contrast the weapon characteristics of a scratch versus a graze.
back:
* Scratch: Produced by sharp-pointed objects (fingernail, pin, thorn).
* Graze: Produced by body dragging against broad rough objects (e.g., roads in vehicular accidents).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail, pin or thorn. Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: A victim presents with skin tags at the distal end of a linear abrasion. Interpret the motion.
back:
* The weapon moved from the smooth end towards the end with epidermal heaping.
* Vital in determining relative movement in hit-and-run accidents.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What defines an 'imprint abrasion' and its forensic utility?
back:
* Caused by a perpendicular strike with a rough object.
* The pattern mirrors the object's surface (e.g., tire treads, shoe heel) providing evidence of the causative agent.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like sheo-heel... Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What constitutes a 'friction abrasion' in the context of hanging?
back:
* Combination of skin indentation from pressure.
* Frictional rub from the movement of the ligature material against the neck skin.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: How is an ante-mortem abrasion differentiated from a postmortem one?
back:
* Ante-mortem: Shows vital reaction (redness, hemorrhage, or scab).
* Postmortem: Appears parchment-like, yellow/brown, and lacks inflammatory response.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Postmortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion... with passage of time after drying assume parchment appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Differentiate scavenger 'ant-bite' artifacts from true abrasions.
back:
* Ant-bites: Irregular patches along moist wrinkles, parchment-like, no vital reaction.
* True abrasions: Distinct heaping (if moving) and signs of hemorrhage/inflammation.
citation: Page 140 (Book Page): Denuded area dries rapidly and presents a brown parchment like appearance which may be mistaken for scratches or abrasions.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: State the timeline for soft and hard scab formation in an abrasion.
back:
* Soft scab: ~2 days.
* Hard scab: ~4-6 days.
* Scab retraction/falling away: ~7-10 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What histological finding confirms an abrasion's vital reaction?
back:
* Microscopic invasion of white blood cells (leucocytes) at the injury site.
* Becomes detectable within 4 to 6 hours post-injury.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): another form of vital reaction is initiation of the process of repair. It becomes visible microscopically four to six hours, as invasion of white blood cells at the site of injury.

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What is the defining morphological feature that indicates direction in a moving abrasion?
back: It shows heaping or piling up of the epidermis at the far end of the injury, indicating the direction of abrasive force.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the mechanism and diagnostic value of an imprint abrasion.
back:
● Mechanism: Strike of a rough object or hard material against the skin.
● Diagnostic Value: Provides corroborative evidence of the causative agent (e.g., shoe heel, rope).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like sheo-heel ... Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Contrast the appearance and cause of a graze versus an imprint abrasion.
back:
● Graze: Irregular epidermal removal via dragging/moving against rough objects.
● Imprint: Geometric mark mimicking the striking object via direct vertical compression.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging ... This abrasion is also called a graze.] Page 55 (Book Page): [imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: How do you differentiate a postmortem abrasion from an antemortem one clinically?
back:
● Antemortem: Shows vital reaction (swelling, redness, inflammation).
● Postmortem: Lacks vital reaction and assumes a parchment-like appearance after drying.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion ... Post-mortem abrasion ... after drying assumes parchment appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: List the chronological time-frame for scab progression in a healing abrasion.
back:
● Soft scab: Formed in ~2 days.
● Hard scab: Formed in 3–4 more days.
● Retraction/Falling: Occurs after another 3–4 days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What features define an imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material in hanging?
back: It manifests as a mark showing both indentation (pattern of the material) and frictional rub against the neck skin.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Explain why postmortem abrasions on the neck might lead to forensic errors.
back: They can be mistaken for antemortem throttling injuries, but lack vital reaction; often caused by jewelry or rough handling of the corpse.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion especially when on Vital region like neck... Police during initial inquiry labeled her death due to throttling]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: How does the presence of serum affect the color of an aging abrasion?
back: Drying effused serum (sometimes mixed with blood) causes the abrasion color to transition from straw-yellow to brown.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum ... Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of a Friction Abrasion in the context of ligatures.
back: It involves a sliding or rubbing action of the ligature material against the epidermis, causing superficial erosion often seen alongside indentation.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What specific skin layer is exclusively involved in a mechanical abrasion?
back: The epidermis; abrasions are superficial injuries characterized by the removal of the outermost layer of skin.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasivy force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: What are the three primary types of abrasions based on mechanism?
back:
- Moving abrasion
- Imprint abrasion
- Friction abrasion
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Types of abrasions are; Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: How is the direction of force identified in a moving abrasion?
back: By observing the heaping or piling up of the epidermis on the far end of the injury.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Differentiate between different types of abrasions
front: Q: Contrast a scratch from a graze based on the causative agent.
back:
- Scratch: Produced by fingernails, pins, or thorns.
- Graze: Result of body dragging against rough objects (e.g., roads in accidents).
