category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Describe the internal vascular mechanism of bruise production.
back: Sudden compression ruptures small capillaries in the dermis or subcutaneous layers, allowing blood to extravasate into surrounding interstitial tissues.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Extravasations of blood from the broken small blood vessels (capillaries) are broken and blood from the broken vessels spread into the surrounding tissue.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Contrast the behavior of blood in a bruise versus postmortem lividity upon incision.
back: In a bruise, extravasated blood is in interstitial tissue and cannot be washed away; in lividity, blood remains intravascular and flows out or washes away easily.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Bruise] Blood is present in tissue... cannot be washed away. [Lividity] Blood is within the vessels and when incised, it flows out of the cut mouths of the blood vessel as it is only an accumulation of blood... can be washed away.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: A victim presents with a black eye 24 hours after a scalp strike. Identify this phenomenon.
back: Gravity shifting (ectopic bruise). Extravasated blood moves from the impact site along tissue lines of least resistance under the influence of gravity.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to below region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What enzymatic process causes a bruise to turn greenish after 4–5 days?
back: Tissue enzymes act on extravasated blood to chemically convert hemoglobin into secondary blood pigments (biliverdin/bilirubin).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: List the two essential criteria to diagnose 'pseudo-bruising' during autopsy.
back:
1. Localized postmortem lividity displaced by gas pressure.
2. Total absence of vital reaction (inflammation/swelling).
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Pseudo-bruising may appear in skin, internal organs and other tissue spaces by accommodation of intense localized postmortem lividity. It is due to displacement of internal pools of blood by gas pressure into areas away from actual hypostasis... Area showing pseudo-bruising lacks vital reaction.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Why does 'police battering' cause a deep blue/black color faster than accidental bruising?
back: Repeated strikes to the same site break tissues and interfere with oxygenation/enzyme action, causing rapid darkening rather than standard sequential color changes.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Repeated strikes to body part... breaks body tissues, interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and causes rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue/black color. It should not be confused with normal vital reaction occurring with passage of time.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Distinguish 'Tardieu's spots' from general contusions.
back: Tardieu's spots are internal petechial hemorrhages occurring under serous coverings of organs, specifically characteristic of asphyxial deaths.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): These petechial hemorrhages were noticed first by Tardieu and are identified with his name as Tardieu’s spots. They occur in the substance of the organs, but are more readily seen under their serous coverings.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: How do systemic diseases like liver cirrhosis influence bruise presentation?
back: Diseases causing coagulation defects lead to excessive bleeding, resulting in larger, more severe-looking bruises that may mislead the examiner.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): State of health (coagulation defect, disease of blood vessel and liver cause more bleeding giving false impression about severity).

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: In which specific tissue layer is a bruise anatomically located?
back: Interstitial tissue (dermis) or subcutaneous tissue, as the epidermis is avascular and cannot bleed.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Lies in the inter-statius tissue below epidermis or even deeper to it, as epidermis is without blood vessels.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Define a bruise (contusion) in the context of forensic mechanical wounding.
back: A closed wound caused by blunt force impact. It involves tissue indentation and recoil, resulting in swelling and pain without breaking the skin surface.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Bruise also called contusion is a closed wound caused by strike of a blunt weapon. It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil. Area struck becomes swollen, red and painful withoutt solution of continuity of covering skin.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism that creates a bruise?
back: Blunt impact ruptures small capillaries. This leads to the extravasation of blood from the broken vessels into the surrounding interstitial tissue spaces.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): It results from broken capillaries. Extravasations of blood from the broken vessels spread into the surrounding tissue.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Contrast the color changes of a bruise at 4-5 days versus 7-10 days.
back: At 4-5 days, tissue enzymes convert hemoglobin into pigments, turning the bruise greenish. By 7-10 days, the color fades to yellow.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: A victim presents with a 'black eye' 12 hours after a forehead strike. Explain this.
back: This is 'gravity shifting.' Blood from the foreheadtracks down along tissue lines of least resistance to the lax periorbital area within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to below region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Why does a fresh bruise darken to purple within the first two days?
back: The darkening is a biochemical step where oxygen is removed from the extravasated capillary blood, converting oxy-hemoglobin into reduced hemoglobin.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Capillary blood is dark red in color and a recent bruise appears purple in color; it darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: List three factors that determine the severity and visibility of a bruise.
back: 1. Quantity of effused blood. 2. Tissue type (lax areas show more). 3. Skin color (visibility is better in fair-skinned individuals).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): 3. Quantity of effused blood 4. Type of tissue (blood spreads easily in lax area around eye and lips)... 6. Skin color (visibility better in fair people)

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Describe the characteristic findings of bruises caused by repeated 'police battering'.
back: Strikes cause rapid darkening to a deep blue color within hours. This is due to interference with tissue oxygenation and enzyme action, bypassing normal color stages.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): repeated strikes to body part... is called battering. It breaks body tissues, interferes with tissue oxygenation/enzyme action and causes rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue color.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: How is 'pseudo-bruising' distinguished from a true ante-mortem bruise at autopsy?
back: Pseudo-bruising lacks vital reactions (swelling/inflammation). It is caused by gas pressure displacing postmortem lividity into areas away from actual hypostasis.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): Pseudo-bruising... simulates ante-mortem bruising... Area showing pseudo-bruising lacks vital reaction. Importance in distinction lies in the fact that bruising is an ante-mortem phenomenon indicating violence before death.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What does finding a bruise on internal organs (liver/kidney) indicate regarding time of injury?
back: It indicates a 'vital reaction,' proving the force was applied while the victim was alive (ante-mortem) as it requires active circulation to effuse blood.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): bruising of internal organs like liver and kidney also occurs... bruising is an ante- mortem phenomenon indicating violence before death.

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: At what timeframe does a typical bruise disappear completely from the skin?
back: Typically disappears in 14 to 15 days. This duration varies depending on the site, size, and depth of the initial injury.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): finally disappears in about 14 to 15 days depending upon site, size and depth.

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What three factors determine the appearance and mechanism of a mechanical wound?
back:
1. Subject (architecture and movement of the part struck)
2. Object (weight, velocity, and type of weapon)
3. Contact (manner and direction of force application)
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients... Weight and velocity... Movement of the part]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the physics of the object's velocity influence the severity of a wound?
back: Kinetic Energy ($K.E. = 1/2 mv^2$) dictates that velocity is more critical than mass; doubling velocity quadruples the damaging energy transferred to tissues.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2. A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone bigger in size with less velocity shall produce greater damage.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why does a strike to the scalp produce a laceration while the same force to the buttocks produces a bruise?
back: Subject architecture determines the result: Scalp is thin tissue stretched over rigid bone (split/crush mechanism), while buttocks contain thick, elastic soft tissue (indentation/recoil).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Head has scalp stretched over a bone whereas buttock comprises mostly of soft tissues of skin, fat and muscles... Strike with a club... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast the outcome of a moving object striking a stationary head versus a moving head striking a stationary object.
back:
Moving Object: Produces local scalp injury and possible deep structural damage.
Moving Head (Fall): Produces minimal local scalp injury but widespread internal brain trauma (deceleration effect).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page)-54: [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact... hit against a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head having soft scalp over it will not produce much of local injury.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Differentiate between direct and indirect contact in the mechanism of injury production.
back:
Direct: Injury occurs at the exact site of impact.
Indirect: Force is transmitted, causing damage away from the site (e.g., clavicle fracture from falling on the hand).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Indirect causes injury at a place away from the site of contact... fracture of clavicle produced by fall on hand.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Which subject-related anatomical factor determines whether an incised wound will gape or remain linear?
back: The cleavage lines of Langer; wounds perpendicular to these lines gape into a spindle shape, while parallel wounds remain linear.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Wound is generally linear or spindle shaped, gaping in the center depending on cleavage lines of Langer.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does subject age affect the mechanical response of bones during object contact?
back: Infant bones are elastic and often suffer greenstick fractures or indentations. Elderly bones are brittle and calcified, fracturing more easily under similar force.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast the mechanical wounding response of solid organs versus hollow sacs in the subject's abdomen.
back: Solid organs (liver/spleen) suffer crushing or bruising. Hollow sacs (stomach/heart) are prone to rupture depending on the density of their fluid or gas contents.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Stomach, intestine, heart... are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids of different density in them... they have different behavior character]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the mechanism of wound production in high-velocity ballistic contact with dense tissue?
back: Higher tissue density increases energy discharge, causing explosive shattering and the creation of secondary projectiles from fragmented bone or displaced fluid.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page)-70: [Greater the density of the tissue, greater is the amount of energy discharged. When high velocity bullet strikes a bone... the bullet shatters its target more effectively.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What defines an 'Object' as a blunt weapon versus a sharp cutting edge in mechanical wounding?
back: Sharp edges produce incised wounds (clean-cut margins). Blunt objects cause lacerated wounds characterized by irregular margins, bridging tissue tags, and crushed hair bulbs.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with irregular margins... and walls that have bridging tissue tags... hair bulbs of hairs are crushed.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: What are the two primary categories of factors that control the shape of a mechanical injury?
back:
1. Factors in the weapon (Object).
2. Factors in the part struck (Subject).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients, (Table 6.1)]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: How does the architecture of the 'subject' (part struck) influence the wounding outcome?
back: The outcome depends on tissue consistency: soft/elastic (skin, fat) absorbs force or bruises; rigid/hard (bones) breaks or fractures depending on age and calcification.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Architecture of part struck with its behavior following a strike has specific relationship to the outcome. Human body is composed of different types of tissues. They are soft and elastic... relatively rigid and less elastic... and hard and limited elastic like bones.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Contrast the result of a blunt strike on the scalp versus the buttocks.
back:
• Scalp: Produces a laceration (skin stretched over bone).
• Buttocks: Produces a bruise (soft tissue, fat, and muscle buffer).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club, a blunt weapon... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Describe the trauma distribution when a moving 'object' strikes a stationary 'subject' (head).
back: Produces a localized injury of the scalp at the site of contact; damage may extend to deeper structures directly beneath the impact.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact and damage may extend even to deeper structures.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: How does weapon velocity (Object) mathematically relate to its wounding potential?
back: Wounding power is determined by kinetic energy: K.E.=1/2mv². Velocity has a squared influence, meaning a smaller object at higher speed can cause greater damage than a larger, slower object.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sumtotal control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv².]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Define the difference between direct and indirect manners of weapon execution.
back:
• Direct: Injury occurs exactly at the point of impact.
• Indirect: Injury occurs at a site distant from the impact (e.g., clavicle fracture from falling on hands).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution or infliction of weapon; direct and indirect. Indirect causes injury at a place away from site of impact.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Explain why 'Subject' age affects the mechanism of bone fracture production.
back: Infant bones are more elastic and often sustain incomplete 'greenstick' fractures; adult and elderly bones are more calcified and brittle, fracturing completely under less distortion.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bone elasticity depends upon person’s age, extent of calcification and shape of the bone: Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: What occurs when a high velocity 'object' strikes a hollow viscus containing fluid?
back: The fluid particles are displaced explosively in all directions away from the bullet path, behaving as secondary projectiles that disintegrate surrounding tissue.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [When a hollow viscus containing fluid is hit by a high velocity bullet, its contents get separated into particles, which get displaced explosively in all directions away from the bullet path and behave as secondary projectiles.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Outline the mechanical sequence of events leading to a comminuted depressed skull fracture.
back:
1. Local deformation forms a shallow cone.
2. Inner table (apex) stretches and fractures first.
3. Outer table (periphery) compresses and fractures second.
4. Both tables break together.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. Apex of cone stretches the inner-table... fractures before the outer table, whereas at the periphery the outer table fractures first.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: In mechanical wounding, which factor determines whether a strike produces an incised or lacerated wound?
back: The type of weapon (Object): Sharp-edged weapons produce incised wounds, while blunt-edged weapons produce lacerated wounds.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factors in weapon: Type of weapon directly controls and determines the appearance of the wound. Examples are incised and lacerated wounds produced by sharp edged and blunt edged weapons.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Define a medical abrasion.
back: The destruction or removal of the epidermis (outer skin layer) caused by a blunt weapon with moving abrasive force.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Removal of the outer surface of the body, which is skin... result of a strike of a blunt weapon having moving abrasive force... causes solution of the continuity of the skin.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Classify abrasions based on the mechanism of production.
back:
1. Moving abrasions (scratches/grazes)
2. Imprint abrasions (stamping/contact marks)
3. Friction abrasions (rubbing marks)
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [There are of three types: Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Contrast moving abrasions from imprint abrasions.
back: Moving abrasions involve dragging and epithelial heaping at the far end; imprint abrasions are static 'stamps' reflecting the object's shape (e.g., shoe heel).
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end... imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like sheo-heel.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: A corpse has dry, parchment-like skin loss on the neck without inflammation. Assessment?
back: Post-mortem abrasion. It lacks vital reaction (bleeding/swelling) and hardens/dries due to air exposure after death.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion... Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying... different appearance. Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: How is the direction of force determined in a moving abrasion?
back: By observing the heaping/piling up of detached epidermis; the epithelial tags point in the direction the force was traveling.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What defines a 'Graze' abrasion?
back: A moving abrasion covering a wide area caused by body surface dragging against a rough object, commonly seen in road accidents.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the appearance of an abrasion at 48 hours.
back: Formation of a soft scab composed of dried serum and blood.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Why is an imprint abrasion forensic significance high?
back: It acts as a signature, providing corroborative evidence of the specific causative agent (e.g., tire patterns, rope weaves).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What is the typical healing timeline for an abrasion to fall away?
back: Approximately 8–10 days (2 days for soft scab, 3-4 days to harden, 3-4 days to retract and fall).
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days. Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What is the biological composition of a friction abrasion mark in hanging?
back: It includes both a physical indentation and a frictional rub resulting in epithelial loss.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Pathologically define an abrasion and identify the specific layer of skin involved.
back:
• Definition: The removal of the surface layer of skin caused by a strike or rubbing against a rough object.
• Anatomic Layer: Exclusively involves the epidermis.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Abrasion is defined as removal of the surface layer of the skin (epidermis) as a result of a strike or rubbing against a rough object.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What are the three primary classifications of mechanical abrasions based on mechanism?
back:
• Moving abrasion.
• Imprint abrasion.
• Friction abrasion.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Classified into three types: • Moving abrasion • Imprint abrasion • Friction abrasion

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Which specific microscopic feature indicates the direction of force in a moving abrasion?
back:
• Heaping or piling up of the epidermis at the far end of the injury.
• This characteristic feature confirms the path of the abrasive object.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end. Appearance is characteristic.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Define a 'graze' and its typical causative scenario in forensic medicine.
back:
• Definition: Irregular removal of the epidermis during body surface dragging.
• Common Scenario: Vehicular accidents where the victim is dragged against a road.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: How do imprint abrasions provide corroborative evidence regarding the causative weapon?
back:
• They reflect the pattern of the rough object (e.g., shoe-heel or rope weaves).
• They show indentation and frictional rub consistent with the agent's shape.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Its pattern provides corroborative evidence of causative agent. Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Contrast the diagnostic features of ante-mortem and post-mortem abrasions.
back:
• Ante-mortem: Displays a vital reaction (signs of inflammation/blood flow).
• Post-mortem: Lacks vital reaction and acquires a dry, parchment-like appearance over time.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Post-mortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion... with passage of time after drying acquires parchment appearance. Ante-moriem abrasion shows vital reaction.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What is the typical timeframe for soft and hard scab formation in a healing abrasion?
back:
• Soft Scab: Forms in approximately 2 days from effused serum.
• Hard Scab: Develops after 3 to 4 more days.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): It is followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: An unconscious accident victim has abrasions with heaping of skin toward the head. Determine the direction of dragging.
back:
• The dragging force moved from the feet toward the head.
• The epidermis piles up at the end point of the abrasive stroke.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: A corpse has neck abrasions matching a heavy necklace but no internal vital reaction. Differentiate this from throttling.
back:
• Diagnosis: Post-mortem abrasion.
• Reason: These occur by rubbing against hard objects after death and lack the vital inflammatory response seen in homicidal throttling.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): She... had three post-mortem abrasions... caused by heavy sliver necklace. Police during initial inquiry labeled her death due to throttling... Post-mortem abrasion lacks vital reaction.

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the changes in effused serum color used to estimate the age of an abrasion.
back:
• Initial: Straw-colored or yellow.
• Transition: Becomes brown as the fluid dries and mixes with blood components.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): Age estimation would depend upon changes that take place in the effused serum... Fluid when dry varies in color from straw to yellow to brown.

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What two primary factors control the shape and appearance of a mechanical injury?
back:
- The Weapon/Implement used.
- The Body Part struck.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does velocity influence the mechanism of wound production?
back:
- Velocity dictates Kinetic Energy (K.E. = 1/2 mv²).
- A small bullet at high velocity produces greater damage than a larger, slower object.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv²]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Differentiate between direct and indirect manners of weapon execution.
back:
- Direct: Injury occurs at the point of contact.
- Indirect: Injury occurs distant from the impact site (e.g., fractured clavicle from a fall on the hand).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution of infliction of weapon; direct and indirect. Direct causes injury at site of contact. Indirect causes injury at a place away from contact site]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why does a club strike produce a laceration on the head but a bruise on the buttocks?
back:
- The head has scalp stretched over rigid bone (crush mechanism).
- The buttocks consist of thick soft tissue/fat which absorbs force (indentation/recoil).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the movement of a body part affect wound severity?
back:
- A strike to a stationary head (fixed against an object) causes more severe trauma due to lack of energy dissipation.
- A free-moving part allows some force to be converted into kinetic motion.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact and damage may extend even to deeper structures... as compared to one that is free to move.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What three categories of consistency determine organ behavior during impact?
back:
- Solid (Liver, Spleen).
- Spongy (Lungs).
- Hollow sacs containing fluid (Stomach, Bladder).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid. Lungs are spongy and contain air in them. Stomach, intestine, heart, gall and urinary bladder are hollow sacs having fluid or semi-solids]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does bone elasticity vary the wounding mechanism between infants and adults?
back:
- Infant bones are elastic, often producing "greenstick" fractures.
- Adult/elderly bones are brittle and break easily at points of maximum convexity.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Bone elasticity depends upon person's age... Bones of infants are relatively elastic than those of adults and old persons, which become brittle and thus, break more easily.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: In a fall from a height onto the feet, which bone typically fractures indirectly?
back: The base of the skull (specifically the ethmoid/cribriform plate) due to transmission of force upward through the spine.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Another example is transmission of force upward through spines after a fall from height on feet or buttocks fracturing base of the skull.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Describe the wounding cycle for a bruise (contusion).
back:
- Sudden tissue indentation by blunt force.
- Followed by immediate recoil.
- Results in extravasation of blood into surrounding tissue without breaking the skin.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil... Area struck becomes swollen, red and painful withoutt solution of continuity of covering skin.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Which tissue layer typically piling up in a moving abrasion indicates force direction?
back: The epidermis (surface layer) heaps or piles up at the far end of the force application.
citation: Page 54 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Define a "wound" from a medical and pathological perspective.
back:
* Any break in body tissue, either externally or internally.
* Both "wound" and "injury" are synonymous pathological entities.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does weapon velocity mathematically influence wound production energy?
back:
* Governed by kinetic energy formula: K.E. = 1/2 mv².
* Velocity increases energy exponentially, causing greater tissue destruction than mass alone.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2. A bullet in flight though small has greater velocity than a stone bigger in size with less velocity shall produce greater damage.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast the direct and indirect manners of weapon execution.
back:
* Direct: Injury occurs at the exact site of impact.
* Indirect: Injury occurs at a site remote from contact (e.g., clavicle fracture from falling on hands).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution of weapon; direct and indirect. Direct impact causes injury at the site of contact... Indirect causes injury at a place away from impact.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why does architecture of the part struck determine the specific wound type?
back:
* Scalp (stretched over bone) splits into lacerations under blunt force.
* Buttocks (soft tissue/fat) absorb force, typically producing bruises instead of skin breaches.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference... is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of "temporary cavitation" in high-velocity wounding.
back:
* High energy dissipates radially.
* Tissues are pushed laterally, creating a cavity larger than the projectile diameter before collapsing.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally... period of cavitation is extremely short and soon after the passage of the bullet, tissues recoil... leaving a permanent cavity.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What are the two primary factors controlling the shape of an injury?
back:
1. Factors in the weapon (Object): weight, velocity, type.
2. Factors in the part struck (Subject): architecture, movement.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury are either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients. (Table 6.1)]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the movement of a body part (stationary vs. motion) affect trauma?
back:
* Stationary head: Local injury at contact site, potential deep damage.
* Moving head striking stationary object: Resultant trauma is typically severer.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact... When a moving head strikes a stationary object, the resultant trauma... is severer.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain the "Blowback Phenomenon" in contact firearm wounds over bone.
back:
* Explosive gases enter tissue but are resisted by hard bone.
* Gases return with extreme force, distending and splitting skin into a stellate shape.
citation: Page 72 (Book Page): [When there is hard bone as in scalp or cheek, it resists entry of gases, which return with extreme force; blowback phenomenon causing stellate or ragged wound with everted margin.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why do long bones in children produce "greenstick" fractures?
back:
* Higher physiological bone elasticity.
* Force causes the bone to bend and break only on the side opposite the impact.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Long bones of children are comparatively more elastic and show less damage to only one side of bone close to application of force resulting into green stick fracture.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What is the defining mechanical difference between incised and lacerated wounds?
back:
* Incised: Caused by sharp objects/cutting edges with linear movement.
* Lacerated: Caused by blunt objects/impact causing tissue crushing and tearing.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Type of weapon directly controls and determines the appearance of the wound. Examples are incised and lacerated wounds produced by sharp edged and blunt edged weapons.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Define an abrasion from a forensic pathological perspective.
back: A closed wound characterized by the partial or complete loss of the epithelial layer of the skin or mucous membrane.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Abrasion is defined as and is a closed wound, showing partial or complete loss of the epithelial layer of the skin or mucous membrane.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What are the three primary types of abrasions based on mechanism?
back:
1. Moving abrasion
2. Imprint abrasion
3. Friction abrasion
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Classification: Moving abrasion, Imprint abrasion, Friction abrasion.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: How is the direction of force determined in a moving abrasion?
back: The direction of movement is indicated by the 'heaping' or piling up of the epidermis at the far end of the wound.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Moving abrasion indicates direction of abrasive force, showing heaping of piling up of the epidermis on the far end.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Identify the specific type of abrasion caused by a shoe-heel strike.
back: Imprint abrasion (also known as a contact or pressure abrasion), which mirrors the pattern of the causative object.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion is caused by strike of rough object on skin like shoe-heel.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Define a 'graze' and its common causative mechanism.
back: A type of moving abrasion caused by the body surface dragging against a rough object, such as a road in vehicular accidents.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Another example is irregular removal of the epidermis occurring during body surface dragging against the rough object such as road as seen in vehicular accident. This abrasion is also called a graze.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What is the defining feature of a 'scratch' abrasion?
back: A linear moving abrasion typically produced by a sharp-pointed object like a fingernail, pin, or thorn.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Example of this variety is a scratch produced with fingernail pin or thorn.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What feature distinguishes an ante-mortem abrasion from a post-mortem one?
back: Ante-mortem abrasions exhibit a 'vital reaction' (signs of living tissue response), which is absent in post-mortem abrasions.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Ante-mortem abrasion shows vital reaction.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: Describe the appearance of an imprint abrasion from hard ligature material.
back: It presents as both an indentation (pressure) and a frictional rub, providing corroborative evidence of the causative agent.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck in hanging shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: What is the typical timeframe for soft scab formation in an abrasion?
back: Approximately two days following the injury, resulting from the drying of effused serum and blood.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [It is followed by formation of a soft scab in about two days, which hardens in about another three to four days.]

category: Define and classify abrasions
front: Q: When does an abrasion scab typically retract and fall off?
back: The hard scab usually retracts in 3-4 days and typically falls away within 7 to 10 days of the injury.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Hard scab retracts in another three or four days and finally falls away. Time relation of these changes... is only an indicator for duration/age of abrasion.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Define a wound from a medical perspective.
back: Any break in the body tissue, whether external or internal. Medically, the term is synonymous with injury.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does weapon velocity influence kinetic energy and wound production?
back: Velocity determines kinetic energy ($K.E.=1/2mv^2$). A high-velocity projectile like a bullet produces greater damage than a larger, slower object like a stone.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv2.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Contrast 'Direct' versus 'Indirect' manners of weapon execution.
back: Direct: Injury occurs exactly at the point of impact. Indirect: Injury occurs at a distant site (e.g., clavicle fracture resulting from a fall on the hand).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [There are two manners of execution of weapon; direct and indirect. Direct... causes injury at site of contact... Indirect causes injury at a place away from site of impact example fracture of clavicle produced by fall on the hand.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why does the same blunt force produce different wounds on the scalp versus the buttocks?
back: Architecture of the part: The scalp is thin tissue stretched over bone (causing laceration), while the buttocks consist of soft fat and muscle (causing a bruise).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Strike with a club... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain 'Local Deformation' as a mechanism of skull fracture.
back: Force at the impact site causes the outer table to crush into the diploe, creating a shallow cone that stretches the inner table until it breaks.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Local deformation at the site occurs, if the force applied is sufficient to cause crushing of outer table into diploe or a bend of the skull bone. Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Identify the three primary factors in the 'part struck' that influence wounding.
back:
* Architecture (tissue types like elastic skin vs rigid bone)
* Consistency (solid vs hollow organs)
* Movement (stationary vs in motion)
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factors in part struck: Architecture of part struck... Consistency... Movement of the part also affects the outcome.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does the movement of a body part (Subject) modify injury outcome?
back: A strike to a stationary head causes local contact injury and deep damage. If the head is moving, the resulting trauma is typically less severe.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Movement of the part also affects the outcome. Difference can be appreciated by noting injuries produced when the part is stationary or in motion... A strike to a’stationary head will produce a local injury.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain 'General Deformation' as a mechanism of skull wounding.
back: The skull is compressed in one plane, behaving like an elastic sphere. It bulges out and fractures in the perpendicular plane at sites distant from impact.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [General deformation of whole skull occurs due to compression of the skull. When skull is compressed in one plane, it behaves as an elastic sphere and bulges out in other plane. where fracture occurs.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What defines the 'Object' (Weapon) factors in the mechanism of wounding?
back:
* Type (Sharp vs Blunt edge)
* Weight
* Velocity
* Manner of application (Direct vs Indirect)
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck... Factors in weapon: Type of weapon... Weight and velocity... Manner of execution.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does organ consistency (Subject) affect injury in body cavities?
back: Solid organs (liver/spleen) respond differently than hollow sacs (stomach/bladder) or spongy tissues (lungs), as fluids or air transmit force explosively.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [These cavities have organs in them, which are again of different shapes and consistency... Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Lungs are spongy... Stomach, intestine, heart... are hollow sacs.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How is a mechanical injury defined in forensic medicine?
back:
- A break in body tissue (internal or external) caused by a mechanical weapon.
- Synonymous with the terms 'wound' or 'injury'.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [From medical point of view, any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury. Both words are synonymous in meaning and are a single pathological entity.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: How does weapon velocity influence the mechanism of wound production?
back:
- Velocity determines kinetic energy (K.E.=1/2mv²).
- Higher velocity produces significantly greater tissue damage than mass alone (e.g., a small bullet vs. a large stone).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv².]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Why does the same blunt force produce different wounds on the scalp versus the buttocks?
back:
- Due to tissue architecture.
- Scalp: Stretched over bone, leading to tissue splitting (laceration).
- Buttocks: Soft fat and muscle absorb force, leading to crushing of vessels (bruise).
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Head has scalp stretched over a bone whereas buttock comprises mostly of soft tissues of skin, fat and muscles. This difference in the shape of wound is due to the difference in architecture of the body part.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain the wounding mechanism when a moving object strikes a stationary head.
back:
- Energy is transferred at the site of contact.
- Results in local injury (scalp laceration or skull fracture) restricted to the impact area.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact and damage may extend even to deeper structures.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Describe the biochemical step used to identify vital reactions in wound production.
back:
- Histochemical detection of increased enzyme activity.
- Key enzymes: Alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, and non-specific esterase at the wound periphery.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Mallik (1968) applied them to skin burns. Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien aminopeptidase and non-specific esterase.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: List the three factors in a weapon that determine wound appearance.
back:
1. Type of weapon (sharp vs. blunt).
2. Weight of the weapon.
3. Velocity at the moment of impact.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factor controlling shape of injury either weapon or part struck each having its ingredients... Factors in weapon: Type... Weight and velocity.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of a 'split laceration' in wound production.
back:
- Occurs where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone.
- The tissue is crushed between the weapon and the bone, splitting the skin like an incision.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues between the weapon and the underlying bone split them. It may resemble an incision wound.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Distinguish between 'coup' and 'contrecoup' injury mechanisms in a mobile head.
back:
- Coup: Injury at the site of impact.
- Contrecoup: Injury distant from impact (opposite side) caused by brain movement against skull partitions.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [The resultant trauma to the mobile head produces lesion at the site of impact (coup) and also at the place distant from it (contre-coup).]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of temporary cavitation in high-velocity bullet wounds.
back:
- High energy radiates laterally, creating a large temporary cavity.
- Tissues collapse back shortly after passage, leaving a permanent cavity larger than the bullet diameter.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues pushing them more laterally... tissues recoil and collapse back leaving a permanent cavity.]

category: Explain mechanism of wound production with reference to subject, object and contact
front: Q: What defines the 'subject' factor in the mechanism of wound production?
back:
- Architecture: Tissue density (soft/fat vs. rigid/bone).
- State of Health: Coagulation defects or pre-existing disease.
- Movement: Whether the body part is stationary or in motion.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Factors in part struck: Architecture of part struck with its behavior following a strike... Movement of the part also affects the outcome.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Define a bruise (contusion) from a forensic medical perspective.
back: A closed wound caused by blunt force. It results from sudden tissue indentation and recoil, causing swelling and redness without breaking the skin surface.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Bruise also called contusion is a closed wound caused by strike of blunt weapon. It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil. Area struck becomes swollen, red and painful withoutt solution of continuity of covering skin.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Describe the underlying pathophysiological mechanism of blood extravasation in a bruise.
back: Blunt impact causes sudden indentation and recoil, which breaks capillaries and leaks blood into the surrounding interstitial tissue spaces.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Extravasations of blood from the broken capillaries/blood vessels spread into the surrounding tissue.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: How is an ante-mortem bruise distinguished from post-mortem pseudo-bruising?
back: Ante-mortem bruises exhibit vital reactions like swelling and inflammation. Pseudo-bruising results from postmortem lividity displacement and lacks vital reactions.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Importance in distinction lies in the fact that bruising is an ante- mortem phenomenon indicating violence before death. ... Area showing pseudo-bruising lacks vital reaction.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: A forehead strike results in a 'black eye' 24 hours later. Identify the mechanism.
back: This is gravity shifting. Extravasated blood moves from the initial impact site along tissue lines of least resistance due to gravitational influence.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to below region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What biochemical process causes a bruise to turn greenish in 4–5 days?
back: Tissue enzymes begin the breakdown process, converting extravasated hemoglobin into various intermediate blood pigments.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Outline the typical chronological healing stages of a bruise by color.
back:
• Fresh: Purple/Dark red
• 2 Days: Dark blue (oxygen removal)
• 4-5 Days: Greenish
• 7-10 Days: Yellow
• 2 Weeks: Disappears
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [recent bruise appears purple in color; darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed. ... in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish ... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Classify bruises based on anatomical location beyond the body surface.
back: Bruises are classified into surface bruises (skin) and internal organ bruises (specifically affecting the liver and kidneys).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Extravasations of blood is more commonly met with on body surface, yet bruising of internal organs like liver and kidney also occurs.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Contrast a bruise and postmortem lividity upon incision of the tissue.
back: In a bruise, blood is in tissue spaces and does not flow out. In lividity, blood remains intravascular and flows from cut vessel mouths.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Bruise: Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue. No flow of blood occurs upon cutting of vessel. ... Postmortem Lividity: Blood is within the vessels and when incised, it flows out from the cut mouths of the blood vessel.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Why does a purple bruise darken significantly within the first two days?
back: The color deepens to dark blue/purple specifically because the oxygen within the extravasated blood is removed by surrounding tissues.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [recent bruise appears purple in color; darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: List three factors that influence the clinical visibility and severity of a bruise.
back:
• Quantity of effused blood
• Tissue type (lax tissues allow easier spread)
• Victim's state of health (e.g., coagulation defects)
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Appearance and severity of a bruise depends upon certain factors: ... 3. Quantity of effused blood. 4. Type of tissue (blood spreads easily in lax area around eye and lips) 5. State of health (coagulation defect...)]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What is the forensic medical definition of a bruise?
back: A closed wound caused by blunt weapon impact, resulting in tissue indentation and recoil without a breach in skin continuity.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Bruise also called contusion is 4 closed wound caused by strike of a blunt weapon. It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil. Area struck becomes swollen, red and painful withoutt solution of continuity of covering skin.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Explain the mechanism and a classic example of 'gravity shifting' in bruises.
back: Blood extravasates and moves along tissue lines of least resistance under gravity. Example: A forehead blow later manifesting as a 'black eye'.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its inig, site along tissue line of least resistance to ben region under the influence of gravity within firs, +; hours. It changes both its position and shape , noticed following 4 blow on the forehead/scalp 2,, later causing black eve.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Contrast an ante-mortem bruise with a pseudo-bruise based on vital reaction.
back: Ante-mortem bruises show vital reactions like swelling and inflammation; pseudo-bruises are postmortem lividity displacements lacking vital reaction.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Pseudo-bruising... simulates ante-mortem bruising and should be differentiated... Area showing pseudo-bruising lacks vital reaction. Importance in distinction lies in the fact that bruising is an ante- mortem phenomenon indicating violence before death.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Why might a victim of repeated police battering show deep blue bruises within hours?
back: Repeated strikes break tissues and interfere with oxygenation and enzyme action, causing blood to darken rapidly to deep blue/black.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [yeated strikes to body part... by police during investigation... breaks body tissues, interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and... causing rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue/black color. It should not be confused with seth color reaction occurring with passage of ie (Photo 6.10)]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: List the chronological color changes in a bruise used for age estimation.
back: Purple (recent), Darkens (2 days), Greenish (4-5 days), Yellowish (7-10 days), and Disappears (2 weeks).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [recent bruise appears purple in co 0T- darkens in two days because oxygen in the bl dis removed. Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in ‘pout four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish Fading of the bruise occurs because of absorption... within seven to ten days, sree yellow and finally disappears in abou! the i]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What three primary criteria dictate the appearance and severity of a bruise?
back: Applied force, weapon type, and tissue characteristics (e.g., blood spreads more easily in lax areas like eyes).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [1. Force applied 2. Weapon type... 4. Type of tissue (blood spreads easily in lax area around eve and lips) 5. State of th (coagulation defect... cause more bleeding giving false impression about severity)]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Can bruises occur internally, and which organs are frequently involved?
back: Yes; blunt force can cause extravasations of blood in internal organs, most commonly the liver and kidneys.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Fxtravasations oft broken blow... more commonly met with on body surtace, vat bruising Of 2 internal organs like liver and kidney also Occurs. (Photo 6.8)]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: In a differential diagnosis, how does a tissue incision distinguish a bruise from lividity?
back: In a bruise, blood is extravasated into interstitial tissue and will not flow or wash away upon cutting the vessel.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (anti-mortem): 1. Blood vessels are broken and blood is: present in bloc surrounding inter-statius tissue. 2. No flow of blood occurs upon cutting of vessel... Lies in i= inter-statius tissue below epidermis]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What physiological process governs the fading and ultimate disappearance of a bruise?
back: Tissue enzymes convert hemoglobin into blood pigments, followed by the absorption of effused blood and fluids.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments... Fading of the bruise occurs because of absorption . af fd, oe within seven to ten days, sree yellow and finally disappears in abou! the i upon site, size and depth]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What determines the morphological pattern of a contusion?
back: The shape of the striking blunt weapon typically dictates the configuration of the resulting bruise.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [A bruise generally acquires the shape of striking weapon.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: What is the characteristic color of a fresh bruise and why?
back:
* Purple or dark red.
* Caused by the accumulation of dark red capillary blood in the surrounding tissue.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Capillary blood is dark red in color and a recent bruise appears purple in color.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: What pathophysiological change causes a bruise to darken after two days?
back:
* Conversion of hemoglobin to reduced hemoglobin.
* Occurs because oxygen is removed from the extravasated blood.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: Contrast the timing and chemical cause of greenish vs. yellow hues in a bruise.
back:
* Greenish (4-5 days): Hemoglobin changes into biliverdin via tissue enzymes.
* Yellow (7-10 days): Biliverdin further breaks down into bilirubin.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: A victim presents with a faint yellow bruise. Estimate the duration since injury.
back:
* Approximately 7 to 10 days.
* Yellow indicates the final stage of pigment breakdown before absorption.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: How do tissue enzymes contribute to the color sequence of a bruise?
back:
* They biochemically degrade hemoglobin into secondary blood pigments.
* This process is responsible for the transition from purple to green and yellow.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: List the color stages of a bruise in chronological order.
back:
1. Purple/Dark Red (Fresh)
2. Dark Blue (2 days)
3. Greenish (4-5 days)
4. Yellowish (7-10 days)
5. Disappears (14-15 days).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [recent bruise appears purple... darkens in two days... four/five days... becomes greenish... seven to ten days, it becomes yellow.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: Explain the 'gravity shifting' phenomenon in bruise color identification.
back:
* Blood follows tissue lines of least resistance.
* Blood may migrate to a dependent region (e.g., forehead blow causing a 'black eye') within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to dependent region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: Differentiate the color of 'police battering' from natural bruise aging.
back:
* Battering: Deep blue color appearing within hours due to repeated strikes preventing oxygenation.
* Natural: Slow sequence of red, green, and yellow over many days.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [repeated strikes... interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and causes color change from first two days to few hours causing rapid darkening... to deep blue color.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: What physiological process results in the total disappearance of a bruise?
back:
* Complete absorption of the effused blood and degraded pigments into the system.
* Typically occurs around the 14th day.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Fading of the bruise occurs because of absorption of the effused blood.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: Identify two systemic factors that can cause exaggerated bruise coloration.
back:
* Coagulation defects (Hemophilia/Vitamin K deficiency).
* Liver disease or vascular disease.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [coagulation defect, disease of blood vessel and liver cause more bleeding giving false impression about severity.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a bruise or contusion?
back: A closed wound caused by blunt force, characterized by tissue indentation and recoil without a break in skin continuity, resulting in localized swelling and pain.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Bruise also called contusion is 4 closed wound caused by strike of a blunt weapon. It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil. Area struck becomes swollen, red and painful withoutt solution of continuity of covering skin.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Describe the underlying vascular mechanism that produces a bruise.
back: Blunt impact causes extravasation of blood from ruptured vessels into the surrounding interstitial tissues beneath the intact skin surface.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Extravasations of blood from broken blood vessels spread into the surrounding tissue.] Page 57 (Book Page): [Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: How is a true bruise distinguished from post-mortem pseudo-bruising?
back: True bruises exhibit vital reactions like swelling and inflammation, whereas pseudo-bruising consists of stagnant blood displacement without inflammatory response.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Pseudo-bruising... lacks vital reaction. Importance in distinction lies in the fact that bruising is an ante- mortem phenomenon indicating violence before death.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: A forehead strike results in a "black eye" 24 hours later. Identify this phenomenon.
back: Gravity shifting (Ectopic bruise). Blood tracks along tissue lines of least resistance under gravitational influence, changing position from the original impact site.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to lower region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What biochemical process dictates the color change to greenish in a healing bruise?
back: Tissue enzymes act upon the extravasated blood, converting hemoglobin into blood pigments (biliverdin) typically around four to five days post-injury.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: List four primary factors that influence the severity and appearance of a bruise.
back:
1. Applied force and weapon velocity
2. Quantity of effused blood
3. Tissue type (lax vs. firm)
4. State of health and skin color.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Appearance and severity of 4 bruise depends upon certain factors... 1. Force... 3. Quantity of effused blood 4. Type of tissue... 5. State of health... 6. Skin color]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Why do bruises around the eyes and lips typically appear larger than those on limbs?
back: Blood extravasates more extensively in lax tissues (loose subcutaneous spaces) where there is minimal resistance compared to firm, dense areas.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Type of tissue (blood spreads easily in lax area around eye and lips)]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Differentiate the color progression of "police battering" bruises from standard healing.
back: Repeated strikes interfere with oxygenation and enzymes, causing rapid darkening to deep blue within hours instead of the multi-day sequence.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [repeated strikes... interferes with oxygenation/enzyme action and speed of color change from first two days to few hours causing rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue color.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Outline the chronological color stages used for estimating bruise age.
back:
Recent: Purple/Red
2 Days: Darkens
4-5 Days: Greenish
7-10 Days: Yellowish
2 Weeks: Disappears.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [recent bruise appears purple... darkens in two days... four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish... within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Where in the skin anatomy is the blood of a bruise specifically deposited?
back: In the interstitial tissue below the epidermis; the epidermis itself remains bloodless and acts as a translucent covering.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Lies in the inter-statius tissue below epidermis or even deeper to it, as epidermis is withoutt blood vessels]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a bruise (contusion)?
back: A closed wound caused by blunt force impact resulting in tissue indentation and recoil, characterized by pain and swelling without a breach in skin continuity.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Bruise also called contusion is a closed wound caused by strike of a blunt weapon... withoutt solution of continuity of covering skin.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Describe the physiological mechanism behind the formation of a bruise.
back: Blunt force ruptures capillaries, leading to the extravasation of blood from broken vessels into the surrounding interstitial tissue spaces while the overlying skin remains intact.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Extravasations of blood from the broken vessels spread into the surrounding tissue.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: How does the color of a recent bruise contrast with one that is 4-5 days old?
back:
• Recent: Purple or dark red (capillary blood).
• 4-5 Days: Greenish (enzymatic conversion of hemoglobin into blood pigments).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Capillary blood is dark red in color and a recent bruise appears purple... in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: A victim sustains a blow to the forehead but develops a 'black eye' later. Explain this.
back: This is 'Gravity Shifting,' where extravasated blood tracks along tissue lines of least resistance to dependent regions within the first 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to dependent region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: List four factors that influence the appearance and severity of a bruise.
back:
• Amount of force and weapon size.
• Tissue laxity (e.g., lax area around eyes).
• State of health (e.g., coagulation defects).
• Skin pigmentation.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [1. Amount of force 2. Size of striking weapon... 4. Type of tissue 5. State of health... 6. Skin color]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What is the typical timeline for a bruise to turn yellow and eventually disappear?
back:
• Yellow: 7 to 10 days.
• Disappears: Approximately 2 weeks (depending on site, size, and depth).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [within seven to ten days, it becomes yellow and finally disappears in about two weeks]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: What distinguishes 'police battering' bruises from standard accidental contusions in color progression?
back: Repeated strikes break tissues and interfere with oxygenation/enzymes, causing rapid darkening to deep blue within hours rather than days.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [repeated strikes... interferes with normal oxygenation/enzyme action and causes rapid darkening of effused blood to deep blue color.]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: How is a true ante-mortem bruise distinguished from postmortem pseudo-bruising?
back:
• Ante-mortem Bruise: Shows vital reaction (swelling/inflammation) and blood is in interstitial tissue.
• Pseudo-bruising: Lacks vital reaction; due to displacement of blood by gas pressure.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Area showing pseudo-bruising lacks vital reaction... Bruising (anti-mortem)... vital reaction (swelling and inflammation)]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Why does a bruise darken to purple in the first two days?
back: The color darkens because oxygen is removed from the blood and tissue enzymes begin changing hemoglobin into blood pigments.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed. Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments]

category: Define and classify bruises
front: Q: Contrast the location and pressure dependence of a bruise versus postmortem lividity.
back:
• Bruise: Occurs at the site of injury; independent of pressure.
• Lividity: Occurs at dependent (unsupported) parts; absent in pressure areas.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Bruise (anti-mortem) 5. Occurs at the site of injury... 6. It occurs independent of pressure... Lividity (post-mortem) 5. Occurs at dependent parts]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: What is the primary medical definition of a bruise (contusion)?
back: A closed wound caused by blunt weapon strike, resulting from tissue indentation and recoil that causes capillary rupture and extravasation of blood without breaking the skin.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Bruise also called contusion is a closed wound caused by strike of a blunt weapon. It results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil. Area struck becomes swollen, red and painful withoutt solution of continuity of covering skin.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiology behind a bruise turning greenish after 4-5 days.
back: Tissue enzymes act upon the extravasated blood to chemically break down hemoglobin into secondary blood pigments (biliverdin).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Tissue enzymes begin to change hemoglobin into blood pigments and in about four/five days, the bruise becomes greenish.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: Contrast the color of a fresh bruise with one that is 2 days old.
back:
* Fresh: Purple/Dark red (recent capillary blood).
* 2 Days: Darkens/Deep blue (due to the removal of oxygen from the extravasated blood).
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Capillary blood is dark red in color and a recent bruise appears purple in color; it darkens in two days because oxygen in the blood is removed.]

category: Explain pathophysiology of color changes in the bruise
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of a "black eye" resulting from a blow to the forehead.
back: Gravity shifting; blood moves from the initial injury site along tissue lines of least resistance into the lax peri-orbital tissues within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to below region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.]
