front: Q: What is the primary mechanical force that causes neck constriction in hanging?
back:
* Weight of the body
* Applied indirectly through a ligature
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Hanging is defined as constriction of the neck by a ligature, constricting force being applied indirectly through weight of the body.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Explain the dual vascular mechanism of cerebral anoxia in hanging victims.
back:
* Compression of jugular veins (blocks venous return)
* Compression of carotid arteries (blocks arterial supply)
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Death in most cases results from combination of two causes: Cerebral anoxia by compression of jugular veins and carotid arteries]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Contrast the ligature mark direction in hanging versus ligature strangulation.
back:
* Hanging: Oblique, directed upward toward the knot
* Strangulation: Transverse and horizontal
citation: Page 152 (Book Page)-153: [Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot... directed transversely across it (strangulation).]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: How is an ante-mortem hanging confirmed when a ligature mark is present?
back:
* Presence of vital reactions
* Hyperemia and ecchymosis along the edges of the groove
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Area of hyperemia and ecchymosis along the edges of the groove is a definite ante-mortem sign and its presence can be confirmed by histology.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What is the physiological mechanism of immediate death via reflex cardiac arrest in hanging?
back:
* Stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve
* Results in vagal inhibition
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Death by vagal inhibition resultant from pressure over carotid sinus or vagus nerve]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: State three specific diagnostic criteria of a hanging ligature mark.
back:
* In-continuous (absent at the knot position)
* Oblique direction
* Non-uniform depth (deepest opposite the knot)
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Characteristic is that it is in-continuous and absent at the place against knot. Direction of the mark is oblique... depth of the groove is not uniform being deepest at a point opposite to the knot]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Where is postmortem lividity classically distributed in a hanging suspension?
back:
* Hands and feet (Glove and stocking distribution)
* Tip of penis (males)
* Labia (females)
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Postmortem lividity will appear at an area of neck above ligature mark and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males and labia in females.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Differentiate between Typical and Atypical hanging based on knot positioning.
back:
* Typical: Knot at the occipital region
* Atypical: Knot at the side of the face or chin
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Typical hanging, ligature knot is at occipital region whereas in atypical mostly at side of face.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Describe the mechanical airway obstruction loop that occurs during hanging.
back:
* Lifting of the glottis and root of the tongue
* Tongue is forced into the pharynx, blocking the airway
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Asphyxia by lifting of glottis and tongue into pharynx and obstructing airway]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What is the reported incidence of hyoid bone fractures in forensic hanging autopsies?
back:
* Rare finding
* Occurs in only 3% to 5% of cases
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Fracture of hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage is a rare finding occurring only in about 3-5% cases.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What is the characteristic direction of the ligature mark in hanging?
back:
• Oblique direction.
• Goes upward towards the knot.
• Usually situated in the upper neck above the thyroid cartilage.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot. It is an imprint abrasion usually situated in upper part of the neck above thyroid cartilage.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: How is mechanical asphyxia produced during the process of hanging?
back:
• Lifting of the glottis and tongue into the pharynx.
• This action obstructs the airway.
• Compression of jugular veins and carotid arteries causes cerebral anoxia.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Asphyxia by lifting of glottis and tongue into pharynx and obstructing airway... Cerebral anoxia by compression of jugular veins and carotid arteries]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Differentiate Typical from Atypical hanging based on the position of the knot.
back:
• Typical hanging: The knot is at the occipital region.
• Atypical hanging: The knot is mostly at the side of the face.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [In typical hanging, ligature knot is at occipital region whereas in atypical mostly at side of face.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Where does postmortem lividity appear in a body suspended for a long period?
back:
• Hands and feet ('Glove and Stocking' distribution).
• Tip of the penis (males).
• Labia majora (females).
• Area of neck above the ligature.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [postmortem lividity will appear at an area of neck above ligature and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males and labia majora in females]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What is the mechanism of immediate death in judicial hanging?
back:
• Sudden drop causing fracture/dislocation of upper cervical segments.
• Separation of the spinal cord.
• Prevents development of usual postmortem asphyxial signs.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [sudden drop in judicial hanging causing fracture/dislocation of upper cervical segment separating spinal cord is immediate leaving no time for development of usual postmortem findings.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Describe the specific physical characteristics of a hanging ligature mark.
back:
• In-continuous (absent at the knot position).
• Depth is non-uniform (deepest opposite the knot).
• Hard material (rope/wire) produces a well-defined groove.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [characteristic is that it is in-continuous and absent at the place against knot... depth of the groove is not uniform being deepest at a point opposite to the knot]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What internal soft tissue injuries are typically found in the neck during a hanging autopsy?
back:
• Bruising of connective tissues and muscles.
• Rare tears in blood vessels.
• Rare fractures of hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage (3-5%).
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Injuries to the soft tissues of the neck immediately below the ligature include a degree of bruising of connective tissue and muscles and rarely tears in the blood vessels. Fracture of hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage is a rare finding occurring only in about 3-5% cases.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Why might an autopsy of a hanging victim be classified as 'negative'?
back:
• Severe emotional disturbance causing vagal shock.
• Rapid death from vagal inhibition/reflex cardiac arrest.
• These cases show no internal or external anatomical findings.
citation: Page 113 (Book Page): [Cases arising from severe emotional disturbances, especially the vagal shock and fright are true negative autopsies] and Page 152 (Book Page): [Death by vagal inhibition... is immediate leaving no time for development of usual postmortem findings.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: How much force is required to occlude the carotid arteries in a hanging victim?
back:
• 11 pounds.
• Compare to jugular veins (4.4 lbs) and windpipe (33 pounds).
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [jugular veins close by 4.4 pounds, carotid artery by 11 pounds and windpipe by 33 pounds]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What are the common nonspecific asphyxial findings noted in hanging?
back:
• Cyanosis.
• Visceral congestion.
• Petechaeal hemorrhages (face and conjunctivae).
• Fluidity of blood.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion... Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera, Fluidity of blood] and Page 152 (Book Page): [Petechaeal hemorrhages are on the face and conjunctivae.]

category: Explain its medico legal importance
coreConcept: Definition and Status of Forensic Medicine
front: Q: Define Forensic Medicine and its primary medico-legal objective.
back:
* Application of medical knowledge to law.
* Core goal: Furthering of justice through unique public service necessity.
citation: Page 2 (Book Page): "defined as, 'a subject that deals with application of principles of medical knowledge to purposes of law and furthering of justice'. Its importance is due to its unique public service necessity."

category: Explain its medico legal importance
front: Q: Explain the medico-legal significance of the 'Chain of Custody' in forensic sampling.
back:
* Prevents substitution or adulteration of samples.
* Ensures results are legally admissible and authenticated for court use.
citation: Page 3 (Book Page): "Forensic Medical Examiner has to... adopt necessary precautions during collection, packing and dispatch of samples... and maintains chain of custody of forensic samples, following strictly legal dictates in this respect."

category: Explain its medico legal importance
front: Q: Contrast the medico-legal remedies of Civil Law versus Criminal Law.
back:
* Civil: Compensates personal grievances (e.g., negligence) in terms of money.
* Criminal: Punishes offenses (fine/imprisonment) to safeguard community interests.
citation: Page 7 (Book Page): "Civil law... provides remedies for personal grievances... The damage to aggrieved party is compensated in terms of money. Criminal law involves defining of crimes and laying their punishments... to safeguard the interests of the community."

category: Explain its medico legal importance
front: Q: Clinical Case: A dying victim identifies his attacker. Why is this legally significant?
back:
* Admissible as a 'Dying Declaration'.
* Legal Assumption: Impending death compels the victim to speak the truth when no time for deposition exists.
citation: Page 10 (Book Page): "Victim is the only eye witness and there is no time left to arrange a dying deposition... assumption that impending death compels injured to speak the truth."

category: Explain its medico legal importance
front: Q: State the medico-legal rationale for 'Qualified Privilege' in medical disclosures.
back:
* Rationale: Community interest is superior to individual privacy.
* Examples: Mandatory notification of births, deaths, and infectious diseases.
citation: Page 22 (Book Page): "Rationale... is that the interest of the community is superior to that of an individual. All notifications of birth, deaths or industrial, infectious or contagious diseases are examples of qualified privilege."

category: Explain its medico legal importance
front: Q: What defines the medico-legal importance of a Forensic Medical Certificate?
back:
* Most comprehensive document about an examinee's health.
* Must omit no findings; serves as factual evidence for law enforcement/courts.
citation: Page 4 (Book Page): "It is the most comprehensive document about state of health of examinee... and is based exclusively upon medical facts observed during medical examination. Findings both positive as well as negative should be documented for information of... law courts."

category: Explain its medico legal importance
front: Q: List the 'Five As' of professional misconduct and their legal consequence.
back:
* Adultery, Addiction, Abortion (criminal), Advertising, Association (unqualified persons).
* Consequence: Disciplinary action leading to temporary or permanent erasure from register.
citation: Page 15 (Book Page): "Common professional misconducts... can be remembered as five As. (Table 3.3)... Misconduct proved... RMP/RDP name erased from registered."

category: Explain its medico legal importance
front: Q: Medico-Legal Principle: Explain the doctrine 'Res Ipsa Loquitur' in negligence claims.
back:
* 'The thing speaks for itself.'
* Legal Effect: Shits the burden of proof from the patient to the doctor to prove they were NOT negligent.
citation: Page 21 (Book Page): "common law doctrine 'Res Ipsa Loquitur' meaning thing speaks for it. This doctrine creates an inference that negligence has occurred and places responsibility on the medical practitioner to prove that he is not negligent."

category: Explain its medico legal importance
front: Q: Why is the identification of post-mortem artifacts vital in forensic toxicology/autopsy?
back: * Prevents misinterpreting agonal or post-mortem changes (e.g., ant bites, vomiting) as ante-mortem trauma or criminal signs.
citation: Page 129 (Book Page): "Recognition is important and necessary to avoid misinterpretation of medically significant ante-mortem findings."

category: Explain its medico legal importance
front: Q: List three criminal purposes for forensic age estimation.
back:
* Determining criminal responsibility (immaturity).
* Eligibility for capital punishment (e.g., whipping).
* Proving age of consent in sexual offenses.
citation: Page 38 (Book Page): "criminal nature like criminal responsibility and capital punishment i.e. whipping... Role of age... especially in sexual offences."

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What are the primary characteristics of a ligature mark in a typical hanging?
back:
* In-continuous (absent at the knot site)
* Oblique direction (upward toward the knot)
* Imprint abrasion situated above the thyroid cartilage
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Its characteristic is that it is in-continuous and absent at the place against knot. Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot. It an imprint abrasion usually situated in upper part of the neck above thyroid cartilage.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: List the three primary physiological mechanisms leading to death in hanging.
back:
* Cerebral anoxia (compression of jugular veins/carotid arteries)
* Reflex cardiac arrest (vagal inhibition from carotid sinus pressure)
* Mechanical asphyxia (lifting of tongue/glottis obstructing airway)
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Mechanism of death in hanging includes cerebral anoxia, reflex cardiac arrest and asphyxia. ... Results from combination of two causes: Cerebral anoxia ... Asphyxia by lifting of glottis and tongue ... Vagal inhibition]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Contrast the direction of the neck ligature mark in hanging versus strangulation.
back:
* Hanging: Oblique direction, running upwards toward the knot site
* Strangulation: Horizontal/transverse direction, typically running all around the neck
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging ... Direction: Oblique. Strangulation ... Direction: Horizontal. ... All around the neck, directed transversely across it.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Which specific finding along the ligature mark edges confirms antemortem suspension?
back: * Vital reaction: A line of hyperemia, redness, or ecchymosis bordering the edges of the groove.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Presence of vital reaction to the skin ... will point to the occurrence of the hanging during life. Area of hyperemia and bruises along the edges of the groove is a definite ante-mortem sign.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What is the specific weight required to occlude the jugular veins and carotid arteries?
back:
* Jugular veins: 4.4 pounds
* Carotid arteries: 11 pounds
Note: The weight of the human head is sufficient for total occlusion.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [According to Brouardel, jugular veins close by 4.4 pounds, carotid artery by 11 pounds... Thus total weight of the head is sufficient.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What are the general, nonspecific asphyxial findings observed during a hanging autopsy?
back:
* Generalized cyanosis and vascular congestion
* Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu's spots)
* Fluidity of blood and pulmonary/visceral edema
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Autopsy findings mostly are general pathological asphyxial i.e; cyanosis, congestion, fluidity of blood, petechaeal hemorrhages and edema of lungs/other tissues.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Where does postmortem lividity typically distribute if the body remains suspended for hours?
back:
* Areas above the ligature mark
* Distal extremities (hands/feet)
* Distal genitalia (tip of penis or labia)
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [In case dead body remains hanging for some period, postmortem lividity will appear at an area of neck above ligature and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males and labia in females.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Differentiate Typical hanging from Atypical hanging based on knot position.
back:
* Typical: Knot is located at the occipital region (back of head)
* Atypical: Knot is located anywhere else, most commonly on the side of the face
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [In typical hanging, ligature knot is at occipital region whereas in atypical mostly at side of face.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Describe the specific skeletal trauma produced by Judicial Hanging.
back:
* Fracture-dislocation of the upper cervical segment
* Separation of the spinal cord (due to the sudden long drop)
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Vagal inhibition ... and due to sudden drop in judicial hanging causing fracture/dislocation of upper cervical segment separating spinal cord is immediate.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What is the incidence and primary sites of bone fractures in suicidal hanging?
back:
* Incidence: Rare (only 3-5% of cases)
* Primary Sites: Greater cornua of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Fracture of hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage is a rare finding occurring only in about 3-5% cases. ... Page 150 (Book Page): Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What are the general non-specific pathological findings in fatal asphyxia from hanging?
back:
• Generalized cyanosis and vascular congestion
• Edema of tissues/viscera
• Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu's spots)
• Fluidity of blood
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion, Edema of the tissues and viscera, Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera, Fluidity of blood]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of death involving carotid artery compression in hanging.
back:
• Direct pressure occludes carotid arteries
• Blocks arterial supply to the head
• Results in rapid cerebral anoxia and unconsciousness
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Mechanism of death in hanging includes... Cerebral anoxia by compression of jugular veins and carotid arteries]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Contrast the direction and continuity of a hanging ligature mark with strangulation.
back:
• Hanging: Oblique direction (upward to knot) and in-continuous (incomplete at knot)
• Strangulation: Transverse (horizontal) and continuous (complete)
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging: Site High up, Direction Oblique, Extent Incomplete. Strangulation: Site Middle of neck, Direction Horizontal, Extent Complete]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: How is an antemortem hanging ligature mark differentiated from a postmortem one?
back:
• Presence of 'vital reaction'
• Areas of hyperemia and bruising along the edges of the groove
• Microscopic evidence of cellular repair processes
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Area of hyperemia and bruises along the edges of the groove is a definite ante-mortem sign and its presence can be confirmed by histological examination]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What specific internal soft tissue injuries are typically found under a hanging ligature mark?
back:
• Tearing/bruising of neck muscles and connective tissue
• Rare transverse intimal tears in the carotid arteries
• Lividity above the mark level
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Injuries to the soft tissues of the neck immediately below the ligature include a degree of tearing of connective tissue and muscles and rarely tears in the blood vessels]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Why is the ligature mark in hanging often described as an 'imprint abrasion'?
back:
• Hard material (rope/wire) creates a well-defined groove
• Pattern of weaves or knots is embossed on the skin
• Provides corroborative evidence of the ligature type
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [It is an imprint abrasion... Weaves of the rope or studs of the belt may be imprinted on the skin]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What is the forensic incidence and typical location of fractures in hanging cases?
back:
• Rare finding (3–5% of cases)
• Involves greater cornua of the hyoid bone or superior horns of thyroid cartilage
• More common in elderly due to calcification
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Fracture of hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage is a rare finding occurring only in about 3-5% cases]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Describe the specific distribution of postmortem lividity in a body left suspended in hanging.
back:
• Lividity above the ligature mark in the neck
• Distal extremities: Hands ('gloves') and feet ('stockings')
• Tip of the penis in males
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Postmortem lividity will appear at an area of neck above ligature mark and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males and labia in females]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What anatomical structure stimulation causes immediate reflex cardiac arrest in hanging?
back:
• Pressure on the carotid sinus or vagus nerve
• Triggers parasympathetic stimulation
• Results in sudden vagal inhibition and instant death
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Death by vagal inhibition resultant from pressure over carotid sinus or vagus nerve... is immediate leaving no time for development of usual postmortem findings]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Differentiate between typical and atypical hanging based on knot position.
back:
• Typical: Knot is at the occipital region (midline, posterior)
• Atypical: Knot is at any other site (e.g., side of face, chin)
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [In typical hanging, ligature knot is at occipital region whereas in atypical mostly at side of face]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What are the common nonspecific (general) asphyxial findings observed during an autopsy of hanging?
back:
• Generalized cyanosis
• Visceral congestion
• Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu's spots, often less marked in hanging)
• Fluidity of blood
• Pulmonary edema
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [General pathological changes in asphyxia • Generalized cyanosis • Vascular congestion • Edema of the tissues and viscera • Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera • Fluidity of blood]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Describe the specific features of the ligature mark characteristic of hanging.
back:
• Oblique direction (upward towards the knot)
• In-continuous (absent at the knot site)
• Situated in the upper neck above the thyroid cartilage
• Deepest opposite the knot
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Its characteristic is that it is in-continuous and absent at the place against knot. Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot... usually situated in upper part of the neck above thyroid cartilage.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: How is postmortem lividity specifically distributed in a body that remained suspended for a long period?
back:
• Found in dependent parts: hands, feet, and distal limbs (stocking and glove distribution)
• Tip of the penis in males
• Labia majora in females
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [In case dead body remains hanging for some period, postmortem lividity will appear at an area of neck above ligature and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males and labia majora in females.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Contrast the ligature mark of hanging with that of strangulation regarding its direction and continuity.
back:
• Hanging: Oblique direction, in-continuous mark.
• Strangulation: Horizontal direction, continuous mark all around the neck.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging: Direction Oblique, Extent Incomplete; Strangulation: Direction Horizontal, Extent Complete]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: A victim is found suspended with the knot at the side of the face. Identify this specific type of hanging.
back: Atypical hanging. Typical hanging requires the knot to be positioned in the occipital region (back of the head).
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [In typical hanging, ligature knot is at occipital region whereas in atypical mostly at side of face.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What specific internal neck structures are rarely fractured in cases of suicidal hanging?
back:
• Hyoid bone
• Thyroid cartilage
These are rare, occurring in only approximately 3-3.3% of cases.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Fracture of hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage is a rare finding occurring only in about 3-3.3% cases.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Which specific finding on a ligature mark indicates it was inflicted ante-mortem?
back: • Vital reaction: Presence of an area of hyperemia (redness) and ecchymosis (bruising) at the edges of the groove.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Presence of vital reaction to the skin and deeper tissues in relation to ligature mark will point to the occurrence of hanging during life. Area of hyperemia and ecchymoses along the edges of the groove is a sign of an ante-mortem effect]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Compare the depth of the ligature groove in hanging versus ligature strangulation.
back:
• Hanging: Groove depth varies, becoming shallower toward the knot.
• Strangulation: Depth is uniform all around the neck.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging: Depth of the groove Decreases towards knot; Strangulation: Uniform]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Describe the physiological mechanism of airway obstruction in hanging beyond simple external pressure.
back: The constriction forces the larynx upward, causing the root of the tongue to lift and press against the posterior pharynx, effectively blocking the airway.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Usual mechanism is for larynx to be lifted up so that tongue blocks back of the throat.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What defines 'Complete Hanging' in terms of the body's position during autopsy findings?
back: Complete hanging occurs when the victim's entire body is suspended and no part of the feet or body touches the ground.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [In complete hanging, victim's whole body is suspended with feet off the ground]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: List the general nonspecific pathological findings identified during an autopsy of hanging.
back:
• Generalized cyanosis
• Vascular congestion
• Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu’s spots)
• Edema of the lungs and viscera
• Fluidity of blood.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [General pathological asphyxial i.e; cyanosis, vascular congestion, fluidity of blood, petechaeal hemorrhages and edema of lungs/other tissues.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Describe the characteristic direction and continuity of the ligature mark in hanging.
back:
• Direction: Oblique, typically running upward toward the knot.
• Continuity: In-continuous, often absent or disrupted at the site of the knot.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Ligature mark... in-continuous and absent at the place against knot. Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: How does the anatomical level of the ligature mark help distinguish hanging from strangulation?
back:
• Hanging: Situated high in the neck, above the thyroid cartilage.
• Strangulation: Situated lower, typically in the middle of the neck or below the thyroid.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [It is an imprint abrasion usually situated in upper part of the neck above thyroid cartilage. In partial hanging, it may be lower down even below the thyroid cartilage.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: A body presents with a non-continuous, oblique neck groove that is deepest opposite the knot. What is the interpretation?
back:
• This is a specific ligature mark of hanging.
• The non-continuity identifies the knot position.
• Depth variation occurs because the weight is least effective directly under the knot.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Ligature mark... in-continuous and absent at the place against knot... depth of the groove is not uniform being deepest at a point opposite to the knot.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Explain the physiological mechanism of cerebral anoxia in hanging.
back:
• Compression of the neck by the body's weight occludes the jugular veins and carotid arteries.
• This prevents oxygenated blood from reaching the brain and halts venous return.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Mechanism of death in hanging includes cerebral anoxia... results from combination of two causes: Cerebral anoxia by compression of jugular veins and carotid arteries.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: What are the common internal soft tissue findings specific to the neck in hanging?
back:
• Tearing of connective tissue
• Bruising of the neck muscles (fascia and sheaths)
• Rare intimal tears in the blood vessels.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Injuries to the soft tissues of the neck immediately below the ligature include a degree of tearing of connective tissue and muscles of the neck and rarely tears in the blood vessels.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: How is the ante-mortem status of a hanging victim confirmed through the neck groove?
back:
• Detection of a vital reaction.
• Manifested as an area of hyperemia and ecchymosis along the edges of the ligature groove.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Area of hyperemia and ecchymosis along the edges of the groove is a definite ante-mortem sign and its presence can be confirmed by histology.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: A corpse found suspended vertically shows reddish-purple staining in the hands and feet. Identify the finding.
back:
• Specific post-mortem hypostasis (lividity) of hanging.
• Gravity causes blood to pool in the lower dependent extremities, often termed 'glove and stocking' distribution.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Postmortem lividity will appear at an-area of neck above ligature and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males and labia in females after hanging for some period.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Describe the physiological effect of pressure on the carotid sinus during hanging.
back:
• Stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve triggers parasympathetic activity.
• This results in reflex cardiac arrest and instantaneous death.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Mechanism of death in hanging includes... reflex cardiac arrest... Death by vagal inhibition resultant from pressure over carotid sinus or vagus nerve.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: What is the incidence of hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage fractures in hanging cases?
back:
• Fractures of these structures are rare.
• They occur in only approximately 3-5% of all hanging autopsies.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Fracture of hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage is a rare finding occurring only in about 3-5% cases.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What is the defining character of the ligature mark in a typical case of hanging?
back:
- In-continuous (mark is absent at the knot site).
- Oblique direction passing upward toward the knot.
- Usually situated in the upper neck above the thyroid cartilage.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Its characteristic is that it is in-continuous and absent at the place against knot. Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot. It is an imprint abrasion usually situated in upper part of the neck above thyroid cartilage.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Explain the primary pathophysiological mechanisms resulting in death during suspension (hanging).
back:
- Cerebral anoxia: Compression of jugular veins and carotid arteries.
- Mechanical asphyxia: Lifting of the glottis and tongue obstructing the pharyngeal airway.
- Reflex cardiac arrest: Stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Mechanism of death in hanging includes cerebral anoxia, reflex cardiac arrest and pure asphyxia... Cerebral anoxia by compression of jugular veins and carotid arteries. Asphyxia by lifting of glottis and tongue... Death by vagal inhibition resultant from pressure over carotid sinus.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Contrast the depth of the ligature groove at the knot site versus the opposite point.
back:
- Deepest point: Located directly opposite the knot site.
- Shallowness: The groove becomes progressively shallower as it approaches the knot site, where it eventually disappears.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [depth of the groove is not uniform being deepest at a point opposite to the knot and gradually becoming shallower towards it.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: An autopsy of a hanging victim reveals hypostasis in the feet, hands, and tip of penis. Interpret this.
back:
- Indicates vertical suspension for a significant postmortem period.
- This specific 'glove and stocking' distribution occurs because blood pools gravitationally in the most dependent, unsupported extremities.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [In case dead body remains in hanging for some period, postmortem lividity will appear at an area of neck above ligature mark and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males and labia in females.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Describe the specific internal soft tissue injuries and fractures associated with neck compression in hanging.
back:
- Bruising of neck muscles and connective tissue immediately below the ligature.
- Occasional tears in the walls of neck blood vessels.
- Hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage fractures (found in 3-5% of cases).
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Injuries to the soft tissues of the neck immediately below the ligature include a degree of bruising... and rarely tears in the blood vessels. Fracture of hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage is a rare finding occurring only in about 3-5% cases.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: List the four primary nonspecific general pathological findings of asphyxia identified at autopsy.
back:
- Generalized cyanosis and vascular congestion.
- Pulmonary and visceral edema.
- Tardieu's spots (petechial hemorrhages under serous coverings).
- Blood remains in a fluid state (fibrinolysin action).
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion, Edema of the tissues and viscera, Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera, Fluidity of blood.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the primary rule regarding the knot when removing a ligature from a corpse?
back:
• Never untie or disturb the original knot.
• Cut the ligature material at a point well away from the knot.
• Secure the cut ends with thread to maintain the loop's forensic integrity.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Ligature is retained in position in homicidal cases with knot usually firmly tied in front.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Why must the knot of the ligature be preserved intact during forensic collection?
back:
• The knot provides evidence of the specific type of loop (sliding vs. fixed).
• It reveals the level of skill/knowledge of the assailant or victim.
• Helps distinguish between suicidal and homicidal intent.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Ligature is retained in position in homicidal cases with knot usually firmly tied in front.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Contrast the imprint abrasions produced by hard vs. soft ligature materials.
back:
• Hard Materials (e.g., rope, wire): Produce deep, well-defined grooves with distinct indentations.
• Soft Materials (e.g., cloth, silk): Produce diffuse, faint, or pale marks without deep grooving.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material such as rope around the neck... shows both indentation and frictional rub. Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: A ligature has multiple loops. How should the medical examiner proceed with its removal?
back:
• Cut each loop individually away from the knot.
• Label each cut end immediately (e.g., using A-A, B-B).
• Avoid sliding the material over the neck to prevent losing trace evidence.
citation: Page 106 (Book Page): [Locate and record details of observed findings... weather disturbed, torn... and preserve evidence present.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What step is mandatory before sealing wet or blood-stained ligature material in a container?
back:
• The material must be air-dried at room temperature on a hanger.
• Sealing wet material causes decomposition of biological evidence and mold growth.
• Avoid direct heat or sunlight during drying.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Damaged portion encircled, signed with permanent marker, photographed and then cloths are left for air drying on hangers before they are handed over to police as case property.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Identify the mandatory labeling criteria for preserved ligature material containers.
back:
• Date and place of collection.
• Name/Identity of the victim.
• Exact anatomical site of the material (e.g., neck ligature).
• Signature and designation of the medical examiner.
citation: Page 159 (Book Page): [Every container should bear a label with the following entries: Date and place of collection, Name of the specimen, From whom and from where collected... Name and designation of person who collected specimen.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How does the presence of jute fibers on the neck corroborate the cause of death?
back:
• Jute fibers found in the skin indentation link the external weapon (rope) to the injury.
• They serve as trace evidence of the causative agent.
• Matches the texture/pattern of the suspected ligature.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent... if a jute rope is used, it leaves traces on the skin.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Differentiate the ligature mark direction in hanging versus strangulation.
back:
• Hanging: Oblique, non-continuous mark, directed upward toward the knot.
• Strangulation: Horizontal, continuous mark, usually below or across the thyroid cartilage.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot... In strangulation... all around the neck, directed transversely across it.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Describe the handling procedure for ligatures found at a potential crime scene.
back:
• Maintain the 'chain of custody' strictly.
• Document the material in situ with photographs and sketches.
• Hand over only after obtaining a formal receipt from investigating police.
citation: Page 161 (Book Page): [Responsibility of maintaining chain of custody rests on medical officer who collects specimen and must be able to state: What material was removed... What was done with it? Who was it delivered to?]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the significance of measuring the width of the ligature material?
back:
• The width must be compared to the 'imprint abrasion' or groove on the neck.
• Confirms if the recovered material is the actual weapon used in the assault.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Groove may suggest type and width of ligature material, Weaves of the rope or studs of the belt may be imprinted on the skin.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the mandatory rule regarding the knot when removing a ligature from a victim’s neck?
back: The knot must never be untied or disturbed. It should be cut away from the knot, and the cut ends should be secured with thread to preserve the original structure for forensic analysis.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Ligature is retained in position in homicidal cases with knot usually firmly tied in front.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How does the texture of the ligature material influence the characteristics of the resulting neck groove?
back: Hard materials like rope produce well-defined, deep grooves often imprinting weaves or patterns. Soft materials like cloth produce diffuse, shallow, and less defined marks on the skin.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Groove may suggest type and width of ligature material, Weaves of the rope or studs of the belt may be imprinted on the skin... definition is diffuse with soft material like cloth.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Differentiate the ligature mark continuity in hanging versus strangulation during external examination.
back: Hanging typically presents an incomplete/incontinuous mark (absent at the knot site) directed obliquely upward. Strangulation presents a continuous, horizontal mark of uniform depth encircling the neck.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging: Oblique, Incomplete... Strangulation: Horizontal, Continuous, Uniform depth.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: In a decomposed body, what forensic evidence must be prioritized if the ligature is still in situ?
back: The material must be photographed in position before removal. Once removed, the examiner must check for trace fibers on the skin and verify if the material matches the observed pattern.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent... If a jute rope is used, it leaves traces on the skin.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What documentation step is essential before the physical removal of a ligature during autopsy?
back: Detailed photography of the ligature's position, the exact site of the knot, and the relationship between the material and the surrounding clothing must be completed and recorded.
citation: Page 127 (Book Page): [Close-up of injuries, damages and staining of clothes and full view of injured or intoxicated are essential.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What diagnostic sign on the skin indicates that a ligature was applied ante-mortem?
back: The presence of a vital reaction, characterized by an area of hyperemia and ecchymoses (bruising) specifically along the edges of the ligature groove, confirms ante-mortem application.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Area of hyperemia and ecchymoses along the edges of the groove is a definite ante-mortem sign.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How is jute rope ligature evidence specifically processed to preserve trace materials?
back: Any traces or fibers left on the neck skin are collected and preserved between glass slides. The rope itself is sealed in a labeled container to maintain the chain of custody.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [If a jute rope is used, it leaves traces on the skin... Page 113 (Book Page): Maintenance of proper chain of custody of collected samples.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: A victim has a faint horizontal neck mark; how is this differentiated from a postmortem artifact like a tight collar?
back: The examiner must inspect the underlying subcutaneous tissues for bruising and verify the mark against the specific width and weave of the removed suspected ligature material.
citation: Page 148 (Book Page): [Situational: Pseudo groove on the neck by tight collar... Differential diagnosis: Ligature mark.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the typical anatomical location of the ligature mark in a standard hanging case?
back: The mark is usually situated in the upper part of the neck, specifically above the level of the thyroid cartilage, and is directed obliquely toward the point of suspension.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [It is an imprint abrasion usually situated in upper part of the neck above thyroid cartilage.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What labeling information is mandatory for the container holding the preserved ligature?
back: The label must include the date and place of collection, the name of the specimen, the identity of the deceased, and the name of the authorized collecting officer.
citation: Page 159 (Book Page): [Every container should bear a label with the following entries: Date and place of collection... Name of the specimen... Name and designation of person who collected.]

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Define hanging in the context of mechanical asphyxia.
back: Hanging is the constriction of the neck by a ligature, where the constricting force is applied indirectly through the weight of the victim's body (complete or partial suspension).
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): Hanging is defined as constriction of the neck by a ligature, constricting force being applied indirectly through weight of the body. Hanging can take place with victim in standing, semi-reclining or sitting position.

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: List the four primary mechanisms of death in hanging.
back:
1. Cerebral anoxia (jugular/carotid compression).
2. Asphyxia (tongue/glottis lifting).
3. Reflex cardiac arrest (vagal inhibition via carotid sinus).
4. Spinal cord separation (judicial hanging fractures).
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): Mechanism of death in hanging includes cerebral anoxia, reflex cardiac arrest and asphyxia... Death by vagal inhibition... drop in judicial hanging causing fracture/dislocation of upper cervical segment separating spinal cord.

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Differentiate between typical and atypical hanging by knot position.
back: In typical hanging, the ligature knot is at the occipital region. In atypical hanging, the knot is positioned at the side of the face or anywhere else.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): typical hanging, ligature knot is at occipital region whereas in atypical mostly at side of face.

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: A victim is found in a sitting position with a low door-knob ligature. What specific external finding is expected?
back: A ligature mark may be found lower down on the neck, potentially below the level of the thyroid cartilage, due to partial suspension.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): In partial hanging, it may be lower down even below the thyroid cartilage. It is well-defined groove with hard material like rope, wire or belt.

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Describe the specific characteristics of the ligature mark in hanging.
back: It is typically an in-continuous, oblique imprint abrasion situated in the upper neck, running upward towards the knot and deepest opposite the knot site.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): its characteristic is that it is in-continuous and absent at the place against knot. Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot. It is an imprint abrasion usually situated in upper part of the neck.

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What are the nonspecific pathological autopsy findings of general asphyxia?
back: Findings include generalized cyanosis, vascular congestion, tissue edema, petechial (Tardieu's) hemorrhages in the skin/viscera, and complete fluidity of the blood.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis; Vascular congestion; Edema of the tissues and viscera; Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera; Fluidity of blood.

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What internal vital reaction confirms an ante-mortem hanging?
back: The presence of hyperemia and ecchymoses (bruising) in the skin and subcutaneous tissues along the edges of the ligature groove confirms vital response.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): Area of hyperemia and ecchymoses along the edges of the groove is a definite ante-mortem sign and its presence can be confirmed by histological examination.

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: A victim remains suspended for several hours post-death. Describe the resulting lividity pattern.
back: Postmortem staining (hypostasis) appears in a 'glove and stocking' distribution, specifically in the hands, feet, tip of the penis, or labia.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): In case dead body remained in hanging for some period, postmortem lividity will appear at an area of neck above ligature and in hands, feet, tip of penis in males and labia in females.

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: Explain the physiological role of the carotid sinus in hanging death.
back: External pressure on the carotid sinus stimulates the vagus nerve, causing parasympathetic discharge that precipitates immediate reflex cardiac arrest and circulatory collapse.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): Increased tension precipitates strong parasympathetic stimulation and produces inhibitory circulatory effects such as slowing of pulse, depression of myocardial contractility... leading to circulatory failure.

category: Describe nonspecific and specific autopsy findings of hanging
front: Q: What is the forensic significance of hyoid bone fractures in hanging?
back: Hyoid fractures are rare (3-5% cases), typically occurring at the greater cornua, and are more common in older victims with calcified cartilages.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): Fracture of hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage is a rare finding occurring only in about 3-5% cases. Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone.

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the mandatory first step before removing a ligature from the neck?
back:
* Photograph and sketch the ligature in situ.
* Document the knot's location and the direction of the ligature loop.
citation: Page 111 (Book Page): [All findings should be documented as written record, sketches and photographs, wherever necessary.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Why is it a forensic requirement to never untie the ligature knot?
back:
* The knot style provides evidence of the assailant's occupation or skill.
* Untying destroys specific mechanical characteristics required for laboratory comparison.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Ligature is retained in position in homicidal cases with knot usually firmly tied in front.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Contrast the removal site of the ligature versus the site of the knot.
back:
* Knot: Must remain untouched and intact.
* Removal Site: Cut the ligature at a point farthest from the knot to preserve its structure.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Locate and record details of observed findings... weather disturbed, torn, bear knife-cut...]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: A doctor removes a ligature from a homicidal hanging; how are the cut ends managed?
back:
* Secure the two freshly cut ends with separate string or wire.
* This identifies the doctor’s cut versus any original damage to the ligature.
citation: Page 113 (Book Page): [Forensic autopsy is scrutiny of corpse... and further examination of collected body tissues/other material.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the specific step for preserving a wet or blood-stained ligature?
back:
* Air-dry the material thoroughly on clean hangers at room temperature.
* Avoid folding or sealing while wet to prevent bacterial decomposition of trace evidence.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Wet stain is air dried... before they are handed over to police as case property.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What criteria define the proper container for preserving a removed ligature?
back:
* Impervious, clean, and dry glass jar or paper envelope.
* Must be sealed with wax and marked with a distinctive forensic device.
citation: Page 107 (Book Page): [Container of specimen should be impervious, clean and free from contamination... sealed before dispatch.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How does the pattern of the preserved ligature correlate with skin findings?
back:
* Texture/weave matches the 'imprint abrasion' on the neck.
* Allows matching of the causative agent to the specific width of the neck groove.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Distinguish ligature removal in homicidal versus suicidal cases according to text.
back:
* Homicide: Knot is often firmly tied and requires careful preservation in position.
* Suicide: Ligature may be loose but must follow the same non-untying protocol.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Ligature is retained in position in homicidal cases with knot usually firmly tied in front.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Describe the loop of custody for a ligature from collection to the laboratory.
back:
* Collector labels with deceased data and date.
* Seal with distinct device.
* Maintain chain of custody receipts during police transit.
citation: Page 109 (Book Page): [Every container should bear a label with... Date and place of collection, Name of the specimen... Analyst should sign register to maintain chain of custody.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Why is the width of the preserved ligature compared to the groove depth?
back:
* To confirm if the material was hard (deep, narrow groove) or soft (diffuse, wide groove).
* Assists in determining the force of suspension.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Groove may suggest type and width of ligature material... depth of the groove is not uniform.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the primary forensic significance of preserving the ligature material's pattern?
back: The pattern of the ligature material acts as corroborative evidence to identify the specific causative agent or weapon used to create the neck compression.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Why must the knot of a ligature never be untied or disturbed during removal?
back: To preserve evidence regarding the type of knot and the loop size, as the imprint is typically 'in-continuous and absent at the place against knot.'
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [It is in-continuous and absent at the place against knot. Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Compare the ligature mark direction in hanging versus strangulation.
back: 1. Hanging: Oblique, directed upward toward the knot. 2. Strangulation: Transverse (horizontal) and continuous around the neck.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Direction of the mark is oblique going upward towards the knot.] Page 153 (Book Page): [directed transversely across it.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: A ligature found on a corpse is soaked with fluids; what is the correct preservation step?
back: Wet ligature material must be air-dried on a hanger, then the damaged or relevant portions should be encircled with a permanent marker and signed.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [If stains are wet, cloths are air-dried by putting them on hangers... damaged portion encircled, signed with permanent marker, photographed.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What anatomical landmark guide is used to differentiate ligature marks from contact flattening?
back: Identify the 'taches noires' (sclera discoloration) and specific 'imprint abrasions' which show both indentation and frictional rub at the neck site.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Imprint abrasion produced by hard ligature material... shows both indentation and frictional rub.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Which labeling criteria are mandatory for a preserved ligature container?
back: 1. Date and place of collection. 2. Specimen name. 3. Source identity. 4. Type of examination. 5. Name and designation of the examiner.
citation: Page 109 (Book Page): [Every container should bear a label with the following entries: Date and place of collection, Name of the specimen, From whom... Type of examination, Name and designation.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How is a ligature removed from the neck without compromising its evidentiary integrity?
back: The loop must be cut at a point away from the knot (similar to cutting clothes at seams) to avoid interfering with existing perforations or the knot structure.
citation: Page 118 (Book Page): [Removal... should be done carefully, avoiding interference or extension in existing cuts, perforations or tears... clothes should be cut on seams.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: In suspected homicidal garroting, how should the ligature be handled during the autopsy?
back: The ligature should be 'retained in position' initially, and internal damage such as fractured hyoid bone or thyroid cartilage must be documented.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Ligature is retained in position in homicidal cases with knot usually firmly tied in front... Hyoid bone usually and thyroid cartilage occasionally is fractured.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What document must accompany the ligature specimen to ensure its legal admissibility?
back: A schedule showing the identity number allotted to the specimen and a forwarding letter must be enclosed to maintain the 'chain of custody.'
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [If specimens are more than one, then each... identified with an identity number and schedule... enclosed with forwarding letter... maintain chain of custody.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What type of container is required for the final preservation of the ligature material?
back: An impervious, clean, non-contaminated glass container with a screw-type stopper to avoid any leakage or contamination during transit.
citation: Page 109 (Book Page): [Container of specimen should be impervious, clean and free from contamination... Stopper of container should be screw-type to avoid leakage.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How must a ligature be removed from the neck during autopsy?
back:
• Cut the loop away from the knot.
• Never untie the knot or cut through it.
• Preserve the knot's integrity for technical analysis.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Ligature is retained in position in homicidal cases with knot usually firmly tied in front.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the mandatory procedure for a ligature with multiple loops?
back:
• Each loop must be labeled sequentially.
• A single cut is made in each loop at a distance from the knot.
• Relative positions of loops must be maintained.
citation: Page 106 (Book Page): [Record details of observed findings on examinee’s cloths, over his body... preserve evidence present.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Why must a ligature be preserved separately from the body?
back:
• To allow matching of the material's weave to the imprint abrasion.
• To identify specific pattern imprints (e.g., rope weaves or belt studs).
• To prevent cross-contamination.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: A ligature is found damp with fluids at a crime scene. What is the preservation step?
back:
• Air-dry the material completely on a hanger.
• Do not heat or use chemicals to dry.
• Place in a labeled paper envelope or non-airtight container once dry.
citation: Page 107 (Book Page): [Wet stain is air dried and encircled with permanent marker before dispatch to the laboratory.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What specific action is required after cutting the ligature for removal?
back:
• Bind the cut ends with string or wire.
• Reconstruct the original circumference for measurement.
• Ensure cut edges are marked to distinguish them from original tears.
citation: Page 111 (Book Page): [Documentation of findings is mandatory. All findings should be documented as written record, sketches and photographs.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What labeling information is required on the ligature container?
back:
• Case yearly number and bio-data.
• Site of recovery and date/time.
• Name and designation of the recovering officer.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Every container should bear a label with the following entries: Date and place of collection, Name of the specimen, From whom and from where collected.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Which trace evidence should be searched for on the ligature’s inner surface?
back:
• Loose hairs from the victim or assailant.
• Skin epithelium or blood stains.
• Synthetic or natural fibers from clothing.
citation: Page 106 (Book Page): [Observe presence/absence of any trace evidence on examinee’s cloths and on body like blood stains or other such as hair and synthetic fiber.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How is a ligature handled when the loop is very tight and obstructing removal?
back:
• Place a grooved director or a soft pad under the loop.
• Cut through the material against the director to protect the neck skin.
• Cut at a point opposite the knot.
citation: Page 106 (Book Page): [Procedures should be carried out with dignity, decorum and efficiency. Job require neatness and precision.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What legal protection is necessary when transferring a ligature to the laboratory?
back:
• Strict chain of custody must be established.
• Each handler must sign a receipt.
• Evidence must be kept in a locked, secure facility.
citation: Page 161 (Book Page): [Safe custody of specimen is applicable... All those who hold custody of these materials have to declare on oath in the court of law that no tampering of evidence took place.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What type of container is ideal for dry ligature material to ensure preservation?
back:
• A chemically clean glass container or a paper envelope.
• Seal with wax and a distinctive device to prevent tampering.
citation: Page 159 (Book Page): [Sealing of each container is under taken by wrapping it with heavy paper... seal applied over the knot with sealing wax.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the cardinal rule regarding the knot when removing a ligature from the neck?
back: The knot must never be untied or cut through. It must be preserved intact to identify the type of knot and the skill of the assailant/deceased.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Ligature is retained in position in homicidal cases with knot usually firmly tied in front.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Describe the specific technique for cutting a ligature for removal during autopsy.
back:
1. Cut at a point farthest from the knot.
2. Bind the cut ends with string/tape.
3. Keep the original loop size for forensic reconstruction.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Observe presence/absence of any trace evidence present... and preserve evidence present]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How must a wet or blood-stained ligature be processed for preservation?
back: The material must be air-dried at room temperature on hangers before being placed in a sealed container to prevent bacterial decomposition.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [photographed and then cloths are kept for air drying on hangers before they are handed over to police as case property.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: A victim presents with a wire ligature. What is the immediate priority before its removal?
back: Detailed photography and sketching of the ligature in situ, noting the exact number of turns and the direction of the loop/knot.
citation: Page 111 (Book Page): [All findings should be documented as written record, sketches and photographs... Close-up of injuries... are essential.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Why is the pattern of a hard ligature material (like rope) forensic gold?
back: The imprint abrasion provides corroborative evidence of the causative agent by matching the weave or texture to the suspected weapon.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Pattern of ligature material provides corroborative evidence of causative agent.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What documentation is required on the label of a preserved ligature specimen?
back:
1. Date/place of collection.
2. Specimen name.
3. Identity of the deceased.
4. Type of examination required.
5. Examiner's designation.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Every container should bear a label with the following entries: Date and place of collection... Type of examination required...]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How is the 'ligature sore' or vital reaction preserved for forensic analysis?
back: A skin section showing the mark and adjacent healthy tissue must be preserved in 10% formal saline for histological verification of ante-mortem suspension.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [identification of the occurrence of vital reaction to the skin and deeper tissue in relation to ligature mark will point to ante-mortem hanging... preservation of ligature and sore.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: If multiple turns of a ligature are found, how should they be removed?
back: All loops must be cut at one single point away from the knot, and the relative arrangement of the strands must be maintained during packing.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Observe presence/absence of any trace evidence... on body like blood or other such as hair and synthetic fiber and preserve evidence present]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the procedure for handling a ligature found at a suspicious scene?
back: Encircle any damaged portions, sign with a permanent marker, and maintain a strict chain of custody during transit to the laboratory.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [damaged portion encircled, signed with permanent marker, photographed and then cloths are kept for air drying... before they are handed over to police]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Which tool is essential to identify minute trace evidence on a ligature during removal?
back: A magnifying lens (ordinary or illuminated) is required to locate fibers, hair, or blood prior to the removal process.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Above evidence is sought both with naked eye and with the help of a magnifying lens, depending on its magnification.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the mandatory initial step before removing a ligature from a deceased person?
back:
- Record findings with photography and sketches.
- Note the material type, loop position, and knot location.
- Do not disturb trace evidence during the process.
citation: Page 111 (Book Page): [All findings should be documented as written record, supported with markings on sketches and photographs, wherever necessary. Close-up of injuries, damages and staining of clothes and full view of injured or intoxicated are essential.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How must the medical examiner mark specific findings on a ligature or associated clothing?
back:
- Encircle the damaged portion or stain.
- Sign the area using a permanent marker.
- Use photography to document these markings for the court.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Any finding regarding its clothes, being an important item of evidence... damaged portion encircled, signed with permanent marker, photographed.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the correct preservation protocol for a ligature found damp with biological fluids?
back:
- Air-dry the material on hangers before packing.
- Avoid packing while wet to prevent bacterial destruction.
- Ensure the environment is free from contamination.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Photographed and then cloths kept for air drying on hangers before they are handed over to police as case property.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: In a clinical scenario, which authority must personally supervise the sampling and storage of a ligature?
back:
- The authorized Forensic Medical Examiner.
- The examiner ensures no contamination, substitution, or loss occurs during transit.
citation: Page 3 (Book Page): [Choice of sampling, its collection, preservation and storage for at least under his personal supervision.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What type of container is required for preserving and transporting forensic ligature materials?
back:
- Impervious glass containers or specifically designed sealed covers.
- Use screw-type stoppers to prevent leakage or gas escape.
citation: Page 107 (Book Page): [Samples collected in impervious glass container... processed in sealed cover.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What four identifying details must be present on the label of a preserved ligature container?
back:
1. Date and place of collection.
2. Victim's name/identity.
3. Type of required examination.
4. Name/designation of the collecting officer.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [Every container should bear a label with the following entries: Date and place of collection; Name of the specimen; From whom and from where collected; Type of examination required.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How is a ligature container secured to ensure its integrity in a court of law?
back:
- Wrap in heavy paper and tie with cotton cord.
- Apply a wax seal with a distinctive device.
- Tampering must be immediately detectable.
citation: Page 159 (Book Page): [Sealing of each container is under taken by wrapping it with heavy paper, tie its top and bottom with a cotton cord, seal applied over the knot with sealing wax and mark wax seal with some distinctive device.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the primary objective of maintaining the 'chain of custody' for a ligature exhibit?
back:
- Proving that no tampering occurred while in the examiner's possession.
- Confirming exactly where and how the material was recovered.
citation: Page 161 (Book Page): [All those who hold custody of these materials have to declare on oath in the court of law that no tampering of evidence took place while in their possession.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Why are ligatures kept in safe custody or freezing units if they contain biological traces?
back:
- To halt decomposition by autolysis or bacterial action.
- To preserve chemical markers (like blood/saliva) for laboratory analysis.
citation: Page 3 (Book Page): [Before and after receipt samples kept in freezing... to prevent decomposition of biological material.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What bio-data verification is required before starting the forensic examination of a ligature-involved corpse?
back:
- Verification of identity through a National Identity Card (CNIC).
- Documentation of two permanent identifying marks on the body.
citation: Page 106 (Book Page): [Record examinee’s personal identity verified from CNIC and also from his two identification marks.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the mandatory first step before removing a ligature from a body?
back: The ligature must be documented in situ through photography and detailed sketches, showing the knot's position and its relationship to neck structures.
citation: Page 111 (Book Page): [All findings should be documented as written record, sketches and photographs, wherever necessary... Full view of injured or intoxicated are essential.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: How must a ligature be cut during its removal to preserve forensic evidence?
back: It must be cut at a point distant from the knot. One should never cut through or untie the original knot used in the assault.
citation: Page 118 (Book Page): [Removal of clothes from body... carefully, avoiding interference or extension in existing cuts, perforations or tears...] Page 153 (Book Page): [Ligature is retained in position in homicidal cases with knot usually firmly tied in front.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: What is the procedure for marking a ligature as a forensic exhibit?
back: Significant or damaged portions should be encircled with a permanent marker and signed by the medical examiner to ensure integrity.
citation: Page 110 (Book Page): [damaged portion encircled, signed with permanent marker, photographed and then cloths are air drying on hangers before they are handed over to police as case property.]

category: Explain the process to remove and preserve the ligature material used
front: Q: Why is preserving the ligature knot vital in homicidal strangulation cases?
back: The knot provides corroborative evidence of the perpetrator’s skill or occupation and differentiates homicidal intent from suicidal patterns.
